articles.title: Carlos Yulo misses out on World Championship floor exercise medal
articles.summary: Carlos Yulo finishes eight and last in the floor exercise final of the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships, ending his bid to recapture the title he first won in 2019

blocks.text: REACHING FOR GOLD. Filipino gymnast Carlos Yulo performs his floor exercise routine in the 2025 FIG Artistic Gymnastics World Championships.
Jat Tenorio-GAP/Red Ox Media Events
Carlos Yulo finishes eight and last in the floor exercise final of the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships, ending his bid to recapture the title he first won in 2019

MANILA, Philippines – Carlos Yulo fell short of reclaiming the world title in men’s floor exercise, settling for eighth place at the 54th Artistic Gymnastics World Championships on Saturday, October 24, in Rotterdam, Netherlands.
Yulo scored 13.233 points to finish last in the eight-man final, recording 7.633 in execution and 5.800 in difficulty, along with a 0.10 stick bonus. But he also incurred a 0.30 penalty.

Yulo first captured the floor exercise world title in 2019 in Stuttgart, Germany, establishing himself as one of the sport’s biggest stars before going on to win two Olympic gold medals at the Paris Games.
Just a month ago, Yulo won gold in both the men’s floor exercise and vault at the 2026 Asian Games in Japan. He also finished fourth in the parallel bars.
Fred Richard became the first American in 23 years to win the world title in floor exercise, scoring 14.633 points.
Great Britain’s Jake Jarman took silver with 14.600, while Israel’s Artem Dolgopyat claimed bronze with 14.466. Japan’s Ryosuke Doi finished fourth with 14.366.
Yulo still has a chance to claim a world title in Rotterdam as he is set to compete in the vault final on Sunday, October 25. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Northern Olympics campaign to get £7m in Healey’s budget
articles.summary:
Fund will support feasibility study for potential bid to host Games in the 2040s, backed by northern mayors and top athletes

John Healey is to announce a £7m fund to examine a potential…

blocks.text: John Healey is to announce a £7m fund to examine a potential future bid to host the Olympics in northern England in his first budget as chancellor.
The fund will be used to carry out a full feasibility study for a northern Games, which, if successful, would be held in the north of England in the 2040s.

In May, before Andy Burnham entered No 10, the government commissioned an assessment by UK Sport which could inform a bid for the international sporting event in the 2040s. If the campaign were successful, it would be the first time the Olympic Games and Paralympics were hosted in Britain since London 2012.
There was further momentum behind the idea in June when mayors from across the north of England met in Sheffield to discuss the possibility of a northern Olympic bid.

More than 40 Olympians, Paralympians and elite athletes, including Laura Kenny, Jason Kenny, Sarah Storey, Beth Tweddle and Tom Pidcock, have signed a joint statement “to express our strong and united support” for the idea to hold a “box office Games” in the north of England.
Announcing the fund, Burnham said an Olympics bid would “unlock opportunity across our towns and cities” and that “we can put on the greatest show on Earth”.

He continued: “Few things bring a country together quite like the Olympics. I want people to feel that sense of excitement again, and to experience it in their own towns and communities, not just watch it on the telly.
“The Games would unlock opportunity across our towns and cities for the whole country. From north to south, it would be something everyone could get behind and be proud of.
“We know we can put on the greatest show on earth. Now we want to explore how we can do it again, with the whole country behind it.”

The full feasibility study will look in greater detail at how the Games would work in practice, including types of venues and transport links needed and the prospects of developing a winning bid. It will also look into how much it could cost and examine the chances of a bid succeeding.

blocks.caption: Mo Farah winning the men’s 5000m at the 2012 Olympic Games. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

blocks.text: The work will involve the government, UK Sport, the northern mayors and the British Olympic and Paralympic Associations, who would ultimately be responsible for a bid.
Healey said: “The north hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable.
“Britain’s experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I’m picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious Games.
“It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost.”
The British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport released a joint statement welcoming the news.

“Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements,” they said.
Sydney, Tokyo and London are among the mega-cities that have played host to the Olympics in recent years but Brisbane, Australia’s third-largest city, will be hosting the 2032 Games.
The Mayor of London Sadiq Khan has previously criticised plans to explore a bid to host the Olympics in northern England, saying that excluding London would be a “missed opportunity”.

articles.title: Vanessa Trump says she is cancer-free six months after revealing diagnosis
articles.summary: The ex-wife of Donald Trump Jr, with whom she shares five children, announced in May that she had been diagnosed with breast cancer.

blocks.text: Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Donald Trump Jr, has announced that she is cancer-free following her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year.

Trump, 48, who has five children with President Donald Trump's eldest son, shared in a short video on her 19-year-old daughter Kai's Instagram account that her recent tests results "came back clear, so I'm finally cancer-free".

The video, posted on Friday, teases the release of a longer YouTube video to come on Saturday, in which Vanessa and Kai Trump will discuss breast cancer awareness and prevention, Kai wrote in the caption.
Vanessa Trump separated from Trump Jr in 2018 and announced last year that she had begun dating US pro golfer Tiger Woods.
"October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time to raise awareness about early detection, education, and support for those affected by breast cancer," Kai Trump wrote on Instagram.
"I sat down with my mom and Dr. Nicole Saphier to talk about my mom's journey with breast cancer and learn more about prevention and early detection," she continued.
Kai's post received over 20,000 likes and hundreds of comments from people offering support and well wishes, including from American singer and media personality Mary Millben.

In Friday's video, Trump said she was first diagnosed with breast cancer in April. She publicly announced the diagnosis in May, saying in a social media post that she had undergone surgery and was working on a treatment plan with her medical team.

According to the American Cancer Society, the average risk of a woman in the US developing breast cancer is about 1 in 8, or 13%. The disease also accounts for 30% of all new female cancers every year, according to the group.
Surgery cures most breast cancers, but if some disease remains, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and endocrine therapy can reduce the long-term risk.
Treatments have been advancing, including more targeted therapies for early breast cancer, new types of hormonal therapies, and more precise and effective radiotherapy.

articles.title: Ombudsman Remulla to gov't: Outsource visa processing, strip DFA of role
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has called for the outsourcing of visa processing to a third-party service provider, questioning the Department of Foreign Affairs" (DFA) capacity to screen foreigners…

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 10:34pm

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has called for the outsourcing of visa processing to a third-party service provider, questioning the Department of Foreign Affairs’ (DFA) capacity to screen foreigners seeking entry into the Philippines.
In his program on DZRH, Remulla said visa issuance was an immigration concern that fell under the Department of Justice (DOJ).
“The point is we want to get a background of the people entering our country. And if the DFA is not capable of doing that, give it to VFS (Visa Facilitation Services),” Remulla said.

He was referring to VFS Global, a private outsourcing and technology services company that assists governments and diplomatic missions with the administrative aspects of visa applications, including collecting application forms, supporting documents and biometric data.

Remulla made the statement in reaction to reports that the DFA is reviewing its policy on visa-free entry for Chinese tourists amid concerns that it may have contributed to the expansion of Philippine offshore gaming operator (POGO) activities.

"The DFA’s problem is that it seems to have forgotten that its primary job is to be diplomats. In this case, they want something else to happen—they want to do business. They used to turn visa issuance in China into a business,” he added.
Remulla also claimed that the DFA generated substantial revenues through travel agencies.
He described visa processing as a clerical task and said the Philippines lacked the capacity to perform it effectively in other countries, making a third-party provider such as VFS a better option.
“The DFA should no longer assume that visa processing automatically falls under its responsibility. We have to take it away from them,” Remulla said.
GMA News Online has reached out to the DFA for comment and will update this story once a response is received.—MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Turkey's new deal on Mediterranean maritime boundaries with Libya is exacerbating issues with Greece and the EU
articles.summary: Turkey and Libya plan to redraw maritime boundaries in the Mediterranean as part of a new economic corridor. This has sparked strong protests from Greece, and has also drawn the European Union into…

image.caption: Turkey seeks to strenghten ties with Libya in a bid to extract gas from the eastern Mediterranean in futureImage: ADEM ALTAN/AFP

blocks.text: On Tuesday, the parliament of Libya unanimously approved a maritime agreement with Turkey to establish a direct maritime economic corridor between the countries.

Turkey had agreed on the corridor with the UN-recognized Government of National Accord in western Libya in 2019. However, the agreement faced opposition from the rival Libyan government in the country's east. Now, though, the eastern parliament has reversed its previous opposition.
The decision, which was welcomed by Turkey's Foreign Ministry, is likely to contribute to tensions with other countries in the eastern Mediterranean — especially Greece .

blocks.caption: Ties between Turkey and Libya have improved through joint projectsImage: DHA

blocks.text: 'Null and void'

The agreement establishes a direct maritime corridor between the southern coast of Turkey and the northern coast of Libya. Large oil and gas deposits have recently been discovered in the region in question — estimates suggest that natural gas reserves worth several hundred billion US dollars may lie beneath the seabed. Turkey and Libya aim to secure their economic rights to these raw materials and are seeking to jointly exploit the resources.

The planned corridor disregards Greek islands such as Crete, Karpathos and Rhodes. Greece's government insists that it possesses a comprehensive exclusive economic zone, or EEZ, around these islands and has already announced its opposition to the accord.

In a post on X, the Foreign Ministry announced that Greece firmly rejects the agreement and has the support of the European Union in doing so. "The European Union has described the Turkish-Libyan memorandum as null and void, stressing that it violates the sovereign rights of third states and is not consistent with the Law of the Sea," the ministry posted.

Similar wording came straight from Brussels. "I raised yesterday's Libyan vote on a maritime MoU with Türkiye and stressed that it infringes upon the sovereign rights of third states," Kaja Kallas, the European Union high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, posted on X.
International maritime law

Whose claims are legitimate in the eastern Mediterranean is the central point of contention. Greece primarily cites the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS. According to Article 121 of the convention, inhabited islands that "support an economic life of their own” have the same rights to an EEZ as the mainland. This applies to Crete, Rhodes and Lesbos.

Athens cites precedents such as a 2022 ruling by the International Court of Justicethat found that Colombia had violated the sovereign rights of Nicaragua by authorizing fishing activities in the Central American country's EEZ. The ICJ found that when interests overlap a fair demarcation must be reached that takes coastlines, geographical conditions and the implications of a potential boundary into account.

Turkey's government argues that the geography of the Mediterranean plays a special role: If every small Greek island off the coast of Turkey and Cyprus were granted a full EEZ, Turkey would be largely cut off from access to the open sea. This, the government argues, must be given greater consideration when demarcating the boundary.

Unlike Greece, Turkey has never signed UNCLOS. Therefore, it does not agree to have the dispute heard by a UN arbitration tribunal. Moreover, even international experts on the law of the sea disagree on what a "fair division” might look like in this specific case.

blocks.caption: Hifter reversed his position on the deal after opposing it for yearsImage: Abdullah Doma/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: When Turkey pushed for the agreement in 2019, a brutal civil war was still raging in Libya. At that time, Turkey intervened militarily in the west to support the government in Tripoli, thereby repelling the offensive by eastern Libyan General Khalifa Hifter.

Since then, the relationship has changed fundamentally: A successful charm offensive by Turkey's government appears to have led to a political rapprochement with Hifter and his camp. Turkey's government now maintains mutually advantageous relations with both parts of Libya. In addition to the countries' plan to develop energy resources in the Mediterranean together, Turkish construction companies have secured contracts worth billions in recent years for Libya's reconstruction. Furthermore, the Turkish state-owned oil company TPAO and the Libyan National Oil Corporation are already working on joint plans for seismic surveys off of Libya's coast.

Turkey's government has established itself as a new military partner for Hifter's forces, supplying weapons and offering training programs. In doing so, Turkey is pushing back against the influence of Egypt and Russia in eastern Libya and strengthening its role as a geopolitical player in the region.
How Turkey quietly became a power broker in Africa

With the agreement now approved in the regional parliament, eastern Libya also aims to secure its share of the lucrative natural resources. This could give Hifter greater international influence in the future. Disputes in the eastern Mediterranean are likely to escalate further as a result of the agreement — particularly once Turkey and Libya begin extracting oil and gas from the disputed maritime area.

The agreement also jeopardizes a major project that is still in the planning stages: the EastMed pipeline, which is intended to transport natural gas from Israel and Cyprus via Greece, thereby making an important contribution to energy security in the European Union. However, the corridor established by Turkey and Libya cuts across the planned route of the pipeline. Turkey has also argued that projects involving cables or pipelines on its claimed continental shelf require its consent.

In the long term, this could lead to a division of the eastern Mediterranean region into two competing energy and defense blocs: The Turkey-Libya axis might be countered by an EU-supported alliance of Greece, Cyprus, Egypt and Israel.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: DOTr: Gov't to retain MRT-3 ownership, fare-setting authority under privatization plan
articles.summary: The Department of Transportation (DOTr) said Saturday that the government will retain ownership of the Metro Rail Transit Line 3 (MRT-3) and the authority to set fares under its proposed…

blocks.text: The Department of Transportation (DOTr) said Saturday that the government will retain ownership of the Metro Rail Transit Line 3 (MRT-3) and the authority to set fares under its proposed privatization plan.

In an interview with Super Radyo dzBB, DOTr Undersecretary Timothy John Batan said the proposed public-private partnership (PPP) would transfer only the railway’s operations and maintenance, along with investments for capacity expansion, to the winning private concessionaire.

“Pag sinasabi po natin na privatization ng MRT-3 ay hindi po natin ibinebenta ito pong asset. Hindi po natin ibinebenta o inililipat ang pagmamay-ari ng MRT-3 sa pribadong sektor, kung sino man po ang mananalo. Mananatili po ang pagmamay-ari ng MRT-3, mananatili po ang pagtatakda ng pasahe, ng service quality requirements, ng performance standards. Ito po ay mananatili sa kamay ng gobyerno,” Batan said.

(When we speak of privatizing MRT-3, we are not selling the asset or transferring its ownership to the private sector, whoever the winning bidder may be. Ownership of MRT-3, along with the authority to set fares, service quality requirements, and performance standards, will remain with the government.)
Batan said the government would also set performance standards for the private concessionaire and impose sanctions or penalties for noncompliance.
He stressed that the primary goal of the proposed privatization was to improve MRT-3 facilities and services, rather than generate revenue for the government.
“Ang pangunahing benepisyo po natin na… nilalayong makita dito sa proyekto na ito ay hindi po pinansyal. Hindi po tayo pumapasok sa proyekto na ito para po kumita ang gobyerno,” Batan said.
(The main benefit we aim to achieve through this project is not financial. We are not undertaking this project to generate profits for the government.)

“Pangunahin po nating layunin na maibigay ‘yung mataas na kalidad po ng serbisyo doon po sa ating mananakay. ‘Yan pong mataas na kalidad na serbisyo na ’yan ay una sa lahat, manggagaling sa capacity expansion,” he added.
(Our primary goal is to provide high-quality service to commuters. This will primarily be achieved through capacity expansion.)
The DOTr said the revenue-sharing arrangements for MRT-3 were still under review and undergoing approval by the Investment Coordination Committee and the Economic Development Council.
Batan, however, said the proposed arrangement would have fare revenues go directly to the government.

The agency assured commuters that the government would retain control over fares to keep them affordable, saying service improvements would be of little use if passengers could not afford to ride the trains.
Capacity expansion

MRT-3 currently has a daily passenger capacity of 500,000, with trains operating in three-car configurations and a signaling system that allows intervals of about three and a half minutes between trains.
Under the proposed PPP, the DOTr aims to increase the line’s daily capacity to as many as one million passengers and reduce train intervals to two minutes.

Batan said technical studies were ongoing with the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the agency’s adviser, to determine whether MRT-3’s capacity could be increased to 800,000, 900,000, or even one million passengers daily.

“Ongoing po ‘yung teknikal na pag-aaral, kasama po ng ating adviser galing sa Asian Development Bank (ADB), kung ito pong kapasidad na nasa 500,000 a day ay maiaakyat po natin to 800,000 to 900,000 or even one million passengers a day,” he said.

(A technical study is underway with our adviser from the Asian Development Bank to determine whether the current capacity of 500,000 passengers a day can be increased to 800,000, 900,000, or even one million.)

Batan said the expansion would involve acquiring additional train cars to convert all trains to four-car configurations and upgrading the signaling system to reduce train intervals from three and a half minutes to two minutes.
The DOTr acknowledged that overcrowding at stations during peak hours underscored the need to replace aging train cars, upgrade signaling equipment, and reduce passenger waiting times.
Batan said tapping the private sector would allow the government to benefit from experienced railway operators and secure additional capital for the necessary investments.
The DOTr said it was finalizing the concession structure, in coordination with the ADB, including arrangements for recovering private investments.
Timeline
Batan said the current maintenance partnership between the government and Sumitomo Corporation for MRT-3 would end in December 2027.
Under the proposed PPP, operations and maintenance would be consolidated under a single private operator to establish a single point of responsibility.
The DOTr aims to finalize the PPP terms and secure the necessary approvals by December 2026, before proceeding with an open, solicited bidding process for prospective concessionaires.
The agency targets awarding the MRT-3 PPP concession contract by the third quarter of 2027. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Met police confirm giving Duchess of Sussex letter about father’s alleged offending
articles.summary:
Scotland Yard says it shared information about Thomas Markle Sr allegations in 2019 but did not pass claims to other agencies

The Metropolitan police have confirmed they gave a letter to the…

blocks.text: The Metropolitan police have confirmed they gave a letter to the Duchess of Sussex in 2019 concerning “alleged offending” involving her father, after accusations arose on Friday about Thomas Markle Sr having child sexual abuse images.
Scotland Yard said it had received a letter in January 2019 making a number of allegations about offending outside Britain.
The police force said it had passed the information on to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s office, but it did not pass it on to “other law enforcement agencies”.
The Sun newspaper published claims that Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, claimed he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.
On Friday, Meghan said she had been made aware of these allegations by the Met, and that she was “deeply distressed” by them.
The Duchess, who is estranged from her father said in a statement she had broken off contact to protect her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. He has never met them.
Meghan and Prince Harry recently moved back to the UK from the US.
Meghan’s father has denied the allegations and told the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”.
The Met said it was considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to review its actions.

In a statement, a Metropolitan police spokesperson said: “Following a thorough review of Met police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. It was sent to the MPS (Metropolitan Police Service) Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.

“The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.
“The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach.”

In a statement on Friday, issued through her spokesperson, the duchess said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.
after newsletter promotion

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection [Rasp]. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”

Sources said that although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2019, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.

The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.
Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.

articles.title: Israeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homes
articles.summary:
PM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpoint

Israeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of…

blocks.text: Israeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of families, in collective punishment for a militant attack on an army checkpoint outside the West Bank city, local Palestinian authorities said.

The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry.

Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags.

blocks.caption: Israeli forces demolish a Palestinian house in Hebron on Friday. Photograph: Mussa Qawasma/Reuters

blocks.text: People said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters.

The large-scale demolitions follow an attack on Friday on an Israeli military checkpoint outside Hebron by two gunmen. After a 20 minute gunfight, two Israeli soldiers were killed, three injured and the two gunmen were also killed.

The attack came four days before Israeli elections, and the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the extreme-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, travelled to the site of the attack to promise an immediate and ferocious response.

Netanyahu said Israel would “act to destroy this place”. Smotrich who is standing for election in a smaller coalition party, had himself filmed wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished. He said he had ordered “the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”.
Smotrich also called for “a comprehensive military campaign … exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon”. Ein Deir Baha, the focus of the demolitions, was alleged to be the home district of the two gunmen.

A spokesperson for the Hebron municipality said that about 300 families had been evicted. Some had taken refuge in the homes of friends and relatives, while the municipality said it had opened community halls and children’s play areas to shelter others.

A Palestinian news agency, Wafa, reported Israeli plans to displace a further 2,500 people. “We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported,” a Hebron civil rights activist, Issa Amro, said. “Our suffering is being turned into political material for Israel’s elections, while innocent families pay the price.”
Amro said his sister’s family was one of the hundreds driven out of their homes.

“We are talking about hundreds of families who left their homes because of this, and they are not at all connected to what happened yesterday [Friday],” Amro said in a telephone interview. “It’s a very big area and we don’t know what’s going on, whether it is only election propaganda or if it’s a serious plan from decisions on what to do after the election.”
The Israeli army was approached for comment on the operations and on videos showing extensive devastation.

articles.title: FFCCCII warns against declaring Chinese envoy Jing Quan persona non grata
articles.summary: The Federation of Filipino-Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Inc. (FFCCCII) on Saturday cautioned against declaring Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata, warning that the move…

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 8:34pm

The Federation of Filipino-Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Inc. (FFCCCII) on Saturday cautioned against declaring Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata, warning that the move could prompt reciprocal action against the Philippine ambassador to Beijing.

In a social media update by GMA News reporter Vonne Aquino, FFCCCII president Victor Lim urged the Chinese Embassy and the Philippine government to engage in dialogue and ease tensions instead of trading accusations online.
Lim also warned that the dispute could affect trade relations between the Philippines and China.
“Sana ’wag… calm down na lang para our economy will be moving forward,” Lim said.
(I hope they don’t. They should just calm down so our economy can continue moving forward.)
On Tuesday, a Senate resolution was filed urging President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. to declare Jing persona non grata or ask the Chinese government to recall him.
Calls for the ambassador’s expulsion intensified after he said Beijing could “easily win” if it resorted to force against the Philippines.
In response to the Senate resolution, the Chinese Embassy in Manila warned of reciprocal action if its diplomats were declared unwelcome.
“Since you don’t welcome us, we don’t welcome you, either. Fair enough,” the embassy said in a Facebook post.
Malacañang has deferred to the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on the matter, noting that Marcos does not favor declaring foreign envoys persona non grata.

“Hindi rin nais ng Pangulo itong mga pangyayaring palitan ng mga maaanghang na salita. Nais ng Pangulo, again, maganda na relasyon,” Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said earlier this week.
(The President also does not want these exchanges of harsh words. The President wants good relations.)
The Palace also maintained that the President and his administration consider relations between the Philippines and China to be good.
The DFA summoned Jing on Monday to convey the Philippines’ “serious concern and strong objection” to his remarks. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: France deploys thousands of police amid a new wave of protests
articles.summary: Paris braced for a fresh march by students and workers over school funding and soaring living costs Saturday, one week after violent unrest left shops looted and cars burned. The new march was…

image.caption: Protesters hold placards on Saturday during an authorized demonstration organized by labour unions in Paris as part of nationwide protests against the rising cost of living. French high school and university students launched demonstrations earlier this month to protest against current education sta

blocks.text: World·New

Paris braced for a fresh march by students and workers over school funding and soaring living costs Saturday, one week after violent unrest left shops looted and cars burned. The new march was restricted to the city's southeastern edge, away from the centre, as police deployed in force across France.
Major museums, including the Louvre and Grand Palais, closed Saturday over protest-related concerns

Paris braced for a fresh march by students and workers over school funding and soaring living costs Saturday, one week after unrest left shops looted and cars burned. The new march was restricted to the city's southeastern edge as police deployed in force across France.

Scenes of looting, burned-out cars and attacks on public buildings left the impression that the government had lost control, as groups of masked vandals targeted businesses in Paris and other city centres.
Police imposed the new route Friday between Porte d'Italie and Porte de Vincennes, replacing the planned march from Bastille to Nation.

The movement began last month over staff shortages at one high school southeast of Paris. It now reaches well beyond the classroom. Students want more teachers, better school buildings and more university places. Unions are demanding higher wages and pensions to help people meet the cost of living.
‘It’s utter chaos': Protests in France evolve into anger over broader economy

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said as many as 70,000 officers will be deployed nationwide, along with helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons. In central Paris, a few dozen gendarmes, or military police officers, were stationed beneath the Arc de Triomphe and along the nearby avenues.
A massive turnout is expected again after more than half a million took to the streets last week.
Museums are closed and shopkeepers are worried

Major museums, including the Louvre, Musée d'Orsay, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais — where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display — are closed Saturday. Art Basel, one of the world's most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.

items: Tear gas, arrests and chaos as protests grip France

blocks.text: Parisian shopkeepers have been barricading their stores all week. Near the Saint-Lazare train station, Akram Ahmed, a 34-year-old contractor, was boarding up an optician's shop.
"I got the call last night," he said. "The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life."
Why thousands of high school students in France are protesting

Following the unrest, Paris police prefect Patrice Faure urged Parisian shopkeepers to hire security guards. He later clarified that protecting business owners and their establishments is the responsibility of the government.
Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted last weekend.
Some protests have been banned

Protest marches are scheduled in Paris and Marseille, but some other rallies, including in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier, have been banned by local authorities. In Lyon, French media reported that police used tear gas Saturday morning.

Cities outside Paris were hit hard by the unrest. Two suspects in the fire that nearly destroyed Limoges's 19th-century city hall were placed under formal investigation and held pending trial, French media reported. The probe includes attempted murder of a public official.
Tourist office in Lyon, France, set on fire
Trade unions have criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.

French President Emmanuel Macron, a centrist, has entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term, with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures are needed to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings.
French police move people away to prevent gatherings at the Place de la Bastille in Paris as part of nationwide protests that are taking place again on Saturday. (Dylan Martinez/Reuters)

Thousands of people gathered Saturday morning for an anti-far-right protest in the city of Orléans, about 110 kilometres south of Paris. It was organized on the sidelines of a two-day congress of Marine Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party ahead of next spring's presidential election.
Students and workers are angry

Student groups want 250,000 more places in higher education and an end to selection through Parcoursup, the national admissions system. Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.
They are also seeking help with everyday costs: an extra 200 euros (around $313 Cdn) a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing.

High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods. Some also called for a reform of the university admissions system, seen by many as unfair.

items: What's behind the youth protests in France? - Transcript

blocks.text: With the government seemingly unable to respond to students' demands, the movement has morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, just months before the vote to choose Macron's successor.
"The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people," said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University. "And it's not possible anymore."
Students in France clash with riot police amid weekslong education protests

articles.title: Additional 178 cases of measles reported by US health authorities amid outbreak
articles.summary:
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 4,588 cases across the country, more than double the tally in 2025

Federal health authorities reported an additional 178 cases of measles…

blocks.text: Federal health authorities reported an additional 178 cases of measles in the US this week, as the vaccine-preventable illness continues to sicken people across at least 43 outbreaks.

The new data reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) comes as experts criticize the agency for lack of transparency, and as health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr takes steps to further upend US vaccine infrastructure.

The CDC reported 4,588 cases of measles across the country in 2026 as of Friday – more than double the tally for 2025. Pennsylvania alone reported 1,338 cases on the same day. The CDC also reported large outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah, both of which are reporting more than 500 cases.

In spite of rising measles numbers, official tallies represent an undercount of the disease. Measles is widely regarded as one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine. Its most common symptoms – rash, runny nose, fever and cough – may not immediately send the infected to a doctor.

Measles sends one in five unvaccinated people who become infected to the hospital, and one to three people in 1,000 die of disease-related complications. The measles vaccine is 97% effective at preventing the disease. Vaccine side effects include injection-site soreness and low-grade fever. The measles vaccine has been a focal point of anti-vaccine activism for decades.

In Pennsylvania, which has had the worst outbreak in the nation for months, state authorities have reported five measles-associated deaths and are investigating a sixth. The CDC has reported three measles deaths nationally, but has refused to say where the third death took place, obscuring whether it is counting a death in Pennsylvania or elsewhere.
Kennedy reportedly asked senior CDC officials in September to remove a measles death from the official tally after he questioned whether the disease contributed to the death, according to Reuters.

In addition to criticism of how the CDC has tallied measles deaths, Health and Human Services (HHS) this week announced changes to vaccine injury reporting systems. A proposal will allow doctors to bill for reporting suspected vaccine injuries, among other changes.

The “vaccine adverse event reporting system”, or VAERS, has been a long-time fixation of the anti-vaccine movement. The system has proved useful for researchers tracking rare vaccine safety issues. However, it has also become a source of misinformation for anti-vaccine activists, who point to VAERS to make claims, however unfounded, about safety.

All vaccines have risks – a fact acknowledged by vaccinologists. Before Kennedy’s appointment to the health department, an expert panel considered each vaccine change individually to decide whether benefits outweigh risks. Kennedy fired all 17 sitting members of that board. He replaced them with members with whom he ideologically aligned. A court blocked the members’ appointment in March.

In his time as secretary, Kennedy also misleadingly claimed children get more than 90 vaccine doses; linked vaccines to autism in spite of extensive evidence to the contrary; directed the CDC to remove claims that vaccines do not cause autism from its website; claimed the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine contains “aborted fetal debris”; and stated that vitamin A and cod liver oil may help children with measles, which leading physicians described as misleading.

articles.title: Epstein files take back seat in midterms but experts say issue has not gone away
articles.summary:
Other voter concerns have prevailed but return of Congress likely to see renewed focus on late sex offender’s activities

As US voters head to the polls for crucial and fraught midterm…

blocks.text: As US voters head to the polls for crucial and fraught midterm elections, some survivors’ advocates in the Jeffrey Epstein investigation have expressed concern that the scandal could recede into the background.

Political experts believe, however, the Epstein issue is not going away permanently and that many voters can balance day-to-day concerns such as affordability and AI with the scandal involving the late financier and accused sex trafficker whose social circle was widespread among America’s elite.

“My greatest concern is not that the public will forget Jeffrey Epstein, but that the politicians and institutions responsible for accountability will use the chaos of world events as an excuse to move on,” said Spencer Kuvin of Goldlaw, who has represented multiple Epstein survivors.

Kuvin added: “Wars, economic crises and political controversies may dominate the headlines, but they do not erase the suffering of the victims or the unanswered questions about how Epstein and his powerful associates were allowed to operate for decades.

“Justice should not have an expiration date, and it certainly should not be dictated by the news cycle. We cannot allow the Epstein scandal to become yesterday’s news simply because today’s headlines are more urgent.”
Kuvin called for the US government to continue releasing Epstein files – which many have said were excluded from allegedly incomplete disclosures – and for Congress to demand accountability.

“It has been disappointing to have seen attention diverted from Jeffrey Epstein in the past year,” said Jennifer Freeman of Marsh Law, who represents numerous Epstein survivors in litigation surrounding his sexual abuse of teenage girls.

Freeman, however, expressed optimism about the long-term prospects of justice for survivors, saying: “While public attention may have shifted from the Epstein case, given the electoral cycle, I am confident it will command concentration and accountability shortly again.”

Freeman noted that she was continuing to pursue a lawsuit against the US government for alleged negligence “in repeatedly, for decades, dropping the ball on investigating and prosecuting Epstein”. She is also litigating a class-action lawsuit against his estate related to his collection and production of child sex abuse images.
Political experts said that Epstein might get less attention from campaigning politicians and voters, but that it was probably a temporary dip, not a permanent drop-off.

“It really does feel like everything is on fire. I think people can care about several things at once, but what’s directly affecting their lives tends to take priority,” Brittany Martinez, a Republican strategist who works as acting director of Principles First, said. “When they’re worried about gas prices, living costs and whether their government is working for them, that can push Epstein out of the immediate conversation.

“I don’t think the questions or the demand for answers have gone away; they’re just competing for attention. So I’d expect to hear less about it for stretches, rather than see it disappear altogether.”
“There’s just something every day with Trump,” said Shawn Donahue, clinical associate professor in the University at Buffalo’s department of political science.

For Donahue, timing also plays a key role. The US Congress has been in recess and without members on the House floor, so there’s not any discussion of the Epstein Files Transparency Act’s proposed new iteration. This bill, the Epstein Files Transparency Act II, seeks to address what advocates have said are shortfalls in the present EFTA – such as an absence of enforcement mechanisms.

“It kind of feels like whenever Congress comes back into session, this probably starts to become more of an issue again, and especially if Democrats are looking at being in control of one or maybe both chambers of Congress,” Donahue said.
Should Democrats win the house, as polls project, Donahue expects they will swiftly “put Republicans on the spot” with Epstein. “Democrats are ready to start on the investigation from day one.”

For Julie Roginsky, who co-founded the non-profit Lift Our Voices and pursued a sexual harassment lawsuit against the former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes, the significance of Epstein among voters has not gone away.

“I think Epstein is part of the reason that Trump’s numbers are at record lows. I think it’s something that was one of the issues where even Maga Republicans broke with him,” Roginsky said. “I think that if Democrats do get control of at least one house of Congress this year, then starting next year, you’re going to see a lot more conversation about survivors and about Epstein.”
Congressional supporters of survivors said they would keep fighting for truth and justice.

“This is bigger than a moment. It’s a reckoning, and Americans are ready to have this conversation about power, abuse, and who gets protected,” the Democratic New Mexico representative Teresa Leger Fernández said in a statement. “Of course, Americans will vote with their pocketbooks. They’re worried about groceries, gas, and making rent. But they won’t forget that this president was Epstein’s friend and tried to hide the truth from them.

“The survivors have fought for decades to be heard. Our responsibility is to keep fighting alongside them, get the truth out, and hold those responsible accountable. That responsibility doesn’t disappear when the headlines change.”

The Massachusetts Democratic representative Ayanna Pressley said in a statement: “Justice for survivors of Epstein’s abuse has been a prominent issue amongst the electorate because people of conscience see through the cover-ups of the Trump Administration and demand accountability – that won’t change no matter how much they try to flood the zone and distract us.”
Pressley and fellow representatives Leger Fernández and Deborah Ross recently introduced legislation to address survivors’ financial burdens.

The New Mexico Democratic senator Ben Ray Luján similarly commented that whatever might be unfolding, he would keep pushing for the files to be released in full despite the Department of Justice insisting they have released all Epstein investigative files required under the law.
“We cannot lose sight of the need to release the full Epstein files, hold those responsible accountable, and ensure survivors receive the justice they deserve,” Luján said.
Asked for comment, the White House insisted Trump had advocated for survivors.

“Just as President Trump has said, he’s been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein. And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House Oversight Committee’s subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein’s Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him,” the White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement.
The statement then claimed that several Democrats had yet to explain why they were soliciting money and meetings from Epstein after he was a convicted sex offender.

As for the Department of Justice, the department maintains they have complied with disclosure requirements under the original EFTA. They also rejected claims by New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, that the justice department had not been helping the state’s investigation.

“The Epstein Files Transparency Act does not require, and the protective orders in place in the Southern District of New York do not permit, disclosure of victim-identifying information carte blanche, and New Mexico has provided no lawful basis to justify such sweeping disclosures,” the department said in a statement. “Protecting victim privacy remains a top priority for the Department, and neither [legal] requests nor a desire to cooperate outweighs that privacy. DOJ remains available to assist New Mexico’s investigation consistent with the law and binding court orders.”

articles.title: Voters head to the polls for B.C. provincial election
articles.summary: Voters will cast ballots for 93 MLAs after a snap election was called last month.

image.caption: Voters are pictured at a voting place in Vancouver-Quilchena in October 2024. British Columbians will head to the polls on Saturday to elect their next provincial government. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Voters will cast ballots for 93 MLAs after a snap election was called last month.
Polling stations open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time on Saturday
British Columbians will head to the polls on Saturday to elect their next provincial government.
The snap provincial election was called last month, with more than 350 candidates running across 93 ridings.
Polling stations will be open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time on Saturday.
To be eligible to cast a ballot, voters must be at least 18 years old on Oct. 24 and a Canadian citizen who has resided in B.C. since April 23, 2026.
Many voters will have received a voter information card with details on where they can cast their ballot.
Elections B.C. has provided an application for voters to find their nearest voting place.

The provincial elections office has a list of acceptable ID documents that voters would need to prove their identity and residential address when voting. Voters who don't have the required identification can have their identity vouched for by a person who meets specific eligibility requirements.
Anyone who hasn't registered can still do so in person on election day.
CBC News will bring you up-to-the-minute coverage after polls close, with a live election special starting at 7:30 p.m. PT.

Hosts Gloria Macarenko and Jason D’Souza will host B.C. Votes 2026, a special evening of election programming featuring guest interviews and in-depth analysis and broadcast coverage available in ASL across all CBC B.C. platforms.
Where to watch and listen:
Online: Live streaming on CBC News BC, CBC Gem, cbc.ca/bc as well as on YouTube.
TV: Live on CBC Television (check your TV service provider for channel).
Listen: Live on CBC Radio One or listen online.

articles.title: Israelis are leaving the country in record numbers. Could a looming election accelerate the trend?
articles.summary: A record number of Israelis have left the country in resent years, data shows, and experts are raising the alarm ahead of a "watershed" election that they say could add to the trend and put more…

image.caption: Economist Itai Ater, seen in Tel Aviv in September, was the lead author of a study that found 99,000 Israelis left the country between January 2023 and December 2024. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)

blocks.text: World

A record number of Israelis have left the country in resent years, data shows, and experts are raising the alarm ahead of a "watershed" election that they say could add to the trend and put more strain on the country's economy.
A February study found 99,000 Israelis left the country in 2023 and 2024
Sitting at his desk in a sun-filled apartment in Tel Aviv, economist Itai Ater pored over data that shows more Israelis have left the country over the past three years than ever before.

Those have been tumultuous years for the country of around 10 million people, with war, economic uncertainty and a prime minister plagued by corruption charges whose trial started in 2020 and still hasn't reached a verdict.

Ater, a professor at the Coller School of Management at Tel Aviv University, says these departures could accelerate depending on the outcome of next week's legislative elections, destabilizing the country's economy and causing ripple effects throughout the region.

"Israelis are thinking, 'do I want to raise my kids in a country like this?'" Ater said. "Unfortunately, and I understand, I sympathize with their answers, many of them realize that the answer is no. And that's why they're leaving."

In February, Ater and his colleagues published a study using data collected from the Central Bureau of Statistics that found 99,000 Israelis left the country between January 2023 and December 2024. The study looked at Israelis who left for at least three consecutive months and stayed out of the country for more than 270 days during the first year of their departure.
Ater says he understands why people might want to leave: 'Israelis are thinking, "do I want to raise my kids in a country like this?"' (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)

According to the data, 50,000 left in 2023, a year that saw Hamas militants storm southern Israel, killing roughly 1,200 people and kidnapping another 250. Israel responded by embarking on a devastating military campaign in the Gaza Strip that continued until a fragile ceasefire went into effect in October 2025, though Israel still controls roughly 60 per cent of the enclave and engages in regular military activity there.
In 2024, 49,000 left. Ater says preliminary data shows the trend continued in 2025, and he believes the looming election could push those numbers even higher in 2026.
Election fuels uncertainty
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has been a defining figure in Israeli politics for the past three decades and is by far the country's longest serving leader, is once again vying for power.

Polls suggest his far-right bloc will fall short of the requisite 61 seats in the Knesset to form a government and that a rival bloc headed by Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, is currently in position to secure the most seats. As of now, Eisenkot's coalition is expected to be short of a majority.

items: Netanyahu's future uncertain as Israel starts to prepare for national election
Netanyahu faces fresh allegations he ignored warnings about Oct. 7 — right before an election

blocks.text: Israel's multiparty system, in which coalitions are often required in order to form a government, means the election results are often only just the beginning of the intrigue and lead to a jostling of parties and power in the days after the vote.
Netanyahu has long been considered a master at this process.

A supporter of Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the Likud party, displays a flag depicting him at Mahane Yehuda market, ahead of Israel's national election, in Jerusalem on Oct. 22. (Kevin Coombs/Reuters)

"We are really, really, really terrified in the sense that if there is no change in the patterns, then there's no change in October in the elections," Ater said. "These [emigration] numbers will go up dramatically."
Avigail Ben-Porat, 50, said she dreams of leaving but doesn't have the resources to do so.
The single mother lives in Kiryat Shmona, near the Israel-Lebanon border, where she said she still regularly hears the sound of rocket fire.

items: Israeli strikes on southern Lebanese town kill 12, including children, Health Ministry says

blocks.text: "I would go and never look back," Ben-Porat said. "Most of my friends are living abroad, some of them in Portugal, some of them moved to Canada. Some of them are in Thailand and in Goa in India. They pretty much left and fled."
Economic impact
It's not just the volume of people leaving that has Ater and others concerned — it's their jobs.

Ater's study suggests that 2023 and 2024 saw a dramatic increase in the number of doctors, Ph.D. holders and engineers leaving the country, with 2,360 net departures from Israeli engineers and 509 net departures from doctors.
"Israel's economy depends on the human capital," he said. "It's the tech industry, it's academia, it's health care. We need these best individuals to stay in Israel."
Lawyer Liam Schwartz, seen in Tel Aviv in September, says many companies, under pressure from investors, are moving chunks of their business outside Israel. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)
Liam Schwartz oversees the corporate immigration department at Goldfarb, Gross, Seligman, an Israeli law firm based in Tel Aviv. He said Israeli companies are also eying the exit.

"There are a good deal of Israeli companies that are just — they call it business viability," Schwartz said. "They have to answer to their shareholders who are not necessarily Israeli and investors who are not necessarily Israeli and they are concerned about the viability of business operations based in Israel. So they are more willing to move chunks of their workforce to North America or to Europe."
Schwartz believes the discontent started when the government proposed judicial reforms that would have stripped power away from the Supreme Court back in January 2023.

items: Israeli parliament approves key part of divisive judicial overhaul

blocks.text: "People are just disappointed," he said. "They feel like the Israeli government is no longer meeting its part of the social contract."
All of this adds up to making Tuesday's elections one of the country's most consequential.
"I think that the October elections in Israel are going to be a watershed moment in whether … the rate of Israeli emigration increases or not," Schwartz said.
For Ater, the stakes could not be higher.

"I'm saying it. It's a strategic concern, strategic risk," he said. "To the future of Israel as a democracy, as a liberal country, and that's not only a concern for Israel, it's also a concern for the Middle East and also for the world."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Willy Lowry is an award-winning correspondent for CBC News in Washington, D.C., where he provides breaking news and analysis across radio and television. Prior to that, he served as the senior U.S. correspondent at the National newspaper in D.C., where he covered the U.S. State Department, American foreign policy and its impacts on the Middle East and the wider world. Willy covered the Israel-Hamas war extensively, travelling to Israel and the occupied West Bank several times. He also covered the fall of ISIS in Syria. He started his career at CBC News in Montreal, where he worked his way up from intern to research assistant and eventually to video journalist.

articles.title: Will Guinea-Bissau remain trapped in political chaos?
articles.summary: Elections scheduled for December 6 in Guinea-Bissau have been postponed indefinitely. No new date has been set, leaving the country's return to civilian rule uncertain.

image.caption: Soldiers patrol the main street in Bissau, the capital of Guinea-Bissau. Following the 2025 military coup, the country's state institutions were suspendedImage: Luc Gnago/REUTERS

blocks.text: The parliamentary and presidential elections scheduled for December 6, 2026, in Guinea-Bissau will not take place as planned. Aly Silva, spokesperson for transitional Prime Minister Ilidio Vieira Te, confirmed to DW that the vote had been postponed until further notice. No new date has been set. The government first intends to discuss the matter in cabinet before publicly announcing when the elections will be held. It remains unclear whether they will take place in 2027 or not until 2028.

The country's political crisis dates back to November 26, 2025. Three days earlier, voters in Guinea-Bissau had elected a new parliament and president. Before the official results could be announced, the military seized power and halted the electoral process. Both then-President Umaro Sissoco Embalo and his challenger, Fernando Dias da Costa, had claimed victory. The military leadership promised a return to constitutional order.

blocks.caption: Guinea-Bissau's General Horta N'Tam (center) was sworn in as transitional leader and commander-in-chief on November 27, 2025Image: Patrick Meinhardt/AFP

blocks.text: For lawyer and political analyst Cabi Sanha, the postponement comes as no surprise. Since the coup, little has been done to create the conditions for credible elections, he says.
"The postponement was foreseeable," Sanha told DW. December 6 had indeed been set as the new election date. "But nothing was done to ensure that these elections could actually take place."
Political freedoms under pressure

The transitional government has justified the postponement by citing the lack of organizational and political conditions necessary for elections. The deadline for submitting candidacies had already passed on October 6. Political parties and potential candidates had not submitted their applications. According to the prime minister, the parties had also failed to hold congresses to select their candidates.

Sanha sees this as more than an organizational problem. He points to restrictions on political activities and the lack of dialogue with key actors in the electoral process. Political parties and civil society have not been sufficiently involved, he says. Mediation efforts by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and Senegal have so far failed to produce a solution.
"Free, transparent and inclusive elections are only possible if the necessary conditions are established beforehand," the lawyer says.

He therefore also views the parties' failure to nominate candidates as a consequence of the political environment. "How are parties supposed to nominate candidates when political activities are restricted in the country? They cannot hold party congresses or organize rallies."

blocks.caption: The funeral of human rights activist Vigario Balanta in Bissau, Guinea-Bissau. His body was found on March 31, bearing signs of torture, in a swamp outside the capitalImage: DW

blocks.text: Leading opposition figures are also staying abroad. Domingos Simoes Pereira, head of the main opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), was allowed to travel to Portugal in July 2026 for medical treatment after being released from detention. He had previously been held in pretrial detention in connection with an investigation into an alleged coup attempt. His defense team denies the allegations and has criticized the proceedings as politically motivated.
The absence of key opposition figures and restrictions on political organizing are making it harder to conduct an electoral process intended to pave the way for a return to civilian government.
An election date without a timetable

What happens next remains unclear. Government spokesperson Aly Silva says the transitional government will first discuss the matter in cabinet. Only afterward will a new election date be announced publicly. So far, there is no concrete timetable.

It is therefore also unclear when political parties will be able to complete their internal selection procedures, nominate candidates and begin campaigning. For Sanha, this is another indication that there is still insufficient evidence of the political will needed to restore constitutional order.
"I do not believe that logistical problems are the main issue. Rather, there appears to be a lack of political will to move the electoral process forward," he says.
Dispute over the constitution

The political crisis has been compounded by a controversial constitutional reform. In a referendum on August 30, 2026, voters approved constitutional amendments that expand the president's powers and reduce the size of parliament from 102 to 65 seats. Critics question the legitimacy of the process because the reform was prepared under military rule and without a regularly elected parliament. The opposition had called for a boycott of the vote.

Fernando Vaz, spokesperson for the National Transitional Council, defends the changes. He says the process was not a comprehensive rewriting of the constitution but a targeted revision. The reform is intended to help overcome the country's political instability, he argues.

"The constitution must be one of the instruments that lead our country toward greater stability," Vaz told DW. The transitional period had provided an opportunity to amend provisions that, in the military leadership's view, were obstructing the country's political development.

Vaz also rejects criticism that the reform gives the president additional powers at the expense of the prime minister. "The president of the republic is the head of state, while the prime minister is the head of government," he emphasizes.

Critics see it differently. The new constitutional framework strengthens the presidency: the president is to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and the government and, under certain conditions, dissolve parliament. At the same time, the number of parliamentary seats is being reduced. It remains disputed whether the reform will genuinely contribute to stability or instead concentrate more power in the presidency.

blocks.caption: Around 70 percent of valid votes in a constitutional referendum on August 30, 2026, were cast in favor of constitutional amendmentsImage: DW

blocks.text: Local elections are not enough

The transitional government has announced plans to hold local elections in 2027. Sanha broadly welcomes the proposal: Guinea-Bissau has never held such elections since independence. Nevertheless, he stresses that they must not replace the outstanding national elections.
"First, parliamentary and presidential elections must take place so that the country can return to constitutional order. Local elections can follow afterward," he says.

Local elections cannot compensate for the lack of democratic legitimacy at the national level. Political freedoms must also be restored so that parties can select their candidates and voters can genuinely choose between political alternatives.
A Transition With No Clear End
Guinea-Bissau has endured decades of political instability, marked by military coups, institutional crises and repeated interruptions of democratic processes. The latest coup continues this pattern.

The renewed postponement of the elections shows how far the country remains from a return to constitutional order. Setting a new election date alone will not be enough. Political activities must be permitted again, parties must be included in the process, and reliable conditions for elections must be established, lawyer Cabi Sanha told DW.
This article was originally published in German.
