articles.title: ICC prosecutor says court making ‘significant progress’ despite US sanctions
articles.summary:
Nazhat Shameem Khan claims some staff are facing ‘banking difficulties’ but their work is unaffected

The deputy prosecutor of the international criminal court has said new US sanctions are…

blocks.text: The deputy prosecutor of the international criminal court has said new US sanctions are beginning to take effect on its staff but insisted they have not hindered the court’s work.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, announced the sanctions this month, accusing the ICC – a frequent target of the Trump administration – of being a “rogue court” and declaring: “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.”
Nazhat Shameem Khan, who is co-running the office pending the appointment of a new chief prosecutor, said the court was so far continuing its work.

She said the Gaza war investigation and others had made “significant progress” since war crimes arrest warrants were issued in November 2024 for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister, Yoav Galant. Further applications from the prosecutor were being kept secret by order of the court, she said.

blocks.caption: The ICC issued a war crimes arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.  Photograph: Amir Cohen/Reuters

blocks.text: Some ICC staff had however encountered banking problems, she said, even though the US sanctions on the court were not due to take effect until six months from 9 October, the date of their announcement. She said the banks were “over-complying” to minimise risk while there was uncertainty over the ultimate scope of the measures.

“These are sanctions imposed on the institutions and, in principle, our individual members should not be impacted directly,” the Fijian deputy prosecutor said in an interview with the Guardian. “But again, what I am hearing from members of our staff is that some of them are experiencing difficulties in banking.”

The court is working on insulating itself from sanctions imposed by a hostile administration in Washington. It has switched its software from Microsoft to European ​alternatives, and is negotiating with relevant service providers over banking and health insurance.

“All the investigations across all situations continue. We haven’t made any decision based on the sanctions to reduce our capability or reduce our output,” Khan said, acknowledging that it was impossible to anticipate the full impact of sanctions when they officially took effect.

The new sanctions target the whole institution of the ICC, but the US first targeted 13 ICC staff in February 2025. Khan was one of them, so is accustomed to dealing with sanctions, which affect aspects of everyday life.

“Life without a credit card is inconvenient. It’s amazing how many things now we cannot do around the world, particularly in relation to travel, without a credit card,” she said, but added that her inconvenience was put into perspective when she visited refugee camps or sites of mass atrocities.
“We see the faces of our victims for whom sanctions and credit cards are completely irrelevant. They just want justice.”

blocks.caption: The former ICC chief prosecutor, Karim Khan.  Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/Reuters

blocks.text: American sanctions are not the only disruption to the ICC prosecutors’ work. Formal investigations began in late November 2024 into allegations of sexual harassment against the former chief prosecutor, Karim Khan. The British jurist (who is no relation to the deputy prosecutor) denied the charges. He was removed in July this year after a vote by member states.

No further charges over the Gaza war have been announced since late 2024. Khan insisted that investigative work on the Israel-Palestine file had only gone quiet because of the court’s ruling earlier this year that all charges and applications for warrants should be kept secret until the judges decide they can be made public.

“Even if we reach a stage of the investigations where it might be imminent, we may not discuss it publicly,” she said. “And so while there might be an appearance that nothing is happening, I can assure you that there’s significant progress in that particular situation as well as others.”

When announcing the sanctions, Rubio gave the ICC a six-month grace period “to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns” but it is unclear what would satisfy the Trump administration, which has exhibited a longstanding hostility towards the court.
Rubio claimed, without evidence, this month that “globalist ‘experts’ an ocean away” wanted the ICC to prosecute US citizens. Khan said it was unclear who and what Rubio had in mind.

blocks.caption: US secretary of state, Marco Rubio: ‘Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.’ Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters/AP

blocks.text: “It is possible that there is a mistaken belief on the part of those who are concerned that we are pursuing Americans, but we certainly haven’t brought any Americans before the court,” she said. “If his reference is to Afghanistan, then in fact the priority for the investigation is in relation to offences committed specifically against women, girls and other vulnerable groups by the Taliban and by the Islamic State Khorasan in Afghanistan.”
This month, four arrest warrants were unsealed by the ICC pretrial chamber against members of the Taliban on charges of gender persecution.

The court registrar for the ICC is in negotiation with the EU over blocking the US sanctions or protecting the court in other ways. There has been support for the court, and on Thursday, the European parliament awarded its Sakharov prize for freedom of thought to the court and its officials.
Khan said the support was “a very important message that the staff at the court need to hear”, as were pledges from other countries to continue to contribute towards the ICC’s costs.

“I think that the fact that there is so much attention on us is a reflection of how relevant we are,” Khan said. “This is a court that provides an avenue of justice for victims who have nowhere else to go, who really want to cut past politics and want their voices to be heard.”

articles.title: Storm Boelo to bring gusts of up to 80mph and heavy rain to parts of UK
articles.summary:
Second named storm in as many days will hit northern parts of UK as thousands remain without power after Friday’s Storm Austen

The UK is bracing for a second storm this weekend, as strong…

blocks.text: The UK is bracing for a second storm this weekend, as strong winds and heavy rain are expected to disrupt travel and cause further power cuts in the north.
Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, is expected to bring heavy, frequent showers and winds potentially exceeding 80mph to northern parts of the UK.
Thousands of homes in the south-west of England have already been left without power after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday.
The Met Office has advised people to stay indoors as much as possible, and said the storm will bring danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves.

The forecaster has issued an amber alert, its second most severe weather warning, covering Scotland, the north of England down to Carlisle from 9pm Saturday to the same time on Sunday. Another amber warning is also in place for the north-east of Northern Ireland from 9pm Saturday to 10am Sunday.

A large yellow warning for very wet and windy weather will cover the whole of the UK’s north from midday Saturday to 9pm on Sunday. Another warning for heavy rain covers Wales and parts of western and southern England from 11am to 11pm Saturday.

Widespread travel disruption is expected on ferries and trains. TransPennine Express has warned against making all but essential train journeys on Saturday and Sunday, while Avanti West Coast has strongly advised users not to travel north of Preston on Sunday.
The Met Office has also warned that power cuts across the south-west of England could be replicated across amber areas in the north this weekend.
In the south-west of England, 31,000 homes were without power at one stage on Friday. More than 3,700 were still without electricity on Saturday morning, according to the National Grid map.

Human-driven climate change has continued to reshape rainfall patterns and weather conditions globally. The UK experienced its hottest summer on record this year, with five heatwaves and a record-breaking 40 days of temperatures above 30C.

Met Office meteorologist Alex Burkill said: “Storm Boelo is arriving. It’s going to bring widespread rain and some very strong winds indeed, and it’s quick on the tails of Storm Austen which is now clearing away towards the east.
after newsletter promotion

“It’s the winds that were perhaps most concerned about, they’re really going to whip up some strong gusty winds across Northern Ireland, northern parts of England and also Scotland through the day – strengthening as we head towards the evening.

“Temperatures will be a little more than the seasonal average but “obviously with the wind and rain it’s going to feel pretty unpleasant out there,” Burkhill added. “A very, well, different side of autumn compared with what we’ve seen through much of the season so far.”
Storm Boelo’s winds are expected to peak from Saturday evening. The wet weather will clear overnight in many areas, while more rain continues to hit Scotland and northern Ireland.
Attending a summit on the summer’s record wildfires on Friday, Andy Burnham warned that the UK could face “a winter of greater flooding”.

The prime minister denied suggestions that the government was playing catch-up with civil preparedness, but said “we’re living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common”.

articles.title: Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits
articles.summary: The slowed Starlink connections had affected the Ukraine's military and drone operations for a week.

blocks.text: Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the satellite network.

Kyiv relies on the Starlink and its military-grade counterpart Starshield for piloting drones and operations within Ukraine, but last week accused US President Donald Trump of telling owner Elon Musk to place limits on it.
This meant drones would lose connection when travelling at 161km/h (100mph) or more, it said. Trump denied doing so before saying Musk had "put it back".
Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that speeds of more than 400km/h were now possible on the network, indicating that full capability had been restored.
"This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he said in a statement on Saturday.
Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield.
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, which Musk said was controlled by the US military when he suggested the Pentagon could be behind the recent issues.
Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

The debacle over Starlink began last week, and emerged during a broader diplomatic row between Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.
Zelensky said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
Meanwhile, fighting on the ground continues.
Russian authorities said on Saturday there were power cuts in Russian-annexed Crimea following a Ukrainian drone attack.
Sergey Aksyonov, the Moscow-backed governor of the region, said restrictions on electricity and water had been put in place.
Separately, Russian-backed authorities said at least three people had been killed and another wounded in a separate Ukrainian strike in Kharkiv.

articles.title: New Trump rule allows hunters to bait bears in Alaska with doughnuts, bacon and more
articles.summary:
Critics decry Trump administration rule that lets hunters lure bears with human foods on federal lands in Alaska

A new Trump administration rule allows hunters to bait bears on federal lands…

blocks.text: A new Trump administration rule allows hunters to bait bears on federal lands in Alaska with bacon, doughnuts, meat scraps or other human foods typically used to help kill the trophy animals at close range.

Opponents say the practice will cause bears to be more aggressive around humans, and allege that the rule change is a political gift to largely rightwing trophy hunters. The rule replaces a 2024 Biden administration rule that banned the practice, and environmental groups criticized the move as “indefensible and inexcusable”.

“We are discouraged to see this rule come back, specifically the bear baiting piece which is cruel and dangerous, not only to wildlife but the public as well,” said Drew Robertson, senior regulatory specialist for Humane World for Animals.

The US interior department on Friday published the rule on the federal register, and it will take effect in mid-November. It marks the latest in a series of rule changes at the state and federal levels since 2023 that allow trophy hunters to use what critics say are barbaric and unethical practices to kill animals.

Doug Burgum, the secretary of the interior, wrote in a press release that the latest rule was developed in response to demands by Alaska residents and it was a “commonsense framework and gives Alaskans a stronger voice in decisions affecting the lands, wildlife and traditions they know best”.

The federal rule does not list specific foods that are allowed, but it defers to state rules, which allow for baiting, and hunters typically use “the cheapest and most effective food, which is high fat and high sugar”, said Nicholas Arrivo, a managing attorney at Animal Protection Law. Hunters typically put food in a steel drum or garbage can, monitor the bait, then set up from a nearby blind from which they kill the bear at short range, Arrivo said.
The practice raises broader ethical questions around the spirit and intent of sport hunting.
“It is a more extreme practice than the hunting traditions that people think of, and many hunters would not see this as a fair chase,” Robertson said.

The move comes after Alaska and federal officials in recent years started allowing sport hunters to hunt big game with controversial practices, like shooting bears from helicopters, shooting swimming caribou from motor boats, killing wolf pups in their dens and using artificial lights to draw bears out of the dens to kill them. The bear baiting is not highly unusual as about a dozen states allow similar practices, but more do not.
The rule change came at the direction of Donald Trump in an executive order, called Unleashing Alaska’s Extraordinary Resource Potential, which was issued in his second administration’s early days.

“It was a priority for the president … and he included direction to reissue this rule, which says that there is a political motivation, not something that seems to be derived from careful consideration,” Robertson said.

This baiting rule has a long history. A ban was first put in place by Barack Obama’s administration, then undone by the first Trump administration. Litigation upheld the Obama rule and overturned the Trump rule. The Biden administration then reimplemented the rule in 2024, largely because science shows that the practice will make bears more aggressive, and put park visitors’ lives at risk.

Though the Trump administration has said the rule was designed to give the state more control over the land, the lands are federal and Congress created the federal land program to give the federal government decision-making power, not state governments, Arrivo said. He said it “is anathema to federal land management goals … of preserving wildlife diversity”.

Though no decision has yet been made about a lawsuit, Arrivo said the interior department’s decision to fully scrap the 2024 rule that underwent a more robust scientific process “doesn’t smell right and raises questions about the legality of this rule”.

articles.title: No unions, low taxes: why some of Britain’s top chefs are opening outposts in Gulf states
articles.summary:
Leading restaurateur says Gulf countries actively help businesses set up, while east Asia has a better work ethic

Some of London’s top restaurants are opening branches in Dubai because of a…

blocks.text: Some of London’s top restaurants are opening branches in Dubai because of a “tax tsunami” in the UK and better work ethic abroad, according to a leading restaurateur.
James Robson, a co-owner of Fallow in St James’s Market, regarded as the capital’s hottest restaurant, serving 1,000 people a day, has just signed a deal to open an outpost in the Gulf.

Other restaurants have opened in Dubai, including the celebrity hotspot Scott’s in Mayfair, the two Michelin-starred Indian venue Gymkhana, and the upmarket Chinese restaurant Park Chinois. Isabel’s, a Mayfair institution enjoyed by politicians, has opened in Abu Dhabi. And the trendy Borough Market bakery Bread Ahead has branched out in Dubai.

Despite conflicts in the Middle East, including the US-Israeli war in Iran which caused Dubai to face bombardment and an exodus of expats earlier this year, restaurants continue to open in the emirate.

Speaking from Hong Kong, where he is looking at opportunities in Asia, Robson said: “East Asia, the States and the Gulf are key growth targets for us. America champions business, the Gulf actively encourages and assists, whilst east Asia has a work ethic and taxation system that puts the UK to shame. I’m incredibly keen to start working in these regions over the next few years.”
Fallow has risen to fame partially through Instagram, where it has 650,000 followers, and its striking dishes including a whole cod’s head drenched in a spicy butter sauce.

Restaurateurs have complained of the VAT rate for hospitality in the UK, which at 20% is one of the highest rates in Europe. The European average for restaurants is about 12%. In Italy, it is set at 10% for food sold in restaurants. Chefs are calling for Andy Burnham to use next week’s budget to cut the VAT rate.

blocks.caption: Two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of several London establishments that has opened in Dubai  Photograph: Sophia Evans/The Observer

blocks.text: “We have had a tsunami of taxes that have got to the point where taking business risk simply does not make sense in the UK,” Robson said, “Sadly the country has sleepwalked into multiple anti-growth taxations the last two budgets and likely more will be forthcoming next week.”
The entrepreneur has asked for VAT to be put more in line with Europe. “Add 25% corporation tax and 40%-plus dividend tax, then you start to question why do businesses any more.”
Jason Atherton, a Michelin-starred chef, spends a third of his time at his Dubai restaurant now and says it is easier to make a profit abroad than in London.

But human rights experts have warned of exploitation and poor worker protections in the Gulf. Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK’s director of campaigns, said: “Dubai might look like an attractive place to do business, but the UAE has a very poor record on workers’ rights and protection from labour exploitation. The UAE has spent heavily on polishing its image in the UK, not least through Manchester City, but that glamour shouldn’t distract from how the people who keep its economy running are treated.
after newsletter promotion

“Migrant workers, who make up the majority of the UAE’s population, remain bound by a sponsorship system that ties them to their employers and exposes them to labour abuse. They are denied the right to form trade unions, leaving them few ways to challenge unfair treatment.

“Any UK business expanding into the Gulf has a responsibility to carry out proper human rights due diligence, to make sure the people working in its kitchens are treated fairly, paid properly and able to raise concerns without fear of losing their job or visa.”

blocks.caption: The British Michelin-starred chef Jason Atherton has previously spoken out about high taxes and the UK’s struggling hospitality sector. Photograph: Richard Saker/The Guardian

blocks.text: Some restaurants in Dubai are struggling: Dinner by Heston is temporarily closed and has been since the fallout from the war in the Middle East. The Michelin guide came under fire earlier this month because it included 16 restaurants that were either permanently or temporarily closed. It appears that some visits were undertaken by inspectors at the beginning of the year, before the war started.

Robson said he had no resentment paying UK tax. “I am incredibly proud of the taxes I pay and feel privileged that I can contribute to our country’s deficit and will continue to do so,” he said. “My point is UK growth simply does not have any risk-reward balance any more, therefore it’s play incredibly safe here and focus overseas.”

articles.title: House prosecution submitted formal offer of evidence vs Sara Duterte - Barbers
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel on Saturday confirmed that it had filed its formal offer of evidence in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, days before the October 23 deadline.

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 6:39pm
The House prosecution panel on Saturday confirmed that it had filed its formal offer of evidence in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, days before the October 23 deadline.

“We already filed ‘yung ating formal offer of evidence. Kung hindi ako nagkakamali, Miyerkoles. This is days before the deadline,” House prosecution spokesperson Robert Ace Barbers said at a news forum.
(We already filed our formal offer of evidence on Wednesday, if I’m not mistaken.)
Barbers said the defense would have 10 days to comment on the prosecution’s formal offer before the Senate impeachment court rules on the admissibility of the evidence.

He said the formal offer included all documentary evidence and witness testimonies presented by the prosecution in support of Article 2 of the impeachment complaint, which alleges that Duterte accumulated unexplained wealth through assets not declared in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).
Barbers expressed confidence that the prosecution could secure a conviction.

“Honestly, ang pakiramdam namin, we are confident that we can secure a conviction. Bakit? Doon po sa aming mga nailatag na ebidensiya, matibay at malakas po ang aming paniwala na itong mga ebidensiyang ito ay sumusuporta sa aming alegasyon na merong hindi maipaliwanag na yaman ang ating Pangalawang Pangulo. At merong mga nalabag na probisyon sa Saligang Batas at merong nalabag na mga batas ang ating Pangalawang Pangulo,” he said.

(Honestly, we are confident that we can secure a conviction. Why? Based on the evidence we have presented, we firmly believe that it supports our allegation that the Vice President has unexplained wealth and has violated provisions of the Constitution and other laws.)
The House prosecution panel had initially been allotted 62 trial days to present its evidence but used only 39 days before resting its case on October 13.

The panel had earlier dropped three other articles of impeachment: Article 1, which concerned confidential funds; Article 3, which alleged bribery; and Article 4, which accused Duterte of making grave threats against President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. and his family. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm
articles.summary: The European Union wants to relax rules for pesticides, saying it will be easier for farmers to adopt more environmentally friendly options. But health and environmental experts say the risks are far…

image.caption: In a bid to help farmers, the EU has proposed unlimited, open-ended approval for certain pesticidesImage: Andrii Yalanskyi/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.
Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.

The European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities, not the industry, would bear responsibility.

The commission has said its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.
Why does the EU want to deregulate pesticides?
The European Commission has said it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of new, more sustainable products.
In recent negotiations, EU member states said open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances."
But their stance is still wanting to extend initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, said there is currently a yearslong delay in approving new pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.
The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities."
Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the issue, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation."
He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the new pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.
How do pesticides affect human health, environment?
Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the new regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.
Pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

blocks.caption: In January 2020, beekeepers in Berlin protested the continued authorization of glyphosate by leaving unsellable tainted honey at the entrance to Germany's Agriculture MinistryImage: Adam Berry/Getty Images

blocks.text: When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has said it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides."

However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: A survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation."

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she said regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time.
"The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge," she said.
More than 50 substances banned since 2011

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe, an NGO based in Brussels, said the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.
"New science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews.
That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, previously used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.
Pesticides banned in Europe linked to bees deaths in Kenya
Roynel said it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby.

This echoes a new report by nonprofit research and campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory, which said Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.
Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the issue.
"The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring new ones to the market," Dorfmann said.
Part of that plan, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.
Farmers need 'incentive' to switch to safer pesticides

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.
Can we cut down on pesticide use with 'plant vaccines'?

Roynel also supports the plan to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but said it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these new products, as well as maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides ― not further deregulation.

"If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she said. "It's important to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but… it will not be the silver bullet."

articles.title: Typhoon Rosal exits PAR; ITCZ bringing scattered rain
articles.summary: As of Saturday afternoon, October 24, no new low pressure areas or potential tropical cyclones are being monitored inside or outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility

blocks.text: PHILIPPINE WEATHER. Satellite image as of October 24, 2026, 4 pm.
PAGASA
As of Saturday afternoon, October 24, no new low pressure areas or potential tropical cyclones are being monitored inside or outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility

items: Typhoon Rosal (Champi) exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility on Saturday, October 24.
Rosal's trough or extension and the intertropical convergence zone are causing scattered rain and thunderstorms.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Typhoon Rosal (Champi) exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) on Saturday morning, October 24, then left the weather bureau’s monitoring domain in the afternoon.
At the time of its exit from PAR, Rosal’s maximum sustained winds were already down to 120 kilometers per hour. During its peak, it was a super typhoon with maximum sustained winds of 215 km/h.

Rosal did not make landfall in the Philippines, but it affected parts of Northern Luzon, especially the northernmost province of Batanes. It brought moderate to intense rain, as well as winds up to Signal No. 2.
The trough or extension of the tropical cyclone has also affected various areas in Luzon, the Visayas, and even Mindanao in the past days.

On Saturday afternoon, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said scattered rain and thunderstorms due to Rosal’s trough will only be confined to Batanes, Ilocos Norte, Apayao, and Babuyan Islands in the coming hours.

Rosal entered PAR last Tuesday, October 20, becoming the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. PAGASA earlier estimated the country may have one or two tropical cyclones during the month.
So far, no new low pressure areas or potential tropical cyclones are being monitored inside or outside PAR.

Meanwhile, the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ) is bringing scattered rain and thunderstorms to the Visayas, Mindanao, Sorsogon, Masbate, and Palawan on Saturday evening. Flash floods and landslides are possible.
The ITCZ is a belt near the equator where the trade winds of the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere meet.
The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Senate minority calls for dialogue after P50-M bounty on Bato
articles.summary: Senators from the minority bloc on Saturday urged President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. and concerned agencies to negotiate with the legal team of Senator Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa for a “peaceful…

blocks.text: Senators from the minority bloc on Saturday urged President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. and concerned agencies to negotiate with the legal team of Senator Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa for a “peaceful resolution” amid efforts to bring him before the International Criminal Court (ICC).
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla has declared Dela Rosa “armed and dangerous,” prompting the department to offer a P50-million bounty for information leading to his capture.

“We understand the government’s desire to resolve this situation in the interest of law and order. We believe a peaceful resolution that respects our laws and protects lives remains possible,” the senators said in a joint statement.

“We respectfully appeal to the President and the concerned agencies to work with Senator Dela Rosa’s counsel toward a peaceful resolution. The Minority stands with our colleague and is ready to help facilitate that discussion, confident that our institutions can uphold the law, protect his rights, and pursue justice without needless loss of life,” they added.
Remulla previously warned that an attempt to arrest Dela Rosa could result in the deaths of 10,000 people.
The minority bloc welcomed Remulla’s stated desire to prevent loss of life and called on all parties to exercise restraint and maintain open communication.

“We appeal to everyone concerned—the executive, law enforcement, Senator Dela Rosa and his family and counsel, his supporters, and anyone who can influence events on the ground—to exercise restraint and keep communication open,” the senators said.

The Senate minority, led by Senator Alan Peter Cayetano, is composed of Dela Rosa, Imee Marcos, Robin Padilla, Bong Go, Pia Cayetano, Jinggoy Estrada, Rodante Marcoleta, Camille Villar, and Loren Legarda.

Dela Rosa has remained out of public view since the ICC issued an arrest warrant against him over alleged crimes against humanity linked to the drug war under former president Rodrigo Duterte, who is currently in ICC custody awaiting trial.
The minority senators, however, questioned the validity of the ICC warrant, reiterating that the Philippines withdrew from the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC, in 2019.
Marcos backs law enforcement

Asked about the minority bloc’s appeal, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said Marcos supported the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), the Department of Justice (DOJ), and law enforcement agencies in their efforts to arrest Dela Rosa.

“Walang dapat mamatay sa pagganap sa tungkulin ng mga pulis para maaresto si Sen. Bato, kaya huwag na silang magmatigas dahil hindi aatras ang kapulisan natin. Tumatakbo ang bawat minuto, dapat mas mabilis na pagkilos. Suportado ng Pangulo ang hakbang ng DILG, DOJ at mga law enforcers,” Castro said in a message.

(No one should die while the police are performing their duties to arrest Senator Bato, so they should stop being stubborn because the police will not back down. Every minute counts, and action must be taken more quickly. The President supports the efforts of the DILG, DOJ, and law enforcement agencies.)
Castro also said the P50-million bounty would not have been necessary had Dela Rosa not managed to leave the Senate by hitching a ride in May, when authorities attempted to arrest him.
Meanwhile, ICC Assistant to Counsel Kristina Conti criticized both Dela Rosa and the Marcos administration over their handling of the arrest warrant.

“Ironically, putting a P50 million bounty on Bato Dela Rosa only highlights the incompetence of the Marcos administration in implementing the ICC warrant, before and now. It reminds us how the DILG, NBI, and PNP essentially let Bato go in May 2026, and on the other hand, how powerful Dela Rosa's backers are,” Conti said in a Facebook post.
Conti also asked Dela Rosa to "surrender to Philippine authorities and directly engage in the ICC proceedings."
"There, he can expect the highest standards in human rights and due process. And that is priceless,” she said. — VBL, GMA News

Philip Jr Lustre's Facebook

items: Philip Lustre Jr., a veteran journalist, was arrested for alleged cyber libel, which his lawyer claims is an attack on press freedom in the Philippines.
Lustre, known for documenting extrajudicial killings during Duterte's presidency, was unaware of the complaint against him, raising concerns about media harassment.
The Presidential Task Force on Media Security expressed support for Lustre and emphasized that laws protecting reputation should not be misused to intimidate journalists.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The arrest of Philip Lustre Jr. is an attack on press freedom in the Philippines, the veteran journalist’s lawyer Dino De Leon said.
Lustre was arrested at a restaurant in Quezon City on Saturday, October 24, for alleged cyber libel. He was served an arrest warrant issued by Branch 10 of Davao City’s Regional Trial Court.
The 72-year-old is the author behind Kill, Kill, Kill: Extrajudicial Killings in the Philippines, which documents former president Rodrigo Duterte’s deadly war on drugs.

blocks.caption: Veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. arrested for alleged cyber libel

blocks.text: “This is a sad day for journalism in the Philippines,” De Leon said in an ambush interview on the same day of Lustre’s arrest, as seen in a video by Bilyonaryo News Channel.
“Nararamdaman na naman natin ‘yung pag-atake sa mga members ng media. This is reminiscent of the Duterte administration na nanggaling sa Davao City again ‘yung complainant.”
(We are again witnessing the attacks on members of the media. This is reminiscent of the Duterte administration, where the complainant is from Davao City.)
Lustre had earlier mentioned that he did not know who the complainant was, and was also unaware that there was a complaint being lodged against him.

The Presidential Task Force on Media Security (PTFOMS), meanwhile, expressed support for Lustre’s welfare, access to legal counsel, communication with his family, and medical assistance, given that he is a senior citizen.

“We urge the prompt handling of any application for bail in accordance with applicable rules, with due consideration for his age and welfare. His reported lack of prior knowledge of the complaint also warrants clarification through the appropriate legal processes,” PTFOMS said in its statement.

With Lustre’s arrest coming just a day after Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo “Pulong” Duterte filed a cyber libel complaint against several GMA Network journalists, PTFOMS also stressed that “laws protecting reputation must never be used to harass journalists, suppress legitimate criticism, or obstruct the public’s access to information.”
“The threat of arrest, prolonged litigation, and substantial legal expenses can discourage journalists from pursuing important stories even before a complaint is resolved,” it said.
It also said that it will coordinate with De Leon and the concerned authorities to gather official information on Lustre’s arrest. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: The children were subsequently rescued from the water, police say.

blocks.text: In a statement, posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said: "According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.

"Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.

articles.title: Seven missing after multi-storey building collapses in Kenya's capital
articles.summary: Rescue efforts are under way to find people trapped under the block, which was still under construction when it buckled.

blocks.text: A search and rescue effort is under way to find seven people feared trapped under rubble after a building collapsed in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi.
Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets.

Dozens of builders had been working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but managed to emerge largely unscathed. Those missing were thought to have been in shops that had opened at the base of the building.
The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya.

The block was under construction when it collapsed on Friday afternoon, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors.

Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had been able to get out unharmed, while the other had suffered injuries that were not life-threatening.

Images from the scene, in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, show the concrete floors of the building piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to get to those believed to have been stuck underneath.

articles.title: British woman dies trying to save sons on Bahamas snorkelling trip
articles.summary:
The 36-year-old died after two boys reportedly swept away by strong current near Bimini, police say

A British woman has died in the Bahamas while trying to rescue her two sons after a…

blocks.text: A British woman has died in the Bahamas while trying to rescue her two sons after a current swept them away as they were snorkelling.
The Royal Bahamas police force said it had launched an investigation after the death of a 36-year-old woman on Tuesday.
The force said they believed she was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island of Bimini when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
The police said that in an attempt to rescue her boys, “the woman was also swept away”. The children were later rescued from the water.
The Foreign Office said it was in contact with the woman’s family and was providing support.
Bimini is a small island between the largest landmass in the Bahamas, Andros, and Miami in the US. It is the closest point in the Bahamas to the US mainland.
The island is best known for once being home to Ernest Hemingway and is also home to a world-leading shark research centre.

In a statementposted on social media, the Royal Bahamas police force said: “According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini ferry dock.

“Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.
“Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
“In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.
“She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered. Foul play is not suspected at this time.”
An autopsy would be carried out to help determine the exact cause of death, the statement said.
A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
“We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family.”

articles.title: Kim Jong-un crosses over newly opened bridge into China
articles.summary:
Visit by train over New Yalu River Bridge marks North Korean leader’s first known trip abroad in more than a year

Kim Jong-un has travelled to China over a newly opened bridge marking the…

blocks.text: Kim Jong-un has travelled to China over a newly opened bridge marking the North Korean leader’s first known trip abroad in more than a year, South Korean officials have said.

A government source told the Yonhap news agency on Saturday that Kim had arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong, in Liaoning province, after taking a train from Pyongyang to Sinuiju and crossing the New Yalu River Bridge.
Yonhap also reported that the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, had travelled to the city. Kim’s trip was not announced in advance and had not been confirmed by Pyongyang or Beijing by Saturday evening.
China will mark the anniversary on Sunday of its entry into the 1950-53 Korean war on the North’s side.

Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum devoted to China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted.
Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.

The 3km bridge opened in mid-October, 12 years after China finished building it, after being held up by delays on the North Korean side. In early September, North Korea and Russia opened the first road bridge across their own short border leaving Pyongyang newly linked by road to its main backers.

blocks.caption: The New Yalu River Bridge seen from the Chinese border city of Dandong, in Liaoning province. Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters

blocks.text: The trip is Kim’s sixth visit to China and his first since September 2025, when he attended a military parade in Beijing alongside the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Xi visited Pyongyang in June, his first trip there in seven years.

Relations with South Korea, meanwhile, have deteriorated. Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has issued about 10 statements criticising Seoul since late September, a frequency South Korea’s unification ministry has called unusual, and has also announced plans to resume loudspeaker broadcasts at the border within days.
Xi will host the Apec summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, which has fuelled speculation about a meeting between Kim and Donald Trump.
Reuters reported on Friday, however, that US and South Korean officials see little chance of Kim meeting the US president this year.

articles.title: Ukraine says Starlink and Starshield operating at 400 kilometers per hour after week of throttling
articles.summary: 'Monitoring systems had previously recorded disruptions to the Starlink/Starshield service. The speed metrics have now returned to normal,' the ministry says

blocks.text: STARLINK IN UKRAINE. An artilleryman of the Special Rifle Police Battalion of Zaporizhzhia region sets up Starlink satellite internet system, at a position, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, near the frontline in Donetsk region, Ukraine, October 16, 2026.
'Monitoring systems had previously recorded disruptions to the Starlink/Starshield service. The speed metrics have now returned to normal,' the ministry says

KYIV, Ukraine – The Starlink satellite communications system and its military version Starshield are operating again at speeds over 400 km per hour, Kyiv’s defense minister said on Saturday, October 24, after over a week of service restrictions that slowed connections and disrupted military operations.

“The Ministry of Defense’s monitoring systems are recording a return to normal speed for Starlink/Starshield. We are recording a speed of over 400 km/h. The connection is stable,” Evhenii Khmara told reporters.
The Ukrainian military does not disclose the systems’ maximum operating speeds, and the defense ministry did not say whether service had been fully restored.
“Monitoring systems had previously recorded disruptions to the Starlink/Starshield service. The speed metrics have now returned to normal,” the ministry said.

The restrictions, first reported on October 14, undermined Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones and disrupted frontline communications, Ukrainian officials said. Sources said connection speeds had been reduced to about 160 kph or less.

Ukraine’s problems with SpaceX-owned Starlink came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow while pressing Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries.

Neither SpaceX boss Elon Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.
Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House.
Trump said on Friday that if problems with access to Starlink communications systems in Ukraine persisted, he would “get it straightened out,” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Dónal Lunny, ‘colossus of Irish music’, dies aged 79
articles.summary:
Founding member of Planxty, Lunny went on to play for bands such as Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and Coolfin

The Irish traditional musician Dónal Lunny has died at the age of 79 from…

blocks.text: The Irish traditional musician Dónal Lunny has died at the age of 79 from cancer.

Lunny rose to prominence in the band Rakes of Kildare alongside Christy Moore and his brother Frank. He went on to play in bands such as Planxty, Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and Coolfin among others and toured the world.
A post on his Facebook page confirmed that Lunny died in St James’s hospital in Dublin on Friday morning.

“We are heartbroken to confirm that our beloved Dónal passed away peacefully this morning in Dublin following a short stay in St James’s hospital,” the post said. “Thank you for helping us to remember and celebrate his immense contribution to music, to culture and to so many people’s lives all over the world.”

blocks.caption: Catherine Connolly said Lunny was ‘central to so many of the most influential moments of the last 60 years of Irish music’. Photograph: Niall Carson/PA

blocks.text: The Irish president, Catherine Connolly, expressed her “deepest condolences to the family, friends and many musical collaborators of Dónal Lunny”.

In a statement, she said: “Dónal was one of Ireland’s greatest musical figures, a wonderfully talented musician and producer who was central to so many of the most influential moments of the last 60 years of Irish music.

“Dónal will be particularly remembered for his long partnerships with fellow musicians such as Christy Moore and Andy Irvine and for the innovative music he has left behind both as a musician in groups including Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts and also as a renowned producer.

“This rich musical legacy, including his central role in the introduction of the bouzouki into Irish music, was appropriately recognised by his fellow artists in Dónal’s membership of Aosdána, as well as the well-deserved recognition which he received in being awarded a lifetime achievement award at the 2025 RTÉ Radio 1 Irish folk awards.
“Beyond his music, Dónal will be remembered for his warmth and the strong connection which he had with audiences all over Ireland and beyond. He will be deeply missed.”
The post ended in Irish, saying his likes will not be seen again: “Ní bheidh a leithéid arís ann.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: The Irish folk group Planxty in London in January 1973. From left: Andy Irvine, Liam O’Flynn, Dónal Lunny and Christy Moore.  Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty

blocks.text: Lunny was born in Tullamore, County Offaly, and was a multi-instrumentalist but was best known for his mastery of the bouzouki. He was a talented melody writer and considered central to the revival of traditional music as he produced 17 albums under his record label Mulligan Records.

Paying tribute to the folk musician, the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he was “deeply saddened” to hear of his passing. “A colossus of Irish music, as a performer, songwriter and producer,” he wrote in a post on social media.
“Uniquely gifted, Dónal carried traditional and folk music to new audiences through Planxty and his many other endeavours.”

Sinn Féin’s president, Mary Lou McDonald, also paid tribute online, saying: “Deeply saddened to hear of the passing of Dónal Lunny. A giant of Irish traditional music, Dónal helped shape the sound of Irish music for generations, bringing our rich musical heritage to audiences at home and around the world. His contribution to Irish music and culture will never be forgotten.
“Ar dheis Dé go raibh a anam [may his soul rest in peace].”

articles.title: DA seeks return of 40% tariff on imported pork, two-month import holiday
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) said Saturday it is seeking the return of a 40% tariff on imported pork and a two-month import holiday to give local hog raisers time to recover from falling…

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 4:32pm

The Department of Agriculture (DA) said Saturday it is seeking the return of a 40% tariff on imported pork and a two-month import holiday to give local hog raisers time to recover from falling farmgate prices.

Hog traders earlier this week held a three-day "pig holiday," temporarily suspending their sale of pork. They urged the government to impose higher tariffs on pork imports, cancel pork import permits, and find a solution to stop the smuggling of foreign meat products.

"A two-month import holiday could temporarily reduce foreign supply and give local producers an opportunity to sell their hogs. Higher tariffs could also make imported pork more expensive," the DA said.
"However, the extent of any benefit would depend on implementation, market demand and the availability of domestic supply," it added.

Reading a message from Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr., DA Undersecretary Asis Perez assured hog raisers that the agency is committed to protecting the local industry from what it called unfair import competition.
Perez said the Agriculture Department has been pushing for tariff increases well before the hog traders' protest, rejecting any impression that "the proposals were prompted solely by the protest."

"The DA filed a petition concerning pork jowl imports in August and another in September seeking to raise pork tariffs to 40%... The agency has since attended two hearings, although the approval process remains ongoing," the agency said.
It added that the proposed measures remain under review and require approval from other government entities, including the Tariff Commission.

The Agriculture Department said it is also preparing to launch an investigation under the General Safeguards framework, which could allow legal restrictions on pork imports if they are found to be harming domestic producers.
"The DA's message was clear: it is backing local producers. Whether that support translates into timely relief now rests on the next steps in the approval process," the DA said.
According to the Pork Producers Federation of the Philippines, the industry is losing P350 million a day or P7,000 per pig head because of frozen pork coming from abroad. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Hundreds of protests expected across France, with shops, businesses and tourist sites closed – Europe live
articles.summary:
France will deploy 70,000 officers around the country. Protests are also expected in Italy, Spain, Austria, Portugal, Albania and Ireland

All through the night in neighbourhoods in…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 15m agoOpening summary

blocks.caption: Angelique Chrisafis

blocks.text: Angelique Chrisafis

blocks.caption: A jogger runs past a Societe Generale bank branch with its storefronts protected by wooden panels on the Champs-Elysees avenue in Paris ahead of nationwide protests onOctober 24, 2026.  Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

blocks.text: All through the night in neighbourhoods in the centre and east of Paris, the sound of sawing, drilling and hammering rang out as wooden boards were hastily secured into place to cover windows and shop-fronts.
Businesses being boarded up included opticians, supermarkets and pharmacies as well as trainers and handbag stores.
Hundreds of shops were smashed and looted over two nights last weekend in Paris, and thousands more in cities across France, including Marseille and Bordeaux.
At a public meeting at Paris city hall this week, some shop-owners had cried as they spoke of their fears of businesses being smashed and looted again this weekend.

“I’m afraid there isn’t enough wooden board left to protect shops and the demand is making it so expensive to board up shops,” one optician near Châtelet in the city centre said. “We’ll close up and take all our stock of glasses out of the shop.”

blocks.caption: Workers install wooden panels to protect the windows of the gaming club Partouche Pasino Club in Paris  Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

blocks.text: Opening summary
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of events in Europe – we will be closely following protests across the continent today.

In France, hundreds of thousands are expected at rallies across the country, with high school students, unionists, “yellow vest” demonstrators and others turning out for a fourth weekend of protests demanding more government funding for schools and measures to help with housing and the cost of living.

Desperate to avoid the looting and property damage seen on the fringes of some protests last weekend, French authorities have ramped up restrictions on where protesters can march and which groups are “authorised” to do so. They’ve increased policing 20%, mobilising 70,000 police officers and soldiers to the streets, including both elite units and trainee officers.
Many of Paris’s metro stations and major museums and tourist sites are shut today, while across the country, shops and businesses have been urged to close their doors.

Community tensions are also high following a deadly shooting on Friday west of Paris where the gunman targeted non-white people, killing one person and injuring five others including a child. The French president called it a “racist terrorist attack”.

Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen’s anti-immigration party is also due to hold its national conference in the central city of Orléans. The far-right National Rally’s meeting is expected to draw up to 30,000 counter-demonstrators.
Protests are also being held in Italy, Spain, Austria, Portugal, Albania and Ireland today.
Stay with us for all the developments.

articles.title: NCDA: 2.9 million legitimate PWD IDs issued, outnumbered by fakes
articles.summary: The National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA) said Saturday it has already issued up to 2.9 million legitimate identification cards for persons with disability (PWD), but the number is dwarfed by…

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 4:06pm

The National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA) said Saturday it has already issued up to 2.9 million legitimate identification cards for persons with disability (PWD), but the number is dwarfed by fake ones currently in circulation.
In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB, NCDA spokesperson Walton Jason Alava said the issuance of fake PWD cards has been a pervasive issue, which already cost the government billions in lost revenues.
"Based sa aming data, nasa mga around 2.8… 2.9 million na po, 'yung mga persons with disabilities na nabigyan ng mga identification cards," Alava said.
(Based on our data, around 2.8… 2.9 million persons with disabilities were given identification cards.)
"Nasa mga 8.5 to 9 million in circulation na persons with disability identification cards," he added, citing information reported in a Senate hearing in 2024.
(Around 8.5 to 9 million persons with disability identification cards are in circulation.)
Asked if this discrepancy meant to an estimated 6.5 million fake PWD IDs, Alava said, "yes."
The Department of Justice previously raised an alarm over the estimated 6 million fake PWD ID cards, vowing to go after fraudulent holders.
According to Alava, their basis for the number of PWDs in the country is solely based off the number of PWD cards they have issued.
Citing data from the World Health Organization, however, Alava said that 15 to 16% of a population is likely to be disabled. A number of PWDs in the Philippines are likely unrecorded, he said.

"Some of the persons with disabilities, especially doon sa mga categories natin sa non-apparent, yung mga hindi nakikita…hindi sila kumukuha ng IDs kaya hindi sila nasama sa ating talaan," Alava said.
(Some of the persons with disabilities, especially in the non-apparent categories, those who could not be seen… they are not getting IDs so they are not included in the list.)
In a 2024 hearing of the Senate ways and means committee, Senator Sherwin Gatchalian said the government has lost some P88.2 billion in taxes because of fake PWD IDs. — VDV, GMA News
