articles.title: This Bicolano theater group brings grassroots stories — and disaster relief — to communities
articles.summary: Veteran actor Julie DM Vega of Albay theater group Sining Banwa says it’s time for local governments to invest in their artists and help ‘bring art directly to the masses’

blocks.text: SINING BANWA. Cast members perform in ‘Higit sa Pag-ibig: The Musical,’ one of the multi-arts group’s most successful productions.
CONTRIBUTED PHOTO/Zachary Oliver Gonzales.
Veteran actor Julie DM Vega of Albay theater group Sining Banwa says it’s time for local governments to invest in their artists and help ‘bring art directly to the masses’

items: Sining Banwa (SB) is a community theater collective in Albay, Philippines, founded in 2011 to support local artists and promote Bicol culture through grassroots theater and community engagement.
The organization has provided art relief programs to calamity-stricken communities, particularly after Super Typhoon Rolly in 2020, helping with recovery efforts and trauma processing through art.
SB aims to integrate theater into the educational system in Bicol, advocating for creative spaces for artists and emphasizing the importance of local government support for the arts.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

ALBAY, Philippines – Sining Banwa (SB) began in 2011 as a free space for budding Albay artists to create art and stage progressive productions outside the classroom. Since then, this homegrown collective has evolved into a powerhouse of Bicol culture — using performance not just to entertain, but to bring communities together.

Veteran theater artist Julie DM Vega emphasizes that SB’s soul is rooted in original, grassroots theater that were breathed to life through deep community immersion. For 15 years, the troupe has unearthed and amplified raw, multi-cultural stories that capture the true pulse, pain, and resilience of the region. (READ: 8 plays, 1 reality: Bicol theater unpacks hard-hitting local issues)

“SB is a home for the very communities whose lives we put on stage,” said Vega. “It gives artists the space to sharpen their craft while anchoring every performance to the real, urgent lives of the people they serve.”

Built entirely from the ground up, Sining Banwa was powered by volunteer actors and a crew who personally bankrolled their early productions. In return, some communities they helped gave them harvested rice, sweet potatoes, and fresh vegetables to keep the troupe fed and afloat.

“In those early years, our volunteer members kept the lights on,” recalled Vega. “When we brought our plays to the communities and stood with them in their struggles, strong networks were forged. Grateful locals would send us crops which sustained us through our toughest moments.”

blocks.caption: VLF BIKOL. Julie DM Vega performs in the 2026 Virgin Labfest Bikol, portraying a drag artist-activist who is the child of a desaparecido. Photo by Reinnard Balonzo/Rappler

blocks.text: Remembering SB’s leanest years, Vega highlighted the sheer grit that kept them moving forward when funding was nonexistent.

“We once reached a point where no one had money for a decent meal,” Vega added. “We gathered wild leaves we weren’t even sure were edible just to have something to go with our rice. It’s funny to look back on now, but those extreme sacrifices remind us of our roots and keep us deeply motivated.”

Extending its impact beyond performance art, Sining Banwa launched programs such as Pagtugdon, a Bicolano term for a bird landing or perching, symbolizing the collective’s deep rootedness in the communities it serves.
“By our fifth year, we reflected on our core identity as a community theater,” Vega explained. “We knew we had a responsibility to step up, especially during times of crisis.”

blocks.caption: ART HEALING. Sining Banwa helped numerous calamity-stricken communities across Bicol through its art relief programs following Super Typhoon Rolly in 2020. Photo by Sining Banwa

blocks.text: In 2016, the theater company started providing art relief programs for calamity-stricken communities, particularly as Bicol is regularly battered by storms. In 2020, when Super Typhoon Rolly (international name: Goni) left Bicol with at least 20 people dead and almost P1.1 billion in agricultural damage, SB was among the first groups to respond amid government delays.

“When Rolly hit, lahar heavily impacted our partner community in Busay, Daraga,” Vega said. “The actors and crew were on their feet to save whatever we could salvage from houses that were almost covered in lahar.”

blocks.caption: REBUILDING COMMUNITIES. Alongside creative disaster response initiatives, Sining Banwa members collected supplies and provided manual labor to rebuild storm-damaged homes in Bicol in 2020.  Photo by Sining Banwa

blocks.text: When the group launched a donation drive to help more people, contributions unexpectedly surged to over P400,000 in cash donations, allowing the project to expand to nearby communities, neighboring towns, and adjacent provinces. The group also assisted in relief operations in Tabaco City and Catanduanes province.

“After providing relief goods and hot meals in Busay, we also helped in some areas of Tabaco City and gave victims construction materials to rebuild their homes. It continued until we reached Catanduanes, where we helped a community that couldn’t be reached immediately by other relief groups due to its geographically isolated location,” she added.

blocks.caption: GRASSROOTS RELIEF. Walking for more than half an hour through difficult terrain, Sining Banwa members brought assistance to isolated communities cut off from immediate government aid. Photo by Sining Banwa

blocks.text: After trekking for nearly an hour on foot to reach their target communities, the volunteers worked with residents to help process trauma through art and community-building (READ: Bicol artists bring art relief to traumatized Kristine survivors).

“We weren’t there to pretend or act as if we would save them from what they experienced, so we partnered with them to help them realize their own strength despite going through so much. While the residents were packing relief goods, we had time to conduct art relief programs for children — something the government rarely provides after disasters,” Vega pointed out.

Beyond typhoon recovery, SB also mounted several productions in 2025 to help a village engulfed by fire in Pilar, Sorsogon. That same year, all proceeds from their PedXing: Collab series were donated to disaster victims in the town of Tiwi in Albay (READ: Higit sa Pag-ibig: The Musical’ reveals the pain of Bicol’s flooded, red-tagged communities).

blocks.caption: GIVING LIGHT. As Christmas approached in the aftermath of Super Typhoon Rolly, Sining Banwa distributed lamps to disaster-stricken families.  Photo by Sining Banwa

blocks.text: Fresh off acclaimed shows and expanding productions, Sining Banwa is setting its sights on a bolder ambition: forging a unified regional stage by embedding theater and community arts directly into the Bicolano educational system (READ: Why Bicol theater revived a century-old epic).

“Our vision is to see theater fully woven into the academic curriculum, and brick by brick, that dream is taking shape,” Vega proudly told Rappler. “Our school networks have rallied behind us — bringing their students to our plays and opening their gates for us to perform. Theater is no longer just an extracurricular; it is becoming a vital engine for learning.”

blocks.caption: ELECTION EDUCATION. Sining Banwa actors stage a play about elections during the 2025 Pista nin Teatrong Bikolnon as part of their voter education drive. Photo by Zachary Oliver Gonzales

blocks.text: Looking back on SB’s journey, Vega envisions a future where local theater doesn’t just survive, but thrives. She urged local leaders and communities to address the chronic shortage of creative spaces for grassroots artists.

“What we are truly fighting for is the creative freedom and physical space to hone our craft,” she emphasized. “It is high time that local governments and communities invest in their artists, empowering us to bring art directly to the masses.”

Reaffirming their ties to the grassroots communities that have always been their lifeline, SB vows to continue staging fierce, truth-telling stories that inspire a stronger, more resilient Bicol. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Can millions of people live on the moon? These scientists say yes — but not for very long
articles.summary: Billionaires like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos are claiming that we can expect big cities with millions of people on the moon, but a new study found that that may not be possible, so don’t start packing…

image.caption: This artist’s rendering depicts astronauts, habitats, rovers, power systems and cargo operations supporting sustained human activities at NASA's Moon Base near the lunar South Pole. A recent study found that while a small population of humans can live on the moon, a large city of one million people

blocks.text: Science·New

Billionaires like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos are claiming that we can expect big cities with millions of people on the moon, but a new study found that that may not be possible, so don’t start packing just yet.
Power and water are the main resources needed to live on the moon
Humans have long dreamed about reaching out and exploring space. Most science fiction, more often than not, portrays cities on the dusty lunar surface and Mars.
And if you listen to some billionaires like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, cities on the moon are coming soon.
In fact, in February, SpaceX CEO Musk posted on social media that the company was shifting its focus away from settling on Mars — something Musk has been passionate about for the past decade.

“For those unaware, SpaceX has already shifted focus to building a self-growing city on the moon, as we can potentially achieve that in less than 10 years, whereas Mars would take 20+ years,” he wrote.

For those unaware, SpaceX has already shifted focus to building a self-growing city on the Moon, as we can potentially achieve that in less than 10 years, whereas Mars would take 20+ years. The mission of SpaceX remains the same: extend consciousness and life as we know it to the stars. It is only possible to travel to Mars when the planets align every 26 months (six month trip time), whereas we can launch to the Moon every 10 days (2 day trip time). This means we can iterate much faster to complete a Moon city than a Mars city. That said, SpaceX will also strive to build a Mars city and begin doing so in about 5 to 7 years, but the overriding priority is securing the future of civilization and the Moon is faster.—elonmusk

This statement — and those of Blue Origin CEO Bezos, who has claimed “millions of people” will be living in space by 2045 — intrigued Martin Elvis, senior astrophysicist at Harvard University’s Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory.
He, along with astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell, honorary professor at the Durham University Space Research Centre in England, decided to take a look at the numbers.
But their findings, it turns out, aren't great for a lunar civilization, so don’t start packing just yet.
In their paper, published in the journal Frontiers in Space Technologies, the pair decided to examine power and water needed to sustain humans on the moon.
When it comes to power, they found that solar and nuclear would be enough to sustain one million people on the lunar surface.
But then there's water.
It may be surprising to some, but there is water on the moon. It’s believed that most of it is contained in permanently shadowed regions (PSR), areas at the poles that never see sunlight.
But in this study, they found that there’s not enough on the moon to sustain a large human presence on the lunar surface.
NASA shares plans for moon base

“Our work shows that, yeah, if you want to have an Antarctic base on the moon for the next few hundred years, no problem. If you want to have a small town, that's doable. If you want to cover the face of the moon with cities, like in the best science fiction, then you have to find a way to get the water there, because it's not there right now,” McDowell said.

Assuming that there is roughly one billion tonnes of water on the moon, which is in line with current estimates, they found that a civilization of one million people would only be able to live on the moon for roughly 100 years. And that’s only if we can recycle 98 per cent of the water, which is what is done on the International Space Station.
'A small lake'
Elvis said that while one billion tonnes of water sounds like a lot, you have to put it in perspective.

“If you had a huge aquarium the size of Central Park in Manhattan, you could fill it up to where the Statue of Liberty was just underwater and that's the amount of water you've got. So it's huge in one way, but … it's a small lake. And a small lake is not going to supply a big city for very long.”
That’s not to say that humans can’t ever live on the moon. If it were a town of 10,000, they found that would be sustainable for centuries.
However, that's assuming that the one billion tonnes of water is an accurate estimate.
"Very likely a billion is way overestimating. It's probably 20 or 30 times too big," Elvis said.
How Artemis II is setting up the next stage of space exploration
He also said that it's unlikely that we'd be able to recover all the water that's available. Instead, it would be more like one-third to half of what is present.
"So my best guess is the real amount of water available that we can be fairly confident about is one per cent of what we said before. So instead of 100 years, it's one year."
And there's one other thing: We don't know in what form that water exists. And we need to figure that out.

items: We’ve already been to the moon, so why are we going again?
NASA has set its sights on a moon base. Here's how Canada can play an important role

blocks.text: "It's one thing to detect it from satellites, but ... there are uncertainties in those measurements," said Gordon Osinski, a professor in planetary geology at Western University in London, Ont.

"I think it is there, but let's go and ground-truth that and confirm it. And then there's the bigger unknowns of what form it's in…. Is it more like the permafrost up in the Arctic, where it's basically soil with, you know, sub-millimetre size ice crystals, which are hard to get out of?"
While this may sound like pessimistic news for humanity's plans to explore the cosmos, McDowell said it's best to know what you're dealing with.
"The truth is never negative," he said. "What's negative is to actually go and try and do something that isn't going to work."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Nicole covers all things science for CBC News. As an amateur astronomer, Nicole can be found looking up at the night sky appreciating the marvels of our universe. She is the editor of the Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada and the author of several books. In 2021, she won the Kavli Science Journalism Award from the American Association for the Advancement of Science for a Quirks and Quarks audio special on the history and future of Black people in science. You can send her story ideas at nicole.mortillaro@cbc.ca.

articles.title: 82 days later, no repairs started on washed-out road dividing small Quebec town
articles.summary: Residents in L’Ascension, Que., are still waiting on repairs after August flooding washed away part of their main road. The municipality's mayor blames the delay for repairs on the bureaucracy of…

image.caption: L'Ascension Mayor Jacques Allard points to white spray paint monitoring the ongoing erosion of Principale Street. (Andie Bennett/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal

Residents in L’Ascension, Que., are still waiting on repairs after August flooding washed away part of their main road. The municipality's mayor blames the delay for repairs on the bureaucracy of different levels of government.
L’Ascension, Que., mayor blames delays on bureaucracy of different levels of government
Mayor Jacques Allard stands in front of the 70-foot gap that now divides his town of L’Ascension.
Spray painted white lines on the ground track the ongoing erosion that continues with every rainfall.
It's been 82 days since heavy rain washed away parts of Principale Street and de L’Ascension Road that connects the small municipality to the city of Rivière-Rouge on Aug. 3.
The mayor says on its end, L’Ascension is ready to start work to repair the road.

They have their contractor, the engineer plans are in place and the replacement culvert — twice the diameter of the previous one — is sitting idly by the protective fencing that surrounds the giant crater.
So what's the delay?

items: Situation in L'Ascension, Que., 'stable' after municipality declares state of emergency

blocks.text: The municipality says it's waiting for the green light from the Quebec government to begin the repair, which their contractor expects to take five weeks and cost roughly $3 million.
A report of the required work also had to be sent to Fisheries and Oceans Canada for approval — a report that took 70 days to be approved and was then sent to the government.
The washout is directly in front of the fire hall, impacting emergency services. (Andie Bennett/CBC)
L’Ascension is now awaiting confirmation that they will receive the subsidy from the program that provides financial support to municipalities affected by natural disasters.
Allard says the bureaucracy slowing down this work is unacceptable.
“Normally they have a protocol to fast track. Now it is a very slow track," he said.
300 people cut off
The crater left behind by the rushing water that ripped up sections of asphalt and collapsed culverts is 45 feet deep and 70 feet wide.
Thirty per cent of the small population lives on the other side of the gap, meaning around 300 people are cut off from their community.
Nicolas Côté owns a small grocery store in town. He says business is already down 15 per cent compared to last year due to its inaccessibility.
Residents on the other side of the gap must either take their business to the nearby town of Rivière-Rouge or make a detour of more than an hour to reach their local grocery store.
The gap is 45 feet deep and 70 feet wide and sits where the road used to connect in L’Ascension. (Andie Bennett/CBC)
Côté says when you live in a small town where the population is just shy of 1,000 people, it's more like a family.
He says many people have sent him messages saying they hope the repairs happen soon so they will see him again and be able to shop at their local store.
“Maybe it's tough to fix, but to wait so much time … and we still don't know what will happen," Côté said.
The local grocery store in L’Ascension has already seen a 15 per cent drop in business compared to last year due to the lack of access for residents. (Andie Bennett/CBC)
With winter coming, Allard says there is a lot of anxiety within the community. He is also concerned about the financial impact if the repairs are not completed as soon as possible.

“On the other side, it takes five minutes to get here. Now it's 50 minutes. How will we pay to remove the snow in the winter? The trucks will have to make this detour. We will have a big expense for fuel," he said.

CBC News reached out to the Domestic Security Ministry for comment. It said it is currently reviewing the file and will confirm, as soon as possible, whether the work is eligible for financial assistance.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Andie Bennett is a journalist covering Quebec's Laurentians and Lanaudière regions. Andie lives in Morin-Heights, Que., and has an office space in Piedmont. She can be reached at andie.bennett@cbc.ca

articles.title: Why a new round in the U.S.-Iran conflict could be the most devastating yet
articles.summary: As the U.S. midterm elections approach, intelligence analysts warn that the United States and Israel are preparing for a devastating third round of direct military conflict with Iran. Experts caution…

image.caption: Iranian missiles are displayed next to a banner with a picture of Iranain Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, on a street in Tehran on Sept. 27. (Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency via REUTERS)

blocks.text: The warning signs are flashing red with indications that once the ballots are counted in the U.S. midterm elections, the United States and Israel will relaunch their war with Iran.
The next round of attacks could be more devastating than the first, warn analysts.

"A renewed war seems almost inevitable," said Danny Citrinowicz, an Israeli Middle East and Iran analyst whose earlier warnings and cautions about the risks of a direct conflict with Iran were largely borne out by events.

Citrinowicz, who worked for Israel's military as an intelligence official for more than two decades, had initially warned that any U.S. and Israeli attack on the Islamic regime would not likely lead to regime change but would instead end up engulfing the entire region in a wider conflict — an assessment that proved true.
In an interview with CBC News, he said that assessment still holds.
"The problem is there is no silver bullet solution to the impasse we are now at in the Persian Gulf and in front of Trump he has only bad and worse options."

Under U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, their countries broke with decades of restraint and shadow warfare and launched two distinct wars with Iran over the past 18 months.
Iranian women look at a building, which was damaged in a U.S. and Israeli strike in March, in Tehran on Aug. 22. (Reuters)
The first in June 2025 began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, lasted 12 days and ended with a fragile ceasefire.

The conflict roared back to life in February of this year following a massive U.S. military buildup in the region. It began with Israel's strikes against Iran's senior leadership, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Worst round yet
Citrinowicz, who's with Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, said a third round of war could be the worst yet, based on what Iranian officials are telegraphing.

"They will attack the energy facilities in the Gulf. But more than that, they will cause significant damage to civilian infrastructure, communications, as well as cutting off the internet lines going under [the] Hormuz Strait," he said.
He said there is even a possibility that Iran could push some of its massive land army into the fight with limited assaults against Gulf countries that house U.S. bases, such as Kuwait and Bahrain.
"We'll see a regional war with Iran investing a lot in attacking the U.S. presence in the region to cause maximum economical damage to the U.S. international economy."

Smoke rises from a burning vessel, following what the U.S. Central Command said was a strike on an Iranian-affiliated dhow, at a location given as the Gulf of Oman, in this still image taken from a video released on Oct. 14. (U.S. Central Command/Reuters)
Midterm dynamics

While both sides have largely avoided fresh strikes against each other's bases or territory since the summer truce collapsed, the conflict remains active. The U.S. imposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports and Iran has continued to target commercial shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, driving up global energy costs.

Posting on Truth Social Thursday, Trump blamed Iran for trying to artificially drive up oil prices ahead of the midterms on Nov. 3, elections that many pollsters believe will see Trump's Republicans lose control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate as well.
"They are even making up fake hits, mines and everything else," said Trump, implying that Iran is exaggerating the extent of the damage it's causing.

A report published this week by the Washington, D.C.,-based Critical Threats Project alongside the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) also suggested Iran is trying to use strikes on shipping to weaken Trump's position heading into the elections.

"The increase in Iranian attacks on vessels is part of the ongoing Iranian campaign to pressure the United States to meet Iranian demands, including control over the Strait, by driving up global prices," the report said.
People walk on the beach, with vessels in the Strait of Hormuz visible near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, on Oct. 13. (Razieh Poudat West Asia News Agency/Reuters)
Iran's demands

Iran's government wants relief from punishing sanctions, reparations for the damage caused by earlier U.S.-Israel strikes, the release of billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets and the right to keep its supplies of enriched uranium.
Mediators with Pakistan and Qatar have spent weeks trying to push diplomatic solutions to get the two sides talking again, but to no avail.
For both Netanyahu and Trump, the war with Iran remains unfinished business.

items: Iran says 7 ships have been struck in Strait of Hormuz, Saudis intercept drones in airspace
Iran's president says country won't surrender after Trump threat to 'annihilate' Islamic republic

blocks.text: The Islamic regime not only remains in power, but its leadership has also proven remarkably adept at adapting to both the military strikes and the economic blockade imposed by the West.

"The war in some respects has probably persuaded Iran's leadership to double down on their commitment to the revolutionary ideology that has really forged this regime," said Suzanne Maloney, a vice-president and director of the foreign policy program at the Washington, D.C.,-based Brookings Institution.
Like Citroniwicz, she said if war resumes, Trump won't be able to easily contain it.
"The retaliation as we've seen will come not just from Iran, but from its proxies and partners in the region," she said, referring to the Houthi militias in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
Iran's goal won't just be to hit back at U.S. military targets but also soft economic targets, such as airports, that could undermine Gulf countries for years to come, she said.
How the Houthi-Saudi Arabia conflict plays into broader Middle East war
Maloney and Karim Sadjadpour, a prominent Iran expert with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, were speaking on an online Carnegie panel about the future of the war in Iran.
"I genuinely don't think that President Trump has a clear idea in his head what he's trying to achieve," said Sadjadpour.
"I don't see any possibility of what Trump is looking for — which is like a knockout punch, a military strike — which will essentially force the Iranians into a compromise or capitulation."
Nuclear timeline?
Trump claimed his justification for the initial attacks on Iran was to ensure the country doesn't get a nuclear weapon.

At the time, while Iran possessed enough enriched uranium to theoretically pursue a weapon, many independent experts and U.S. intelligence sources believed it was still likely months away from doing so — and perhaps more importantly, that the regime's supreme leader had not yet made the definitive political decision to cross the nuclear threshold.
Since those initial June 2025 strikes, the human cost of the war has been severe.
Western NGOs claim the death toll in Iran is well over 7,000, including civilians and government figures who have been killed in the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes.
Lebanon has also suffered an especially heavy toll, with local media reporting more than 4,000 fatalities.
Twenty-one U.S. service members were killed, mostly by Iranian strikes on U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf, while more than 70 Israelis have died.
People drive near a billboard depicting U.S. President Donald Trump on a building in Tehran on Sept. 16. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA/Reuters)
There have also been deaths throughout the Gulf countries, including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, as well as in Iraq and Yemen.
The New York Times and other U.S. media are reporting the Pentagon is working on a new battle plan for the possible next round of attacks — but whether Trump will ultimately authorize it is unknown.
'Finishing the job'
Israel's leadership, on the other hand, has made no secret of its push to restart the conflict, with Netanyahu explicitly stating his desire to bring down the Iran regime by "finishing the job."
Netanyahu faces Israeli voters in the coming days, and whether he hangs onto his job could end up in a photo finish.

items: Netanyahu faces fresh allegations he ignored warnings about Oct. 7 — right before an election

blocks.text: Relaunching the war with Iran could offer him a tactical way to stay in power; even if his party loses seats, a widening security crisis could lead to the creation of an emergency unity government with members of the opposition, said Citrinowicz.

"The real risk is that Netanyahu will involve his political considerations together with some other operational development in Iran that he is going to not necessarily invent, but probably [inflate]," he said.
A shopkeeper works at his shop in a local market in Tehran on Sept. 26. (Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency/Reuters)
"And this combination will lead to an unnecessary attack against Iran."
Sadjadpour from the Carnegie panel said there is no obvious military way out of the impasse and says Trump's maximalist goals have closed down diplomatic options as well.

"I believe there's a pretty clear formula under which it [Iran's government] compromises," said Sadjadpour. "It's when it faces what I would describe as existential economic pressure, coupled with a clear, limited diplomatic exit.
"If you're asking them to change their identity, that's not going to succeed."

articles.title: Nature vs. bulldozers: The environment minister's balancing act at UN nature summit
articles.summary: Canada is showing up at this year's international nature summit in Armenia with pledges to protect swaths of land bigger than most countries. But it's also facing criticism for advancing major…

image.caption: Canada's Environment, Climate Change and Nature Minister Julie Dabrusin is heading to Armenia for a major biodiversity conference. (Patrick Doyle/Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics

Canada is showing up at this year's international nature summit in Armenia with pledges to protect swaths of land bigger than most countries. But it's also facing criticism for advancing major projects that put those protections in jeopardy.
Julie Dabrusin heads to COP17 in Armenia looking for ways for Canada to have 'leadership role'

Environment and Climate Change Minister Julie Dabrusin spoke to CBC News about the work she hopes to advance in Yerevan and responded to critics who say the government's actions on the nature file are "incoherent."
Dabrusin is heading to COP17, the United Nations biodiversity conference, on Saturday.
"Canada is the second-largest country in the world. We have the longest coastline in the world. So whatever we do has a real global impact," said Dabrusin before departing to Armenia.

items: Biologists seek justice for forgotten kingdom of fungi

blocks.text: She said international environmental conferences are "real moments" for Canada to have a "leadership role" in "pushing the world" to protect nature and reduce global emissions.
The environment minister attends COP17 on the heels of making a series of announcements to conserve lands and waters.
In October, Dabrusin announced that Canada is conserving an area of forest and peatlands near Kapuskasing, Ont., that's 1.3 times the size of Toronto.

In 2025, the minister said Ottawa would support the conservation of an area of land that's the size of Japan. As part of the initiative Northwest Territories: Our Land for the Future, the Canadian government is funding one of the world's largest Indigenous-led projects, conserving 380,000 square kilometres of land and water.
Policy 'incoherence': Greenpeace
But Dabrusin's attendance at COP17 comes as the Carney government receives sustained criticism for changes it's making to Canada's environmental laws.
"I think the big headline specifically for Canada is policy incoherence," said Salomé Sané, the nature and biodiversity campaigner for Greenpeace Canada.

The Building Canada Strong Act, or Bill C-39, is making its way through the House of Commons. The omnibus bill is proposing to amend several pieces of environmental legislation in order to fast-track pipelines, power lines, mines and other projects that fall under federal jurisdiction.

items: Critics accuse Carney government of proposing 'sacrifice zones' for the environment
Liberal MP calls for more safeguards in new bill to fast-track development projects

blocks.text: "We have the same federal government pushing for a very destructive bill under C-39 that will allow development projects to be built by bypassing, amongst other things, environmental regulations," Sané said.

"So our question to the government is, which is it? Are we protecting nature or are we destroying nature? Because going to COP to talk about nature protection and not defending nature at home will not allow us to deliver nature recovery."

items: Parks Canada plan to cut 500 jobs draws criticism from union

blocks.text: Debrusin responded to that criticism noting the government didn't move forward with some of the amendments it was contemplating due to pushback. She added the bill focuses on how projects get assessed, not weakening environmental standards.
"There's nothing in the policies we're putting forward that reduces our environmental standards," Dabrusin said.

Canada co-hosted with China the UN biodiversity conference in 2022. Countries signed the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which set a target of the world conserving 30 per cent of lands and waters by 2030.

items: Biodiversity agreement to protect planet reached at UN conference in Montreal

blocks.text: Since setting those targets, global progress has been slow according to UN Secretary General António Guterres.

"Even if current national commitments are met, only 26 per cent of terrestrial, and 12 per cent of marine ecosystems would be protected by 2030. That is well short of the promise made in Montreal," Guterres said in the Armenian capital last week.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

David Thurton is a senior reporter in CBC's Parliamentary Bureau. He covers daily politics in the nation’s capital and specializes in environment and energy policy. Born in Canada but raised in Trinidad and Tobago, he’s moved around more times than he can count. He’s worked for CBC in several provinces and territories, including Alberta and the Northwest Territories. He can be reached at david.thurton@cbc.ca

articles.title: The Marineland belugas keep dying. Was it a mistake to move them?
articles.summary: The deaths of six belugas at Marineland have raised questions about the impact of the transfers on their health and well-being and whether they were fit to travel. But was there ever a better option…

image.caption: Tofino, the last whale in captivity in Canada, is transported onto a truck via a sling before being moved to an aquarium in the U.S., in the final transfer of beluga whales out of the closed park, in Niagara Falls, Ont., on Aug. 31. Six of the transferred belugas have since died. (Carlos Osorio/The

blocks.text: A few months after a mass relocation effort that stretched across the Atlantic Ocean, six whales have died out of the 30 that were transferred from the now-shuttered Marineland theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont.

The most recent death, a beluga named Cyprus, was announced on Sunday by SeaWorld San Diego — one of five facilities in the U.S. and Spain that took in the marine mammals after Marineland said it could no longer care for them.

The deaths have raised questions about the impact of the transfers on their health and well-being and whether they were fit to travel, and rehashed concerns about the conditions they were living in during the years they spent at Marineland.
But was there ever a better option for the last captive whales and dolphins in Canada?

Advocacy groups such as Animal Justice have pointed to the federal and provincial governments, as well as Marineland, saying they failed to properly plan for the animals' futures. Experts have said they're worried these deaths are just the beginning. Meanwhile, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans maintains the transfers were the best possible rescue plan.

Cyprus, a beluga whale who was rescued from Marineland in Niagara Falls in August, is shown in an undated photo published to social media by SeaWorld San Diego. SeaWorld announced the whale's death on Oct. 18. (SeaWorld San Diego/Facebook)

"This was, I would say, almost kind of a Hail Mary effort in terms of trying to make sure that we could provide a better life for these whales," Dr. Doug Whiteside, the head veterinarian at the Calgary Zoo and a member of the Canadian Veterinary Medical Association's animal welfare committee, told CBC News.

They were already under chronic stress from the conditions they faced at Marineland, Whiteside said. Transferring them caused additional stress, even though international regulations were followed and they went to high-calibre institutions to receive full-time care, he said.
"Is it a risk? Absolutely ... any sort of acute stress may push them over the edge," he said.

items: 'I tried to say goodbye and tried to tell him I love him': Canada's last captive whales leave Marineland

blocks.text: While we can't underestimate the stress of the transfers on the whales, that doesn't mean it's not in their best interests to try to give them a better life, said Angela Fernandez, director of the Animal Law Program at the University of Toronto's law faculty.
"People knew that there were stronger and weaker individuals in the mix, just like there would be among a group of 30 human retirees," Fernandez told CBC News.
"You would not evacuate an old-age home and take only the strong individuals if there is capacity to take everyone."
Why Marineland's last living belugas are on 'death watch'
What happened to Marineland?
Marineland, once Canada's most popular amusement park, has been the subject of controversy for years, with animal rights activists and others vehemently opposed to its practices.

A federal law passed in 2019 that bans keeping whales, dolphins and porpoises for breeding or entertainment in Canada shuttered its business model. Then it never recovered from the COVID-19 pandemic's tourism slump.

In 2024, the park was put up for sale and began relocating many of its animals. But in 2025, the federal government blocked Marineland's request to export the remaining belugas to an aquarium in China. Marineland responded by asking for emergency funding from Ottawa, warning that it might otherwise have no choice but to euthanize them.

items: Why it’s so hard to find a new home for Marineland’s 30 belugas

blocks.text: Releasing them into the wild would lead to certain death for the mammals raised in captivity, marine experts noted. And there was no appropriate seaside sanctuary for them in North America. A proposed sanctuary in Nova Scotia was still years away from being developed.

In May, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans endorsed a rescue plan to split up all remaining whales between Oceanogràfic València in Spain and four U.S. locations: Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta, Shedd Aquarium in Chicago and two SeaWorld facilities in San Diego and San Antonio, Texas.
By the end of August, the last whale had been shipped out.
PHOTOS | Belugas' journey out of Marineland:

This situation was entirely avoidable, said Camille Labchuk, executive director of Animal Justice, based in Toronto. The animal law advocacy group had pushed for a proactive plan to move the whales to a seaside sanctuary for years, she said, adding there was still time to plan a responsible transition after the 2019 legislation passed.
"It was obvious to everyone that Marineland would one day close, because the public no longer wants to see miserable whales swim in circles in tiny tanks," Labchuk said.
"A seaside sanctuary was always going to be a challenging undertaking ... but these challenges don't excuse the failure to plan for a better option."
Concerns about fitness to travel

Since their transfer, four whales have died at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium, one whale and a dolphin have died at Oceanogràfic València and another whale has died at SeaWorld San Diego — representing one-fifth of the rescued whales.

The first, Peekachu, died on Aug. 25, about two weeks after arriving in Chicago. Rain was next on Sept. 2, followed by Osiris on Sept. 21, both of them also at Shedd. Necropsies for Peekachu and Rain, and preliminary results for Osiris, identified long-standing intestinal and liver issues that began before their rescue, the aquarium wrote in a blog post.

Jelly Bean died on Sept. 17 at Oceanogràfic València, and then Echo, a dolphin, died at the same facility on Sept. 23. They had been experiencing a list of health complications and organ abnormalities that may have developed prior to the transfer, the aquarium said in a news release.

items: Animal Justice urges investigation into Marineland beluga death in Chicago, wants relocation efforts halted
Marineland belugas that died in Chicago had chronic inflammatory disease, preliminary necropsy findings show

blocks.text: On Oct. 9, Shedd announced the death of Caspian two days earlier, noting it had been concerned about her health for weeks. The aquarium hasn't yet released her necropsy results. Cyprus, the sixth ill-fated beluga, died last weekend. SeaWorld San Diego said an ultrasound determined the animal's intestinal tract did not appear to be functioning normally.

There wasn't much transparency around the condition of the whales and dolphins before they were transferred due to their private ownership, U of T's Fernandez said. "After years and decades in captivity, it would be surprising if they didn’t all have significant health problems."
The deaths raise questions about whether the animals were fit to travel and whether every possible precaution was taken, Labchuk said, adding that the public deserves transparency.
'Heartbreaking,' says former trainer
Kristy Burgess, who worked as a trainer at Marineland from 2022 to 2025, called the deaths "heartbreaking."
Burgess has previously spoken out about the conditions at Marineland, noting that the beluga pools were in desperate need of repair and that the whales were eating paint peeling off the walls.

She now says she wishes there had been more opportunity for independent experts to contribute to the decision-making, as well as greater transparency around the planning, risks and ongoing health of the animals.
"Change has to come with a realistic, carefully considered plan for the animals themselves," Burgess said.
Former Marineland trainer Kristy Burgess says the beluga pools were in desperate need of repair and the whales were eating paint peeling off the walls. (Submitted by Kristy Burgess)
Whiteside, the Calgary Zoo's head veterinarian, said his understanding of the situation is that there simply wasn't a better option.
The belugas were in a "horrible situation" crowded into crumbling pools at Marineland, he said.
At least a transfer gave them a chance for a better life, he said, even if some didn't survive.

items: Former Marineland beluga whale dies at California theme park

blocks.text: The experience is a sad example of what can happen when institutions like Marineland aren't held to account, Whiteside said.
By not being held to account, Marineland allowed the animals to get to a state where they were chronically stressed, crowded in pools and eating paint, he said.
"Right from the get-go, this sets you up for potential failure."
'Their best chance of survival'
Before the animals' transport began, federal Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson said she had taken reasonable steps to ensure their safety, including individual health assessments for each animal.
In a statement to CBC News on Wednesday, Thompson said she was still confident in the rescue plan, noting that the transfer was "a significant and complex undertaking."

"Marineland was no longer able to care for these animals. I remain confident that this rescue plan gives these belugas their best chance of survival and that they are being cared for by experienced professionals who are deeply committed to their welfare," she said.
The experts and advocates who spoke to CBC News say their concern now is for the fate of the remaining Marineland whales.
"It's almost a certainty that more belugas and dolphins will die," Labchuk of Animal Justice said.
But Fernandez said "that means 24 are safe, at least for now."
CBC News has reached out to Marineland for comment but has not received a response.
Beluga whales swim in a tank at Marineland in Niagara Falls on June 9, 2023. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)

articles.title: The RDSP was meant to help disabled Canadians save for the future. Yet many don't know it exists
articles.summary: The Registered Disability Savings Plan was intended to be a financial safety net for people with disabilities and the families who care for them. But it's only reaching about a third of those it was…

image.caption: Conservative MP Mike Lake and his son Jaden are seen in this photo. Lake helped spearhead the Registered Disabilities Savings Plan nearly two decades ago, inspired in part by his son and his own desire to others with disabilities. (Submitted by Mike Lake)

blocks.text: Radio

The Registered Disability Savings Plan was intended to be a financial safety net for people with disabilities and the families who care for them. But it's only reaching about a third of those it was designed to help.
Barriers include getting a doctor to fill out paperwork and a 'knowledge gap'

It was when he was a fresh-faced Conservative MP nearly two decades ago — and father to 10-year-old Jaden — that Mike Lake realized he could be in a position to bolster the financial futures of those with disabilities and the families who cared for them.
And he happened to be in a governing party thinking the same way, at the same time.

“Our finance minister, [the late] Jim Flaherty, had three kids, triplets, and one of his sons had an intellectual disability,” Lake told CBC Radio. “So, in the 2007 budget, the RDSP showed up in that — and in subsequent budgets.”
The Registered Disability Savings Plan, a tax-free savings vehicle that includes grants of up to $70,000 and bonds of up to $20,000 from Ottawa, was born.

“In my son's case, he likes to work,” Lake said in a recent interview about his now-adult son, who was diagnosed with autism as a child. “Jaden's not in paid employment right now, but the potential of those things — in combination with the RDSP, really does create an environment where Jaden will be able to thrive and live the life he wants."
But the plan has had poor uptake.

Only about 34 per cent of those who qualify for it have opened one, according to a 2024 investigation by Statistics Canada. Meanwhile, other registered savings plans — like the Tax-Free Savings Account or RRSPs — are being used by roughly 68 per cent of eligible Canadians.

Those who qualify for the Disability Tax Credit (DTC) also qualify for the RDSP, but a report from April by The Canadian Tax Observatory found the take-up rate for the various programs available to that cohort less than 50 per cent — and declining.

Jill Teeple, investment advisor and financial planner, says that one of the barriers is that only the Big Five banks and a handful of local credit unions or wealth management firms offer the RDSP. (Submitted by Jill Teeple)

After spending close to two decades working as an investment adviser and financial planner for people with disabilities and their families, Jill Teeple has identified two consistent barriers to the program.
The biggest: people don’t know it exists, she said, though the federal government has started sending leaflets to those already approved for the Disability Tax Credit, the gateway to eligibility.

“Your financial institutions and, you know, maybe your provincial and territorial income support program for people with disabilities, they're not telling you,” said Teeple, the vice-president of non-profit Inclusion Canada.
“So we have this knowledge gap.”

Until recently, only the Big Five banks and a handful of local credit unions or wealth management firms offered RDSP accounts, largely because there are a lot of checks and balances required for them — and, for smaller ventures, it may not have made financial sense.

For example, they have to monitor whether someone still qualifies for a Disability Tax Credit, whereas as Teeple says, other investment vehicles are a lot more straightforward, both for the bank and the customer.
And there’s the secondary hurdle: navigating the medical and bureaucratic obstacles of applying for the tax credit.

As part of the medical process, you’ll have to meet with a clinician willing to go through a 16-page questionnaire to determine eligibility, which encompasses 10 categories of physical and cognitive disabilities.
“Lots of families or people with disabilities don't qualify right away, so you have to try again,” Teeple said.

In cases where there is a significant disability that is not expected to improve, people are given lifetime eligibility. But on average, people are given between four to six years before having to reapply.
That can be a challenge for applicants, Teeple said, noting that when the Disability Tax Credit was created in 1988, Canadians were not facing the doctor shortage of today.
“We had an entirely different relationship to our family doctor,” she said.
An opportunity for startups
Until recently, applicants had to rely on disability rights organizations, financial planners and doctors for assistance, but startups are starting to enter the picture.
In fact, there are two fintech companies that provide no other services aside from RDSP support. One is Montreal’s Terry.
Co-founder Michel-Alexandre Riendeau said the idea emerged during the pandemic, when people were forced to rely on online support.

“This is when the RDSP project really came into mind, because it's physically impossible to be able to go door-to-door and help all the people with disabilities around the province, around Canada.” he said. “So I think this online shift really enabled us to be able to help more people.”
Co-founder of financial technology company Terry, Michel-Alexandre Riendeau, says his business focuses exclusively on RDSPs. (Submitted by Michel-Alexandre Riendeau)
Understanding how the RDSP works, and who qualifies for grants, can be confusing — especially for first-time investors, he notes.

The RDSP provides the matching grants to those under the age of 49 with a disability — be it visible or invisible, though people can continue to invest in the plan until the end of the calendar year they turn 59 or have made $200,000 in contributions, whichever comes first.
Riendeau advises eligible clients to open an RDSP, even if they are not in a position to contribute right now.
“Over 90 per cent of our clientele, it's their first investment,” he said. “When they get a letter that's really complicated to understand, you're not going to convince them right away."

But in some cases, those who are playing catch-up — and have a lower personal or family income — will receive a substantial amount in government contributions over a 10-year period. As Riendeau put it, those who need the most help, “they can get $10,000 just by opening up the account and not even contributing,” provided they have had the disability tax credit for some time and not opened an account.
And sooner is better, he notes: every day, he sees people who are too old to open an RDSP and wish they did sooner.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Luke Williams is a production assistant and disability radio columnist for CBC Radio. He is a graduate of the Journalism program at TMU. Outside of work, he is an avid walker, and the world's worst bassist.

articles.title: Fjord's Sebastian Stan, Cristian Mungiu on making a movie no one can agree on
articles.summary: Fjord director Cristian Mungiu and star Sebastian Stan talk to CBC News about their divisive and celebrated flick.

image.caption: Sebastian Stan appears in a still from Cristian Mungui's Fjord. (Elevation Pictures)

blocks.text: Entertainment·INTERVIEW
Fjord director Cristian Mungiu and star Sebastian Stan talk to CBC News about their divisive and celebrated flick.
'It's about what happens to all of us in the world of today,' says Mungiu of film
Palme d'Or winner and Oscar hopeful Fjord is not your typical Hollywood critical darling.

Following a Romanian, deeply Christian family at odds with the Norwegian child-care system — which interprets that family's form of child-rearing as potentially abusive — it seems the perfect recipe for controversy.
There's only one problem: No one can figure out who to be mad at.
If you were to ask director Cristian Mungiu, that was the point — to craft a story so even-handed that every audience member would come out thinking he meant to villainize someone else.

And with the response ranging from heralding him as a genius to calling the movie prejudiced and withholding, you could say he was successful. But why make a movie without an obvious point in the first place? CBC News sat down with Mungiu and his star, Sebastian Stan, to understand.
This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.
I'm curious whether you think that objectivity in films is possible, and is it something that you aspired for in making this film?
Cristian Mungiu: I think it's possible to make films, as you see this one, in which you don't tell the story from your personal point of view as a citizen.

If I had taken sides in the film, the other party wouldn't have watched the film like this. I use this film as a trigger for a more important conversation — way more important than what happens in the film — about the society of today. That's the point of the film: Let's listen to the arguments of the other, even if they won't convince us. Because if we continue believing that we are the only ones who are right, we are in this dead end, in which half of the population have conservative views, the other half has progressive views, as in the U.S.

Once you make a film and it's free to be screened anywhere, there are a lot of misinterpretations. You can't correct every one, but whenever I try to speak, I try to make sure that this is not about Norway and Romania. It's about what happens to all of us in the world of today.

Sebastian, it wasn't too long ago the Canadian-produced The Apprentice ended up sweeping the Canadian Screen Awards, but it had a very difficult route to audiences. These roles are both conversation starters, but also fraught and difficult. Was that confluence an intentional choice?

Sebastian Stan: That was a very different film, but I think of equal importance to me. And I think the similarity there, again, is just wanting to work with someone like [The Apprentice director] Ali Abbasi or like Cristian, who I think have a very fearless attitude towards wanting to get to the truth and wanting to do it without judgment. And again, just open the door to conversation.

There is a difficulty to it in a lot of ways, but that is also attractive. And it's what you want in the long run. Especially now, when everybody just wants to be spoonfed how to feel, what to think and all that stuff. So I felt lucky to sort of have something right away to follow that with, and that was of equal measure.

items: Stop-motion movie Wildwood is a staggering masterpiece. It's a miracle it exists at all
Loved You Can See Everything? Thank Canada

blocks.text: Speaking about someone to work with — Sebastian, you disappeared into this character, no less for the fact you shaved your head for the role. Cristian, what made you think of Sebastian Stan, the Marvel superhero, for this character?

CM: Well, because I see beyond the Marvel hero. I met Sebastian some 10 years ago and I have also watched the other things that he did in cinema. Yes, he has the ability of also doing the Marvel stuff. That's great. That's for a different audience. It doesn't mean that actors need to be typecast and always labelled as doing only this and this.

And I wanted to take this — after talking to Sebastian — to the edge. To make people see a different character; not only in the way he embodied this very religious person, but also in the way he looked. I'm sorry to say this, but he's a very good-looking guy [laughs]. I always have this problem with him. And this distracts you from seeing that he can be so possessed by the part. And we came together at the end with this idea that the more distant he looks from his regular self, the more the people are going to see the character.

Yes, it was important for me that the name of Sebastian was there, because without him, we couldn't have financed this film, to be honest. But at the same time, it's important not to exploit that he's so good-looking. I was looking for his talents, and he gave us the opportunity to see what he can do.
Sebastian Stan, left, appears next to Renate Reinsve in a scene from Fjord. (Elevation Pictures)

Of course, Sebastian, I don't mean to minimize your range. You've played difficult roles that are not necessarily villainous, but they're not altogether perfect people. How do you approach, from a craft perspective, the question of who is in the right?

SS: Well, first of all, I think it's really about the filmmaker. I mean, it's a director's medium. Film to me has always been that way. And I think what's interesting is when you can meet someone — through their vision and through what they're exploring — who can make you able to understand something more about yourself.

Life is very complicated. People are complicated. We're capable of good things and bad things. There's no black or white. There's no perfect people, you know? It's very difficult to find movies and stories now that I think really — and I think they do it more in Europe, to be honest, than in the U.S. — where they're not afraid to show how complicated situations are.

People are not heroic all the time the way we like to think that they are. People don't communicate so easily what they feel. They may not have the tools, you know? So I think that's going to be interesting to get the audience to do a little bit of work, and try to figure out how they feel about the movie.
And you have faith they will?
SS: I do, that's why we keep making it.

CM: I hope. Who knows. But the idea is that we need to also to tell them that it's fine to have films in which you get all the answers by the end of the film, and this kind of entertaining film for Friday evening. But cinema shouldn't just be formatted like this. There's space for something else, and we hope that this film also appeals a little bit to your critical spirit.

We don't take you by hand to tell you, 'This is good. This is bad.' Because in life, nobody takes you by hand. This is how life is. It's complex. And cinema should be as complex. So you, as a spectator, need to make this effort of understanding something from the film — and also considering something about your values. Because the film ultimately speaks about you and about your own values that you need to double-check every now and then. To make sure that you think with your own mind.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Will the Alberta referendum feed a more polarized immigration debate?
articles.summary: Beside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith's own political future, the most unresolved questions raised by her referendum concern immigration.

image.caption: While Prime Minister Mark Carney raised some eyebrows when he repeated the 'no to the nine' slogan before Alberta's vote, he had also suggested he was inclined to give all provinces more input on immigration. (John Ulan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Analysis
Beside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith's own political future, the most unresolved questions raised by her referendum concern immigration.
Immigration was on the ballot in Alberta. Now attention turns to the Carney government

Referendums tend to raise as many questions as they answer. And so it may be for the 10-part questionnaire that Alberta Premier Danielle Smith put to her province — although with a series of no's Albertans have seemingly foreclosed on a number of possibilities.
"I am well aware that not every grievance Alberta has with Ottawa has been resolved," Smith told Albertans on Tuesday night. "There are still many political and constitutional battles ahead of us."

On the question of whether Alberta should remain in Canada the answer was not close. The 75 per cent of voters who chose the first option is decidedly more decisive than the 1980 referendum in Quebec.

Of the 25 per cent who voted for another referendum, it is also fair to ask how many genuinely want secession. According to Abacus Data, making Alberta an independent country was the primary motivation for just 32 per cent of Albertans who favoured Option 2.

Whatever Smith's appetite for future constitutional battles, Albertan voters also proved to be unenthusiastic: all four questions about whether Alberta should pursue constitutional amendments were answered with a "no."
Not even a question about abolishing the Senate — possibly the most-maligned public institution in Canada history — was able to muster even a simple majority of Albertans.

"There's a reason to be skeptical that some constitutional amendments would be worth the effort and ... what I'm seeing is that Albertans would just rather that we spend our time focusing on things where we can make some meaningful change," Smith said at a news conference on Wednesday (at the time, two of the four constitutional questions were being answered in the negative as results were still being tallied).
"That's why I think the numbers were so different on the immigration questions versus … perhaps the constitutional ones."

Beside Smith's own political future, the most unresolved questions raised by her referendum concern immigration — and one of the questions now is whether they will feed into a more polarized national debate on Canada's immigration policy.
Immigration on the ballot in Alberta

Of Smith's 10 questions, four concerned either immigration or potential new rules for newcomers. On its official referendum website, Smith's government claimed that "unsustainable immigration levels over the past 10 years" had "a profound impact" on Alberta's ability "to fund and effectively deliver social services like health care and education — directly impacting Albertans' access to these services and costing taxpayers billions of dollars."
Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi argued Smith was "scapegoating" immigrants.

"The reality of the matter is even if you took all the young, healthy temporary foreign workers out of the health-care system, even if you denied public education to refugee children, it's not going to make the emergency room lineups any less," Nenshi told CBC's Power & Politics this week. "It's not going to make your classrooms any smaller. It's not going to make anyone's life better."

Just under 55 per cent of voters supported the proposition that the Alberta government should take "increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels."
Danielle Smith says Alberta separatist UCP members can 'join a different party'

Three questions that floated possible limitations on how or when newcomers or temporary residents can access health care, education and other social services in Alberta were supported by narrower majorities of 52.4, 53.1 and 52 per cent.

Smith's government has a majority in the Alberta legislature and it didn't need a referendum to pursue any of these initiatives. But the results — notably, none of the immigration questions won a majority in Calgary — may give Smith reason to hesitate.

At her news conference on Wednesday, the premier suggested she was prepared to act quickly on the first question, but she would "proceed with caution" in response to questions two, three and four. She said she did not want to impact anyone who was already residing in Alberta.

While Prime Minister Mark Carney raised some eyebrows when he repeated the "no to the nine" slogan before Alberta's vote, he had also suggested he was inclined to give all provinces more input on immigration.

"To be candid, I don't need a referendum to tell us to co-operate more with the provinces on immigration," Carney told Global News a few days before Alberta's vote. "I think that's where we're headed."
But Alberta's immigration questions also caught the attention of Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre.
An increasingly polarized debate

"I thought it was inappropriate for the prime minister to tell Canadians and tell Albertans that they should vote to continue to give deluxe taxpayer benefits to people who are illegally here," Poilievre said. "And for the prime minister to suggest that Albertans vote in favor of continued mass, unvetted, out of control immigration was a mistake."
The Conservative Party also sent a fundraising appeal to supporters on Tuesday that promised a Conservative government would "dramatically reduce immigration."
The Carney government argues that it has immigration "under control" after steps were taken to curb the intake of international students and temporary workers. The Conservatives obviously disagree.

items: Conservatives accuse government of 'cooking the books' over immigration data presentation

blocks.text: But the Alberta referendum also landed between two triggers for renewed debate about immigration to Canada.

First, in discussing immigration policy during an interview with the New York Times last month, Carney said, "now the question starts to become: When do we resume some controlled increase in the population, which is the nature of Canada? So that will happen, and we just want to make sure that we've got it under control."

Now the federal government is due to table its latest immigration levels plan, which sets out targets for the next few years for both permanent and temporary arrivals (technically, a new plan is due by Nov. 1, but last year's plan was included in the fall budget).
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Carney said his government "will not budge from overall levels that are sustainable." But what constitutes "sustainable" is likely a matter of debate.

At a news conference on Thursday, Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner argued "mass immigration" was suppressing wages and driving up rents, to the benefit of corporate profiteers. Conservatives, she said, will "vigorously oppose any attempt by Mark Carney to continue to raise and sustain high immigration levels" and "will push him to lower them."

Claims that the "Canadian consensus" on immigration has been broken are sometimes overstated. Canadians still believe immigration is a net-positive for the economy, but they also believe recent immigration levels have been too high, driven in large part by concerns about the availability and affordability of housing.

Polling by the Environics Institute has also shown a growing gap along the political spectrum, with Conservative voters much more inclined to say there is too much immigration. And the parties themselves may be getting further apart.
That is not the most stable foundation on which to build significant new increases in immigration, however much such increases might be necessary.
If the goal remains to be as open and welcoming as possible — if there is an economic imperative to being so — "proceed with caution" might be good advice for all sides.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Aaron Wherry has covered Parliament Hill since 2007 and has written for Maclean's, the National Post and the Globe and Mail. He is the author of Promise & Peril, a book about Justin Trudeau's years in power.

articles.title: Veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. arrested for alleged cyber libel
articles.summary: The warrant of arrest is issued by Branch 10 of the Davao City Regional Trial Court, Meanwhile, Lustre says he does not know who the complainant is.

blocks.text: PHILIP LUSTRE. Veteran journalist and author Philip Lustre Jr. is arrested for alleged cyberlibel.
Philip Lustre Jr's Facebook
The warrant of arrest is issued by Branch 10 of the Davao City Regional Trial Court, Meanwhile, Lustre says he does not know who the complainant is.

MANILA, Philippines – Veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was arrested by the Quezon City Police Department (QCPD) under the leadership of acting district director Police Brigadier General (PBGEN) Christopher Olazo on Saturday, October 24, for alleged cyber libel.
The Kamuning Police Station 10’s warrant section and the Quezon City District’s anti-cybercrime team both facilitated the arrest.
Lustre, 72, is the author behind Kill, Kill, Kill: Extrajudicial Killings in the Philippines, a book about former president Rodrigo Duterte’s deadly war on drugs.

He had been attending the House of Representatives’ Saturday news forum at a restaurant along Scout Borromeo Street when the police arrived to read his Miranda rights to him, according to a report by GMA News.
The same report also said lawyer Dino De Leon, who was also present at the forum, will serve as Lustre’s legal counsel moving forward.
Notably, the warrant of arrest was issued by Branch 10 of Davao City’s Regional Trial Court.

Lustre’s arrest comes just after Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo “Pulong” Duterte filed a cyber libel complaint against GMA Network’s journalists over a report about bribery claims against him and Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.caption: Paolo Duterte files cyber libel complaint vs GMA Network over Gracioso report

blocks.text: In a video posted by ABS-CBN News, Lustre said he does not know who the complainant is.

articles.title: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un travels to Chinese border city via newly opened bridge
articles.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un travelled to China’s border city of Dandong via a newly opened bridge linking the two countries, where he met a senior Chinese official.

image.caption: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un arrived in China via the newly opened bridge. Image: Florence Lo/REUTERS

blocks.text: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un arrived in China via the newly opened bridge on Saturday. He arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong via the New Yalu River Bridge linking the two countries.
China’s top political adviser Wang Huning met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, Chinese state media reported.
Wang conveyed President Xi Jinping’s "greetings and best wishes to Kim," Xinhua reported.
China and North Korea pledged to "strengthen strategic communication and cooperation to safeguard their sovereignty, security and development interests," Chinese state media said.
The two countries also vowed to expand people-to-people exchanges and economic and trade cooperation through the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge.
The four-lane bridge was completed in 2014 but remained unused for 12 years due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side.
It officially opened about a week ago, marking a step towards strengthening economic ties between the neighbouring countries.

China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and a key source of diplomatic, economic and political support for the isolated, nuclear-armed state, although relations between the two have not always been smooth.
Kim’s trip coincides with key dates in China

The trip coincides with the anniversary of China’s entry into the Korean War, known in China as the "War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea." It remains unclear whether Kim will attend commemorative events.
During the 1950-53 war, Chinese troops fought alongside North Korea against South Korea and US-led United Nations forces.

Kim’s visit also comes ahead of a key political meeting in Beijing on Monday, when Chinese President Xi Jinping and other senior officials gather for the fifth plenary session of the Communist Party’s powerful Central Committee.

blocks.caption: Xi visited Pyongyang in June 2019, the first visit by a Chinese leader in 14 years (File image)Image: Ahn Young-joon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Bridge highlights North Korea's ties with China
The New Yalu River Bridge opened just over a month after North Korea and Russia inaugurated their first road bridge, which Pyongyang hailed as a sign of closer ties.
While North Korea’s trade with Russia largely involves military supplies, trade with China could provide goods needed to develop its civilian economy, analysts say.
