articles.title: Why sports insider Brian Windhorst’s career begins and ends with writing
articles.summary: ‘No one story is worth damaging a relationship that maybe involves 5, 10, 15 years of building,’ says American sports media personality Brian Windhorst, who visited Manila for the NBA on Disney+’s…

image.caption: Why sports insider Brian Windhorst’s career begins and ends with writing

blocks.text: Brian Windhorst has broken some of the biggest sports stories from the least glamorous places imaginable.
Long before he became a renowned NBA insider and a household name among basketball fans globally, he learned that the news doesn’t wait for a convenient time or location.

Over his 20-year career, Windhorst has taken urgent, league-shifting phone calls in chaotic airport terminals, public bathrooms, and cramped stadium broom closets. He even reported a massive NBA development from a hospital room while waiting for his wife, Maureen Ellen Fulton, to undergo a scheduled cesarean section.
“It wasn’t going to be for an hour, so… you’re just killing time,” Windhorst shared to Rappler during a recent Manila visit.
But somehow, that round-the-clock hustle is what a kid from Akron, Ohio wanted — Windhorst decided early on that a conventional life wasn’t going to cut it.
Today, his globe-trotting career is defined by television appearances, the flash of cameras, and millions of social media followers.
Yet, Windhorst insists that all of it — the television sets, the viral moments, and the multi-million-dollar sports spectacles — isn’t exactly complete without the quiet, grinding work of a writer.

To him, sports journalism operates exactly like a ride at Disneyland: before visitors can climb aboard an attraction, there must be a movie. Before the movie, a character; and before that character ever comes to life, someone has to sit down at a keyboard.
“The character doesn’t exist without the writer,” Windhorst said as The Hoop Collective visited the Philippines to launch NBA on Disney+’s 2026-2027 season.
“It all comes from writing,” he said. “Everything that we do comes from writing. You can never stop writing. I will never stop writing, ever.”
Growing up near Cleveland, Windhorst’s future was once mapped out on an ordinary Saturday with a strict $10 budget.

As a high schooler looking to escape his parents’ conventional nine-to-five routine, he would stretch that budget to cover bus fare, a movie ticket, and his favorite, now-discontinued Taco Bell item: the Chilito. He was just a local kid who wanted to get out, see the world, and chase something grander.
“I wanted to be, at some level, extraordinary,” he said.
Basketball offered him that exact path. While studying journalism at Kent State University, Windhorst fell in love with the specific rhythm of the NBA.
The league’s 82-game regular season offered a perfect balance, providing frequent competition alongside unique opportunities to travel.
But he’ll always remember covering high school basketball in Ohio, where he watched a 14-year-old LeBron James play his first high school game.
Windhorst remembers a tall, lanky teenager with big feet who was still growing into his body. What stood out immediately was how smoothly James moved.
“There’s a lot of tall, you know, teenagers — he was barely a teenager — are awkward,” Windhorst said.. “You know, they don’t move that well when they’re growing so tall. He moved so smooth.”

James scored 15 points that night. Afterward, his coach told Windhorst that James was the best player he had ever coached — a sweeping assessment that the young reporter struggled to believe at the time.
James, of course, became one of basketball’s greatest icons, and Windhorst’s coverage of him became a defining pillar of his own career.
Windhorst readily acknowledges that he would not have reached the same professional heights without James. But the experience also taught him to look beyond the box score.

In 2003, Windhorst began covering the Cleveland Cavaliers for the Akron Beacon Journal. He moved to The Plain Dealer in 2008 before joining ESPN in 2010, bringing behind-the-scenes developments to a national audience.
The relentless nature of his national role affected everyone around him, creating a landscape where work never truly stops.
Windhorst recalls a time when Philadelphia 76ers coach Nick Nurse had to abandon a long-awaited round of golf midway through the course just to take an urgent call from James’ agent.
“Sometimes that’s the nature of this job,” Windhorst noted. “It’s a job that doesn’t have nine-to-five hours.”
Yet, despite the intense pressure to break news first, he insists that speed must never compromise accuracy.
“Being wrong once is way worse than being right a hundred times in a row,” he said.
One of Windhorst’s biggest career scoops arrived when Kyrie Irving suddenly demanded a trade away from the Cleveland Cavaliers in 2017.

The news blindsided the basketball world, but as Windhorst points out, trade reporting rarely begins when a deal is officially announced. It begins months in advance by tracking minor shifts in behavior and recognizing when a situation no longer looks the way it did before.
“The real value for me is: can you say what a team is going to do before they do it, or what they might do?”

Sometimes, that deep reporting translates into unforgettable television. During an episode of ESPN’s First Take, Windhorst delivered a brilliant, dramatic analysis of the Utah Jazz’s future, using precise hand gestures to stress his prediction.

He was 98% sure of an impending trade but couldn’t legally report it as confirmed yet, so he teased it cryptically. Within two hours, his prediction came true, and his dramatic delivery instantly became a viral internet meme.
The sudden internet fame caught him off guard.

“It sort of scares you about social media, in all honesty,” he admitted, noting that the viral moment didn’t replace the actual journalistic grinding required to get the information in the first place.

Another important thing in Windhorst’s line of work is trust. Maintaining deep league relationships means showing up to empty arenas, attending grueling training camps, and remaining present during ugly losing stretches.
As he values trust, he would even prefer to miss a major breaking scoop entirely rather than burn a bridge for a fleeting headline.
“No one story is worth damaging a relationship that maybe involves 5, 10, 15 years of building,” Windhorst said.
“Time. Nobody ever wants to talk about time because they want stuff right away.”
Windhorst deeply admires fellow ESPN journalist Michael Wilbon for the decades of respect he has earned from players, coaches, and owners alike by simply being fair to people.
For Windhorst, that kind of legacy is the goal because the game itself is secondary to the people playing it.
“Ultimately, the game is throwing a ball through a ring,” he said. “That’s all it is. It’s a child’s game. The player’s job is to provide the spectacle. My job is to tell the story.”
And for him, that work will always begin with writing. – Rappler.com
Jade Tan is a Rappler intern studying AB Journalism at University of Santo Tomas, Manila.

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 2:37pm

As the public began traveling to their hometowns for Undas, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) warned taxi drivers of penalties for overcharging fares, snubbing, and disrespecting passengers during the All Saints’ Day break.

In a press release on Saturday, LTFRB Acting Chairman Atty. Greg Pua Jr. warned that violations of the agency’s rules and regulations could lead to the suspension or cancellation of a Certificate of Public Convenience, among other penalties.

“We expect more passengers going to bus terminals and other major transportation hubs starting next week. This early, we are giving a fair warning to all taxi operators to behave and stick to the rules and regulations of the authority to operate issued to them,” Pua said.
The Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) previously stated that it is expecting around 1.9 million passengers for this year’s exodus for All Saints' Day.
Meanwhile, up to 2 million passengers are expected at seaports, according to the Philippine Coast Guard.
The LTFRB added that it similarly expects an influx of passengers at major bus terminals in Quezon City, Manila, Pasay City, Caloocan City, and Muntinlupa.
The agency stated that it will actively monitor complaints on social media platforms and conduct surprise inspections using mystery riders.

“The LTFRB is in full force when it comes to monitoring. This should serve as a strong message to both operators and drivers that we are watching you, and that you know what would happen if we catch you,” Pua said.
Pua advised passengers to report any incidents of abuse to LTFRB Hotline 1342 or through the agency’s official social media accounts. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/KG, GMA News

articles.title: Blaze engulfs Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ mountain retreat in Bavaria
articles.summary:
About 200 firefighters deployed to tackle the blaze at former Nazi retreat in a remote part of southern Germany

German police said Saturday they had detained a suspect after a fire at Adolf…

blocks.text: German police said Saturday they had detained a suspect after a fire at Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat, known as the Eagle’s Nest, in the state of Bavaria.
About 200 firefighters were deployed to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote and difficult-to-access Kehlsteinhaus residence, on the peak of Obersalzberg in southern Germany.
Firefighters saw flames rising high into the air as they approached the scene, only to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said.
“A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody,” they said in a later statement, adding that nobody was injured in the blaze.
Police spokesperson Lisa Maier said firefighters struggled to tackle the fire due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000 feet).
The building was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said.
Authorities were alerted to the fire on Friday evening, when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at about 9.50pm (1950 GMT), police said.
No potential reason for the fire was given, but the German media reported that the investigators suspected it was the result of arson.
As snow fell on the Alpine peak, the Eagle’s Nest was still engulfed in flames in the early hours of Saturday, a weather camera showed.
Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat, according to an AFP photographer.
The firefighters found no one inside the building.
Maier said police were still investigating but will hold a news conference later on Saturday.
German tabloid Bild reported that the authorities had arrested a motorcyclist they came across on their way to the scene.

Built between 1937 and 1938, the Eagle’s Nest forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews as well as Roma, LGBTQ people and Communists in the Holocaust.
It was designed to serve as a monument to Hitler’s rule, although the dictator rarely visited the complex.
It survived the second world war undamaged, and since 1952 has hosted an exhibition recounting the house’s Nazi history and a restaurant.

articles.title: Lacson says TESDA offered him P5-M 'allocation fund,' but agency denies claim
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson on Saturday said the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) offered him a P5-million "allocation fund," but the agency rejected the claim.

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 1:56pm
Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson on Saturday said the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) offered him a P5-million "allocation fund," but the agency rejected the claim.
In a statement, Lacson said the proposal was made through his Senate staff earlier this week, but he refused it.
The senator said he would clarify the issue when TESDA's proposed 2027 budget is tackled in the Senate plenary next month.

"When TESDA's proposed 2027 budget comes up for plenary debate, I will seek clarification on the P5-million fund offer made to me through my Senate staff early this week. I declined unequivocally," Lacson said.

Lacson posted on his X account the screenshot of the alleged allocation fund offer from TESDA Secretary and Director General Jose Francisco Benitez, which was supposedly channeled through an individual named "Stephanie."
Lacson said he initially considered an entrapment or sting operation against those involved in the transaction, but took pity on "Stephanie."

"Maybe they thought I'm 'standard practice.' They didn't know me. Now they do. Initially, I considered entrapment, but I took pity on Stephanie who apparently was only following instructions," Lacson said.
Lacson earlier said the Senate would examine the House-approved version of the 2027 budget bill, and address the red flags there, including those related to Foreign-Assisted Projects (FAPs).

When TESDA's proposed 2027 budget comes up for plenary debate, I will seek clarification on the P5-million fund offer made to me through my Senate staff early this week. I declined unequivocally. https://t.co/J1WcjC97RG— PING LACSON (@iampinglacson) October 23, 2026
In a statement, however, the TESDA chief denied giving the go-ahead for such an offer.
"As TESDA Secretary, I did not authorize anyone to offer any allocation or one amounting to P5 million to Senator Ping Lacson," Benitez said.

"We thank the Senator for promptly informing us of these misrepresentations. We welcome the opportunity to get to the bottom of this matter and fully support efforts to establish the facts," he added.
Benitez lauded Lacson for the senator's advocacy for good governance, transparency, and accountability, values which he said are also shared by TESDA.

"Given that it's budget season, TESDA routinely reaches out to members of the Senate to inquire if they have concerns with the agency. Any improper offer, allocation, or solicitation in TESDA funds, or any other unauthorized arrangement, involving any legislator is contrary to this Office's directives," he said.

Benitez said the agency had already ordered an immediate internal investigation to identify those responsible for any unauthorized actions or misrepresentations, and enforce appropriate administrative and, if warranted, criminal cases. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Moonshot curbs hacking ability in new Kimi model as fears grow over AI-powered cyberattacks
articles.summary: Moonshot says it removed cyber-related data from the training corpus and reinforcement-learning environments used to develop the model, while retaining general coding skills

blocks.text: MOONSHOT AI. The Moonshot AI logo is seen in this illustration taken September 5, 2026.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
Moonshot says it removed cyber-related data from the training corpus and reinforcement-learning environments used to develop the model, while retaining general coding skills

items: Moonshot AI has introduced the Kimi K3.1 Pro model with reduced cyber-offensive capabilities by removing cyber-related data from its training, aiming to mitigate hacking risks.
The company plans to publish the model's weights by November 4, allowing developers to run and modify it, while emphasizing that open-weight models can enhance security for organizations.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Moonshot AI has reduced the cyber-offensive capabilities of its newest model, the Chinese startup said on Saturday, October 24, as fears grow that increasingly autonomous AI could turbocharge hacking.

Beijing-based Moonshot announced the curbs while introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, which it describes as its most capable 3-trillion-parameter-class open-weight model. The company plans to publish the model’s weights — files allowing outside developers to run and modify it on their own systems — by November 4.
Moonshot said it removed cyber-related data from the training corpus and reinforcement-learning environments used to develop the model, while retaining general coding skills.
“We aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability,” the company said.

Governments, technology companies and security researchers are growing increasingly concerned that AI could make sophisticated hacking easier and cheaper. Models that can write code, operate software tools and complete long, multi-step tasks may help users identify weaknesses in programs and automate parts of cyberattacks.

blocks.caption: Millions of hacking attempts as companies, governments rush to patch PHP flaws

blocks.text: China proposed export controls last week that would ban exports of AI-driven malware-generation and mutation technology and restrict AI-assisted vulnerability-discovery tools. The draft measures, which remain open for public comment, cite the risk that such capabilities could be used against critical infrastructure, defence-industrial and core government systems, or to bypass security protections.
Moonshot said open-weight models can improve security by helping more organisations inspect and secure their own software, including older systems that receive little attention.

Unlike proprietary, closed-weight AI systems, however, open-weight releases make central oversight more difficult. Once the files are widely distributed, the original developer has less ability to restrict access, monitor use or update safeguards than with a hosted service.

K3.1 Pro scored 81.0% on its internal cyber benchmark, compared with 90.5% for a similar version without the risk-reduction measures, the company said. The test involved finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities in a controlled environment. Moonshot said the comparison showed that filtering cyber-related data reduced the model’s offensive cyber performance, although it still outperformed its predecessor. The results have not been independently verified.

K3.1 Pro has a 1-million-token context window, allowing it to process very large amounts of text at once. Moonshot also released a faster version, K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which it said runs at two to three times the speed of the standard model. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Minneapolis withdrawal was 'surrender', Trump's ex-border patrol chief tells BBC
articles.summary: Greg Bovino was the public face of the controversial immigration enforcement operation in the city earlier this year.

blocks.text: The former US border patrol chief who became the public face of the highly controversial deportation drive in Minneapolis earlier this year has defended the operation, describing the withdrawal of agents from the city as a "surrender" by the Trump administration.

In an interview with the BBC, Greg Bovino also said he was "not responding" to a lawsuit filed by the family of a woman shot dead during the operation. He appeared to dismiss the legal action, praising the officers deployed to Minneapolis and saying "people do lawsuits all the time".
Bovino, 56, was removed from his role shortly after the fatal shootings of US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January.

The two shootings, which were captured on video, triggered a bipartisan backlash and widespread protests. Trump then said he was "going to de-escalate a little bit" and withdrew hundreds of immigration agents from the city.

Earlier this month, Good's family filed two civil lawsuits against the Trump administration over her killing, alleging wrongful death and a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of protesters.

One of the lawsuits names several top officials, including Bovino and Jonathan Ross, the agent who shot Good, "for their respective individual roles in the operation that led to Renee's death". It alleges that the government's operation in Minneapolis created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence".

Asked about Bovino's remarks, the family's lawyers said he was "spewing propaganda" and could not be "judge, jury, and executioner". They added: "Our legal team looks forward to the depositions of Mr Bovino and all of the defendants in this matter".
A White House spokeswoman previously called the lawsuits "baseless".

Speaking in Detroit where he was campaigning for tougher immigration enforcement, Bovino said the administration "threw the towel in" and called for more deportations, which he said were now at a "virtual standstill".
He added that he regretted "not going harder in Minnesota and arresting even more illegal aliens".
Bovino said his agents in Minneapolis were the "real victims" of what he called "the most violence that any law enforcement mission ever in the history of the United States has been up against".

Challenged by the BBC over how immigration agents handled both shooting incidents, Bovino rejected suggestions that video evidence undermined his claim that Good and Pretti had intended to harm the agents.
"The evidence is that violence was perpetrated against agents of the US government, and this is a society of laws and people need to follow the law. If not, there are consequences," he said.

Trump initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, willfully and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents were sometimes "going to make a mistake".
The withdrawal from Minnesota, which saw some 700 immigration agents leave the state, also saw Bovino removed from his post. The operation was taken over by the White House 'border tsar' Tom Homan.
When asked why he was removed, Bovino told the BBC: "You'd have to ask the administration. I still haven't gotten the final word on that."

articles.title: Why Russia's arrest of Japanese journalist is the latest sign of deteriorating ties between the countries.
articles.summary: Japan is demanding access to a journalist who was arrested by Russian security services. The Kremlin claims that Japan is using journalists as spies.

image.caption: Journalist Yuki Imai seen being taken into custody by Russian security agents Image: Russian Federal Security Service/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Japanese Foreign Ministry officials were in Moscow this week in an attempt to contact a journalist arrested in Russia's far east on allegations of spying.

Journalist Yuki Imai was arrested on October 14 by Russia's FSB security service in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin Island. Televised footage of the arrest showed FSB officers barging into his hotel room as he slept.

The correspondent for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper was accused of attempting to obtain information on soldiers in the region, which is near the Kiril islands, a geopolitical sore spot in Russia-Japan relations.

Russian authorities quickly transferred him to Lefortovo Prison in Moscow, where a court ordered him to be held in pretrial detention until at least December 12. If convicted, 34-year-old Imai faces up to 20 years in jail, according to the International Federation of Journalists, which has called for his immediate release.
Officials from the Japanese embassy in Moscow have been denied access to Imai. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has condemned the arrest and dismissed the claim that Imai was a spy.

Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev said Imai had been caught "red-handed," the official TASS news agency reported. Nozdrev has claimed that Japanese intelligence agencies use journalists to collect classified information with the goal of "undermining Russia's security and defense capability."
Russia accuses journalists of being 'spies'

Yoji Gomi, a veteran journalist and author who has reported from across Asia, told DW that Japanese journalists may occasionally meet with diplomats in the course of their work and "share thoughts and impressions." However, he rejects the idea that reporters are paid spies.
"One-party nations often see foreign correspondents as spies because that is exactly what they use their journalists for," he said.

"I can completely see how the Russians decided that Imai was a spy, as it is how they operate, plus he was in a sensitive part of Russia where there are lots of North Korean laborers that they want to keep quiet," Gomi added.
Japan condemns Putin visit to disputed Kuril Islands

Stephen Nagy, a professor of international relations at Tokyo's International Christian University, told DW that Russia might see Imai as a bargaining chip it can use to exchange for nationals detained overseas.
Nagy doubts that Japan will give in to pressure.

"They are going to resist because it means that Russia, or any other country, can then just seize a Japanese national, put them on trial for espionage and demand the release of one of their people," he said.
"It would set a dangerous precedent," he added.
The arrest comes after a member of the Russia-linked hacking group Qilin was arrested in Japan and extradited to Germany to face charges in connection with a 2024 cyberattack on a logistics center.

The last time a journalist was arrested in Russia was in 2019 for "attempting to obtain classified information about Russia's military potential in the Far East," Russia's Interfax news agency reported. However, in this case, the journalist was quickly released.

Imai's case is perhaps the most serious since 2023, when Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich was arrested in Russia and sentenced to 16 years in a penal colony before being released in a prisoner exchange with Western countries in 2024.

blocks.caption: Russia has previously arrested foreign journalists for prisoner exchanges. US reporter Evan Gershkovich is seen here in a Moscow court.Image: Dmitry Serebryakov/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Strained Japan-Russia ties
Imai's arrest is the latest in a series of incidents that have sent bilateral relations into a tailspin.

Nagy said Imai's seizure was designed to put pressure on Tokyo. He added this is part of a coordinated approach with China to isolate Japan at a time when the US is preoccupied with domestic issues and the conflict in the Middle East.

"Moscow and Beijing are coordinating to create the image that Japan is not a reformed member of the international community but still the military state of the 1930s and that it poses a threat to stability in the Indo-Pacific region," Nagy said.

"This is all designed to smear Japan's efforts to lead diplomacy in the region at a time when the US is perhaps distracted," he said. "And it does not even matter much that it is not true; they will just continue to repeat the claim to discredit and weaken Tokyo."
Decadeslong row over disputed islands

Tadashi Anno, a professor of politics at Tokyo's Sophia University, told DW that he believes Japan had been working hard to maintain a stable relationship with Russia, even after Tokyo joined international condemnation of the invasion of Ukraine.
Anno said Russia's timing in turning up the heat on Japan was puzzling.
"Japan condemned the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 because it was a fundamental violation of international law, but Russia is only now pushing back hard," he said.
At the center of deteriorating ties is a territorial dispute about a chain of islands off the far north of Japan that were seized by Soviet forces after Japan's surrender in World War II.

There had been hopes in the past in Tokyo that a concerted diplomatic effort could be sufficient to convince Russia to return the islands — known as the Northern Territories in Japan and the Southern Kurils by Russia — to Japanese sovereignty.
That campaign has faltered in the past couple of years, and was further dented when Japan announced in the spring that it would be joining the NATO initiative to provide nonlethal assistance to Kyiv.

In August, President Vladimir Putin visited the disputed islands, becoming only the second Russian leader to do so. Earlier this month, a delegation of Chinese businesspeople was welcomed on one of the islands, and talks are underway on the possibility of economic cooperation.

articles.title: Taiwan: Typhoon Champi leaves 1 dead, over 500 injured
articles.summary: After killing one person and causing major disruptions in Taiwan, Typhoon Champi is now headed towards China.

image.caption: More than 500 people were injured as Typhoon Champi swept through TaiwanImage: cnsphoto/REUTERS

blocks.text: Typhoon Champi killed at least one person and left more than 500 people with injuries as it passed through Taiwan on Saturday.
Taiwan's fire department said the death toll remained at 1 a man swept ​away by waves from the island of Liuqiu, with 527 injuries during the heavy wind and torrential rain.
Several parts in Taiwan received heavy rain and strong winds that prompted authorities to cut off power, leaving thousands of people without power supply.
Some 280,000 households were knocked out of power, according to United Daily News, a local Taiwanese newspaper. By Saturday morning, the power supply was restored to 80% of the households.

blocks.caption: Despite weakening, Champi is still packing strong winds near its centerImage: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP

blocks.text: Champi also led to 259 flights cancellations, an improvement from Friday, ⁠when ​the number was almost 1,000, the Transport Ministry said.
Several trees were downed amid strong gusts In the capital Taipei.
Authorities in several districts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second day of office and school closures on Saturday.
Champi headed to China
The typhoon continued to weaken as it moved north towards the Chinese coast though it was not expected to make landfall there.
Chinese authorities have sent a team to ​the eastern province of Zhejiang as Champi ⁠approached, warning of strong winds and heavy rain through Sunday.

blocks.caption: Schools and offices were closed in several districts in Taiwan because of ChampiImage: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP

blocks.text: It said it had readied 400 rescue workers and 600 pieces of equipment, ⁠while more than 41,000 firefighters were on ​emergency duty.

Typhoon Champi started out as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the Pacific this year. While it is weakening, Champi is still packing ​gusts of around 78 km/h (126 mph) near its center, according to Taiwan's Central Weather Administration (CWA).

blocks.text: A student at a rally for President Lula da Silva
ByIone Wells
Reporting fromSão Paulo and Rio de Janeiro
In the sprawling former industrial city of Osasco, shuttered factories have given way to a shopping malls and delivery app tech companies in what is now dubbed São Paulo's "Silicon Valley."

The municipality voted for Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in 2022 but switched to the right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of Brazil's presidential election this month. Bolsonaro won that vote - and now the two men face a run-off on Sunday. Since 1989, every first-round winner has gone on to be elected president.
Like many of President Lula's traditional supporters, Gilberto Almazan, who leads a metalworkers' union here, is visibly worried.

He cries when he tells Lula's life story: a boy who grew up in hunger in the north-east, who became a metalworker, then a union leader, then a three-time president. But he's candid about how things have changed here and how the union movement that was so integral to Lula's support base is stuck in the "Middle Ages", and struggling to keep up.
"We had strong deindustrialisation here," Almazan says. "The profile of the working class changed. They are no longer predominantly industrial workers, they are service workers.
"Metal, chemical, textile factories disappeared. And five malls were built."

The word "change" comes up repeatedly among Bolsonaro supporters here. Many struggle to name specific Bolsonaro policies they like but know they want to try something different: frustrated by the economy, crime and corruption in politics – even though Flávio has been faced accusations of corruption too, which he denies.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Tairine says high prices are a problem for her

blocks.text: Tairine says high prices are a problem for her
"He brings the hope of change, that we can have a different Brazil," says lawyer Gisele Bonfim in Osasco, who decided to vote for Bolsonaro after supporting Lula in 2022.

Lula's re-election campaign has been hampered by voters turning away from him. In some cases, their frustration drove abstention, which was higher than average this year, but others like Gisele actively wanted something new.
One major reason for that is Brazil's working class has transformed seismically in places like Osasco.
Near one large shopping mall lies an open-air market where this shift is noticeable. Everyone is touting products, armed with a portable card machine.

Tairine, who sells hot dogs, used to abstain from voting, even though - as voting is compulsory in Brazil - not going to the polls incurs a fine. This year, she plans to vote for Bolsonaro. She points to high taxes paid on "everything" she buys and says these make it "so difficult for a poor person" dealing with inflation, arguing "nothing has changed" since Lula became president again.
Flávio Bolsonaro has proposed cutting government spending, government ministries, and some taxes - though he has said he'd maintain some of Lula's flagship welfare programmes.
A new working class

For his supporters, Lula is a working-class hero credited with advancing workers' rights through organising strikes and lifting millions of people out of poverty with generous social welfare programmes as president.

But across Brazil millions now work in the gig economy, a phenomenon Almazan calls "Uber-isation": driving for Uber, delivering food, or running small businesses from market stalls to providing at-home beauty treatments.
"There are a lot of workers who need more freedom, flexibility of days and hours," he says, rather than the welfare and collective action Lula offered.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Robson used to support Lula but has since switched to support Bolsonaro

blocks.text: Robson used to support Lula but has since switched to support Bolsonaro

Richard Lapper, who has written biographies of both Lula and Jair Bolsonaro – Flavio's father who was president from 2019-2022 - says the rise of individualised work and the decline of manufacturing caused by globalisation are not unique to Brazil. But because Brazil industrialised late and deindustrialised early, he argues, the effects have been sharper here. He calls Lula a "victim of his own success."

Unemployment fell to a record low, and Brazil was taken off the United Nation's Hunger Map during Lula's current presidency. But Lapper describes a crisis of "expectations" where people are now better off but don't feel it because prices have risen and household debt and interest rates are high.
Robson, 53, is a municipal civil servant in Osasco. Originally from Lula's north-eastern home state of Pernambuco, he grew up supporting him.

But he describes a country now running deficits and says its citizens are enduring the "worst phase" of its tax burden, which he blames on the Lula government's "mismanagement" of the economy and high public spending.
"Now you have to make choices: pay an instalment for your car, or put food on the table," he says.
Lula's comeback strategy

In some areas, Lula lost votes compared to 2022, even though Bolsonaro did not gain more than his father did then: 33 million people did not vote in the first round, the highest abstention since 1998.

In response, Lula's campaign has focused on mobilising hundreds of thousands of people – particularly students – on to the streets to get the vote out for round two. It claims one rally in São Paulo attracted about a million people.
"A lot of people didn't vote, they thought it wouldn't change anything," says one supporter, Leila. "Our fight is to make those people believe their vote changes things."
Aerial videos of these huge demonstrations have been plastered across social media. An image of a topless man with a six-pack waving a Lula flag at one has been shared tens of millions of times.
The strategy is that their revolution will not be televised, but it should ideally go viral.

Lula, 80, has also been using social media to dismiss criticisms that he is past his prime: calling himself the "king of selfies" and posting videos showing him running from A to B on the campaign trail.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Some people who live in the favelas fear security forces entering if Bolsonaro is elected

blocks.text: Some people who live in the favelas fear security forces entering if Bolsonaro is elected
In Maré, one of Rio's largest favelas which is controlled by rival gangs, abstention was higher than average.

This dented Lula's support, even though he still won here: among Brazil's very poorest, Lula's welfare initiatives clearly do still resonate. One 18-year-old mother in Maré, Vitoria, earns less than £300 a month and praises Lula's government for increasing the minimum wage, giving workers the right to two days off, and providing essential medicines for free.
She is sceptical of Bolsonaro's plans to designate the gang which controls this part of the favela, Comando Vermelho, as a terrorist organisation, which he lobbied the US to do earlier this year.

She thinks it will lead to authorities entering the favela to "kill, destroy, ruin families, leave blood and bodies on the ground", citing a police raid in Rio last year that killed more than 130 people.
Another resident, Andreza Dionísio, blames high abstention rates here on both last-minute changes to polling station locations, but also "a sense of hopelessness about the future."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Many Brazilians now worship in evangelical churches like the Assembleia de Deus Vitória em Cristo

blocks.text: Many Brazilians now worship in evangelical churches like the Assembleia de Deus Vitória em Cristo

Increasingly, that void of hope is being filled by the growth of the evangelical church: about a quarter of Brazilians are now evangelical. Its mega-churches offer not just a spiritual home but support with issues like childcare, employment advice and even food.
Its conservative pastors are some of Brazil's most powerful political operators.

Silas Malafaia, who has millions of followers on social media, leads the Assembleia de Deus Vitória em Cristo headquartered in the lower middle-class neighbourhood of Penha in Rio de Janeiro. He is being investigated for allegedly obstructing the coup trial of Jair Bolsonaro, which he denies and calls politically motivated.

At one two-hour sermon he preaches messages of self-improvement to an emotional crowd of hundreds, interrupted occasionally for live music interludes and breaks to collect money with card machines. The whole event is live-streamed on YouTube.

Afterwards, in his office adorned with a photo of him and the former president Jair Bolsonaro, at whose wedding he officiated, he told the BBC that without the evangelical church in working-class neighbourhoods the country would be "in a state worse than you can imagine".
"It gives these people meaning. To better their lives."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Pastor Silas Malafaia officiated at Jair Bolsonaro's wedding

blocks.text: Pastor Silas Malafaia officiated at Jair Bolsonaro's wedding
He argues Flávio Bolsonaro shares the church's values: for family, and against gender "ideology" and abortion.

The church is driving some to actively vote for Flávio Bolsonaro, but among much of Brazil's new working class, the first round feels more like a rejection of President Lula than an endorsement of his rival.
"There will never be another Lula," Gilberto Almazan fears. He intends this as a compliment, but Brazil's changing world of work means it's also probably true.
While Lula's past story still stirs great emotion for people like Almazan, his political fate may depend on whether voters think he can now offer Brazil a new one.

articles.title: As a divided Israel prepares to go to the polls, can Netanyahu pull off his greatest political trick yet?
articles.summary:
The prime minister has defined and dominated his country’s politics for three decades and is putting his rivals on the defensive before Tuesday’s general election

They chant his name, they…

blocks.text: They chant his name, they cheer and clap – and yet he is not the most dominant person in the room. Looming over the crowd that has gathered to hear Gadi Eisenkot, the former general who is the lead opposition challenger in Tuesday’s Israeli election, is a man who is not there. It is the man Eisenkot seeks to replace as prime minister, the man who first served in that role three decades ago and who has held it, on and off, for 19 of the past 30 years. It is Benjamin Netanyahu.

Naturally, the warm-up speakers at this evening rally in the modest city of Modi’in, halfway between Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, stress the virtues of Eisenkot, a son of working-class Moroccan Jews who rose through the ranks to become chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces and entered politics only four years ago. But every sentence might as well end with two words that go unspoken: unlike Bibi.

blocks.caption: Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of the Yashar party, delivers an address on the campaign trail. In an obvious reference to Benjamin Netanyahu, he has called for a ‘country without lies’. Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Even the name of Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, meaning straight or direct, carries the implied contrast with Netanyahu, who is regarded by friends and enemies alike as a maestro of the darkest political arts. When Eisenkot calls for “a country without lies”, when he calls for “responsibility and leading by example”, when he suggests US-style term limits for the role of prime minister, “because power corrupts”, everyone knows what – and who – he means.

None of this comes with rhetorical fire or theatrical panache. But the lack of charisma serves only to emphasise that Eisenkot is every inch the un-Bibi. “I think that’s an advantage,” Noa Sadeh, 56, told me after Wednesday night’s rally. “I’m fed up with people who know how to talk – like Bibi. We need someone who will do the doing part.”

Spotting a journalist with a notebook, David Nadler, 74, a retired colonel who served under Eisenkot, insisted I write down the word “integrity”, meaning “he says something, he means it, he will do it”. Another sentence ending with those silent words: unlike Bibi.

blocks.caption: Eisenkot shakes hands with Netanyahu at a swearing-in ceremony in Jerusalem in 2015 attended by the then defence minister, Moshe Ya’alon. Eisenkot has pledged to wipe out Hamas. Photograph: Menahem Kahana/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: It’s hard to overstate Netanyahu’s dominance not only over this campaign but over Israeli politics and political culture. The two blocs in this election are not left and right but Bibi and anti-Bibi. The latter camp includes at least two figures – the former PM Naftali Bennett and the Moldova-born Avigdor Lieberman – whose natural home is on the nationalist right and who both once worked closely with Netanyahu, only to fall out with him spectacularly.

Almost every political figure is defined, or defines themselves, in relation to Netanyahu. Eisenkot offers himself as the antidote, but listen to the pitch made by the far right and it too is all about the prime minister.

Netanyahu is like a shopping trolley, says Yishai Fleisher, of Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, to a group of about 30 orthodox voters in a study hall in Bet Shemesh on Thursday evening. “He has a tendency to go left, so you have to pull him to the right.” Fleischer makes the case for yet more Jewish settlements in the West Bank, to say nothing of settling Gaza; for a “ministry of emigration” that will encourage the “voluntary” departure of Palestinians; for the death penalty; for ever harsher treatment of Palestinian prisoners; for putting more guns and more ammunition into the hands of Jewish Israeli civilians – but all in the context of strengthening the resolve of a new Netanyahu-led coalition. On the right, Ben-Gvir is a moon that is rising, but Netanyahu is still the sun.

blocks.caption: Itamar Ben-Gvir, centre, the leader of the Jewish Power party, on the campaign trail in Ramla. The far-right politician is calling for more Jewish settlements in the West Bank and harsh measures against Palestinians. Photograph: Amir Cohen/Reuters

blocks.text: Partly, that’s a function of sheer longevity. But it’s also down to Netanyahu’s undimmed ability to set the political agenda. Even in this election, he has demarcated the terrain on which battle is fought. His latest poster campaign offers voters a rhyming choice of Yamin, meaning the right, or Falastin, meaning Palestine. On the right side is, of course, his own face and the Israeli flag; on the other, the leaders of the opposition parties, including Bennett and Lieberman who are adamantly opposed to a Palestinian state, all of them surrounding two heads of parties that represent Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the country’s population. The message is not subtle: vote for me, or you’ll get the Arabs.

blocks.caption: Netanyahu campaign posters are put on display in Jerusalem. The prime minister is pitching the election as a choice between himself and the Arabs. Photograph: Kevin Coombs/Reuters

blocks.text: Indeed, the closing weeks of the campaign have centred on the question of whether the anti-Netanyahu bloc of Jewish Israeli parties – currently forecast to do better than the Netanyahu bloc but to fall short of an overall majority in the Knesset – will do some kind of parliamentary deal with the mainly Arab parties, most of which have, historically, both refused to join Israeli governments and not been invited. Backed by that chunk of the media that is loudly and vociferously pro-Netanyahu, most notably the Fox News wannabe Channel 14, Netanyahu has succeeded in putting his opponents on the defensive.

A rare exception to that pattern came just this week when a Netanyahu uber-loyalist, Channel 14’s Yinon Magal, characterised Eisenkot as a Moroccan “monkey”. The racial slur was so crude that had it been used by the left to describe a politician of the right, it would have had Netanyahu denouncing Ashkenazi elitism from the rooftops (even though Netanyahu is, of course, a privileged scion of the Ashkenazi elite).

Tellingly, while the warm-up speakers in Modi’in mentioned the “monkey” remark, Eisenkot himself did not. To his admirers, that was the mark of a decent man reluctant to follow his opponents into the gutter. To the doubters, it was a sign of a politician still playing by Marquess of Queensbury rules – one who doesn’t quite appreciate what, or rather who, he is up against.

For an outside observer, the most puzzling question about this Israeli election is: how is this even close? How can the polls be showing the two blocs, pro- and anti-Netanyahu, neck and neck? Abroad, many will be baffled that Netanyahu can still be in contention given the devastation his government brought down upon Gaza, flattening much of the territory and killing more than 70,000 Palestinians, even if, as Israel says, one-third of them were Hamas combatants.

But even inside Israel, where the impact of the war on the people of Gaza is all too rarely discussed, it is no less of a riddle that Netanyahu is a serious candidate in these elections, let alone one who could emerge on top.

blocks.caption: Eisenkot, who entered politics only four years ago, is defining himself as the anti-Netanyahu candidate in Tuesday’s election. Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: To start with the most elemental fact, the biggest disaster in the country’s history happened on his watch. The massacres inflicted on civilian Israel on 7 October 2023, at the Nova music festival and at a string of southern kibbutzim, are still fresh in the memory. Stickers depicting the faces of those killed on that day adorn bus stops and railway platforms from one end of the country to the other. As Oded Levi, who voted for Netanyahu in 2022 but was in the Modi’in crowd for Eisenkot, put it: “Whoever was prime minister [then] is responsible. He has to go. For this reason alone, we need a change.”

But it hardly ends there. Netanyahu promised a war that would destroy and eradicate Hamas. That didn’t happen. Instead, Israel destroyed its own international reputation, leaving the country isolated and fast becoming a pariah state. Netanyahu promised to destroy Iran’s nuclear threat and that too didn’t happen.

blocks.caption: Raz Zarfati at a memorial to her sister, Ron, who was killed in the 7 October attacks. Netanyahu has shifted blame for the disaster. Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/AP

blocks.text: Add to that the “judicial coup” in the months before 7 October, where Netanyahu tried to weaken the restraint on his power represented by the supreme court, thereby splitting Israel in two, and the Qatargate scandal, in which his closest aides stand accused of taking money from Doha in return for boosting Qatar’s image. Along with his ongoing corruption trial, it all adds up to the mystery of why Netanyahu was not counted out long ago.

Any explanation begins with the loyalty of his base, built over three decades. Their support for him is unshakeable, unmoved even by reports that Netanyahu received credible warnings of a Hamas attack on 7 October and failed to act. They are kept on side by the PM’s enduring skill in crafting a narrative, in the case of 7 October, that everyone else is to blame except him, that he was kept in the dark by army and intelligence chiefs acting out of incompetence or something more sinister, a baseless claim advanced by his “poison machine” of media and online outriders. And he remains a consummate political operator, so gifted in the business of divide and rule that many can foresee him playing the coalition arithmetic on Wednesday morning far better than any of his rivals.

Still, that prospect has prompted a fierce reaction, one whose intensity can be felt thousands of miles from Israel. In the departure lounges of airports around the globe, you can find expat Israelis, many of them liberal and secular, heading home to vote on Tuesday. I saw it for myself as I travelled in a plane packed with those who felt it their duty to fly back and cast a vote to remove Netanyahu. That’s a group not picked up by pollsters and, who knows, in a contest that could turn on the fate of just one of the Knesset’s 120 seats, it may make a difference.

Some of that same determination was visible at the state ceremony in Jerusalem on Thursday marking the anniversary of the assassination in 1995 of the former prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, remembered still as a would-be peacemaker gunned down before a lasting accord with the Palestinians could be struck. It was not well attended – Netanyahu stayed away and sent a low-ranking minister – and it was tempting to view it as further evidence of how far to the right Israel has shifted in these past three decades, in this age of Bibi. Here were the luminaries of the old Israeli left, gathered in a burial ground.

And yet, Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats, successor party of Rabin’s, was dismissive of such talk. A former general who served with Eisenkot, and a hero of 7 October who drove south to rescue people in his own car that fateful day, Golan told me: “I’m optimistic. I never went into battle thinking ‘all right, I’m going to be killed, I’m going to be wounded’. No, I’m going to win, and we are going to win.”

Golan even believes he and his fellow opposition leaders can agree on the beginnings of “some sort of a regional, strategic process in order to bring security for the long run”. He didn’t use the words “peace process”, but it’s clear what he meant.

The word “peace” became tainted for many Israelis, associated with moves such as the 2005 withdrawal from Gaza which Netanyahu and his allies have succeeded in casting as an early step on the road to 7 October. And yet it has not vanished. A video went viral earlier in the week showing scores of young Israelis at a Negev music festival dancing and singing to Shir LaShalom, the song for peace, the anthem of those 1990s peace efforts and the last song Rabin sang before he was shot leaving a peace rally 31 years ago.

Yes, the polls are deadlocked and, yes, Netanyahu is a political magician, but the sight and sound of those young people, like the queues for planes home, have given at least some Israelis the hope that change might be coming – that the age of Bibi might, at last, be drawing to a close.

articles.title: What community means for a wine shop along Maginhawa Street
articles.summary: Through the Maginhawa Food Community, Rose Abes has found support among fellow entrepreneurs navigating the fulfillment and challenges of running their own establishments

items: Rose Abes, owner of La Rosa Vino, emphasizes the importance of community and collaboration with neighboring businesses in Quezon City, as seen in her Wine and Food Hop event.
Since opening in February 2023, Rose has successfully built a customer base and created a welcoming space for wine lovers, particularly women, while navigating a male-dominated industry.

The Maginhawa Food Community (MFC) plays a crucial role in supporting local businesses, allowing Rose to collaborate with other establishments and promote a shared goal of sustaining small businesses in the area.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – For a business owner, sending customers out the door would normally be the opposite of the goal. But for Rose Abes, owner of La Rosa Vino, sharing customers with her neighbors is part of how she does business.

On September 19, La Rosa Vino once again brought guests to walk along Maginhawa Street, Quezon City for its fourth Wine and Food Hop. This year, its day-long event paired wines with signature dishes from six partner restaurants in the neighborhood.
For Rose, these partnerships are built on something simple.
“A good relationship is very important,” she said, referring to her connection with the Maginhawa Food Community (MFC) and fellow business owners.

This is a philosophy that has shaped La Rosa Vino since Rose opened the business in February 2023. What began as her passion for wine came with a goal: to build a community of wine drinkers in Quezon City, where she saw fewer spaces devoted to wine compared with areas like Makati.

blocks.caption: FOR EVERYONE. Guests of the Wine and Food Hop include previous customers and fellow business owners from the Maginhawa Food Community. Photo from La Rosa Vino

blocks.text: But building that community also meant finding her own place in an industry she acknowledges remains largely dominated by men.
“I just need to be me,” Rose said in an interview with Rappler. “Wala akong magagawa (There’s nothing I can do) since it’s really male-dominated. So, I just need to be myself.”
Ever since she opened her wine shop, Rose has continuously grown her customer base and has found consistent support from the MFC.

Before Rose found herself as a wine shop owner, she was working in marketing and events. When the pandemic prompted her to reconsider her career, she decided to turn her passion for wine into a business of her own.
Finally, her lockdown-born passion for wine led her to change careers. She decided to take her knowledge, wine and spirit certifications, and dream to create a little nook for wine lovers.
While Rose admits that La Rosa Vino is still young, she is also proud to share that she has seen a good increase in wine lovers who now frequent her shop.
Beyond selling bottles of wine, Rose has continued introducing activities that encourage customers to explore alcoholic beverages in different ways.
“My goal of bringing my customers an experience remains,” she said.
In 2025, Rose hosted various activities in her shop partnered with the experience of drinking wine, such as vegan dining, yoga sessions, floral arrangements, and more.
This year, Rose leaned more into experiencing the alcoholic beverages themselves — one of which was a whiskey appreciation class.

“A lot of my customers showed interest in appreciation classes. It’s a deeper experience compared to what we hosted before, so I thought maybe it would not be a hit. Surprisingly, we were fully booked within two weeks!” she shared.

blocks.caption: WOMAN-OWNED. Rose Abes (center) joins fellow participants during the Wine and Food Hop. Photo from La Rosa Vino

blocks.text: Rose has also noticed that many of La Rosa Vino’s customers and event participants are women, something she believes may reflect their desire for spaces where they can enjoy and feel safe at the same time.
“I’m happy that La Rosa Vino is a comfortable space for them to enjoy alcoholic drinks. Like me, maybe they are also looking for a place to be themselves freely,” she explained.
“Perhaps the shop being woman-owned adds to that comfort,” she said.
But the intimate community Rose has built extends beyond the customers who visit La Rosa Vino.
Through the MFC, she has also found support among fellow entrepreneurs navigating the fulfillment and challenges of running their own establishments.
While her background in marketing helped her establish La Rosa Vino, Rose admitted that managing a physical business came with its own challenges.
Being part of the MFC, however gave her opportunities to collaborate with neighboring restaurants, including through La Rosa Vino’s annual Wine and Food Hop.
Formed in 2021, this network of business owners has grown from a small group of restaurant owners into a collective of 70 members.

According to its president, Jules Guiang, they started with around five restaurants and initially struggled to establish credibility among restaurant owners. They gradually earned their trust through initiatives involving local government coordination and events such as the Maginhawa Arts and Food Festival.

“We advocate for Maginhawa to remain a hub for micro and small businesses, many of which are family-owned,” said Guiang. “The MFC works to bring these concerns to the local government, especially as the area attracts more customers.”
He said the group wants to help smaller establishments remain in business and potentially grow, rather than be crowded out by larger brands.

blocks.caption: LONG-RUNNING. Wadough owner Wado Siman shares his café’s success. Photo from La Rosa Vino

blocks.text: One of the MFC’s members is Wadough’s, a pastry shop known for its minimalist cakes, including the viral wedding cake it made for actress Bea Alonzo. The shop was also the third stop on La Rosa Vino’s Wine and Food Hop.

“When I opened this café nine years ago, I imagined it as a place where I would sit down with customers and chat with them while having coffee and cake. The goal was that,” said owner Wado Siman, recalling that they never really expected the shop to be famous.

Wado believes that most of his shop’s fame is brought by pure luck, especially with the timing of going viral online during the pandemic. This success led him to gain more customers, which naturally brought customers to nearby restaurants too.

For Rose, the Wine and Food Hop is one way to put that shared goal into practice. By bringing her customers to neighboring establishments, La Rosa Vino helps introduce them to other independent businesses along Maginhawa while giving participating restaurants another opportunity to reach customers.

The event also reflects how Rose approaches running her own business. Rather than focusing solely on bringing people into La Rosa Vino, she sees value in encouraging them to explore the neighborhood and discover what other establishments have to offer.
“The MFC is very supportive with its business owners, both emotionally and physically,” Rose said, recalling that the collective helped her during her first year running a physical establishment.

blocks.caption: COMMUNITY. Guests gather around to toast the start of the Wine and Food Hop event. Photo by Elle Guison/Rappler

blocks.text: Over time, her fellow business owners have also become her friends. When asked how she found her partner establishments, she replied that they were very casual invitations of “isasali kita sa next Wine and Food Hop ko, ha? (I’ll include you in my next Wine and Food Hop, okay?)”
For Rose, these relationships have become part of how La Rosa Vino operates.
She has always envisioned La Rosa Vino developing a community that includes not only the customers who visit her shop, but also the independent businesses that share Maginhawa Street.
After all, she believes that wine is better enjoyed with company. – Rappler.com

articles.title: India news: Neha Bora refuses to sign peace bond, cites right to democratic dissent
articles.summary: Neha Bora says the peace bond violates the right to democratic dissent. The statement comes amid a wider protest calling for the removal of India's election chief. DW has more.

image.caption: Bora disputed the evidence presented by the cops, while claiming that the Central Park protest, which was cited in the police notice as evidence, was not called by AISA [FILE: October 16, 2026]Image: AFP

blocks.text: Student leader Neha Bora said on Saturday they would not sign a peace bond, alleging that the evidence cited by police was factually incorrect.

The All India Students' Association (AISA) leader, who uses they/them pronouns, made the statement a day after the Delhi High Court dismissed their plea challenging a police notice directing them to execute a Rs 10,000 (€94.39) personal bond with surety to maintain peace.

AISA and India's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), along with other organizations, are demanding the resignation of controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar after a newspaper investigation alleged impropriety during a large-scale voter-roll revision, which saw the deletion of more than 130 million names from draft electoral rolls nationwide.
"Our concern is that people may be deprived of one of their most fundamental democratic rights: the right to vote," Bora wrote in an oped in the Indian Express newspaper on Saturday.

Bora said AISA had not called the Central Park protest cited in the notice as grounds for the bond. They also questioned whether peaceful demonstrations against alleged voter deletions under the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise could be considered a breach of peace.

"It is essential that peaceful protests and democratic demonstrations on the streets are not declared a breach of peace," they said, adding that they would challenge the interpretation and enforcement of such bonds in court.
Bora said neither they nor AISA would sign the bond, arguing that it violated the fundamental right to democratic dissent.

articles.title: Pulong Duterte responds to De Lima's remarks on libel, cyber libel raps
articles.summary: Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo "Pulong" Duterte called out ML Party-list Representative Leila de Lima for criticizing his move to file cyber libel and libel charges against GMA Network…

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 12:38pm

Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo "Pulong" Duterte called out ML Party-list Representative Leila de Lima for criticizing his move to file cyber libel and libel charges against GMA Network Inc. and several journalists, saying he was merely exercising his right to defend his name.
In a Facebook post past midnight Saturday, Duterte said every citizen is entitled to such protections under the law.

"De Lima, as a lawyer and former human rights advocate, you know that every person has the right to protect themselves from any accusation. Filing a case through the legal process is not an attack on the freedom of speech, but a right that every citizen has," Duterte said in Bisaya.

On Friday, Duterte lodged a libel and cyber libel complaint against National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag and dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. over claims of cash delivery to their family.
Executives and journalists of GMA Network were also included in the complaint.
Hours after the filing, De Lima issued a statement saying the complaint was meant to strike fear among media practitioners.

"This is clearly an attempt to silence journalists and truth-seekers, depriving them of their freedom of the press. Filing a libel case against a media network and its journalists for doing their job of reporting allegations of corruption sends a chilling message to other media practitioners," said De Lima, who also serves as senior deputy minority leader of the House of Representatives.
However, Duterte insisted that press freedom has its limits when it violates the rights of others.

"Freedom of the press is important for democracy, but it comes with the responsibility to ensure the safety of those who report and give opportunities to the other side to respond. Reporting an allegation and proving it to be true are two different things," Duterte said.
Reminding De Lima she previously faced controversies and allegations, Duterte said he hopes that her stance on justice and the right to defense remains unchanged.

De Lima was a justice secretary and senator who was a staunch critic of the Davao City congressman's father, former president Rodrigo Duterte. She was jailed in February 2017 during the Duterte administration and spent nearly seven years in detention on drug-related charges. All of her charges were cleared in June 2024.

"A person's right should not be defended at the expense of their own safety, which can be used as a pretext to silence the media. In the same way, freedom of speech should not be used to silence others who are asking for justice," Paolo Duterte said, as he called for a fair, evidence-based process to dispute allegations instead of what he called prejudiced judgment.
As a parting shot to De Lima, Duterte said, "Just stay in Congress, be cute, smile, smile."
In a statement, GMA Network said it has yet to receive a copy of the complaint.
"We will review the matter and comment accordingly upon receipt," it said.

Gracioso previously alleged that he delivered cash to former president Duterte, congressman Duterte, and his sister Vice President Sara Duterte upon the instruction of former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
The Davao City lawmaker has dismissed Gracioso's claims as "pure fiction."
The vice president has also denied the allegations and filed her affidavit with the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI).
Velasco's camp has said the allegations against him have "no basis." — VDV, GMA News

Four soldiers were killed and 39 injured on Oct. 17 when a fire that began during a training exercise on an anti-grenade launching range was picked up by fierce winds.

· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 24, 2026 12:09 AM EDT | Last Updated: 21 minutes ago
U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says the United States has offered to help following the deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta.
The military has said the fire took less than a minute to race about a kilometre, where a different training exercise was taking place on the base about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

items: Rapid spread of fire was main factor in CFB Wainwright deaths, injuries: top military commander

blocks.text: Twenty-seven soldiers remain in hospital, including 13 in critical condition, many of them with severe burns.

The military said there are three different investigations into the tragedy and could not say when more answers will be available about how the tragedy occurred.
'Getting the facts right' commander corrects details on deadly Wainwright fire
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre thanked Hoekstra for reaching out to him as MP for the riding of Battle River-Crowfoot, where the base is located.
"We deeply appreciate this gesture of support for our injured soldiers and their families at such a difficult time," Poilievre wrote in a social media post Friday.
The federal Opposition leader said his office has informed the defence minister and the Alberta government of the offer "whether these additional resources and expertise are needed."

items: Canada's top soldier questioned over deadly CFB Wainwright fire

articles.title: Arrest made after fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat
articles.summary: Around 200 emergency personnel are deployed to fight the blaze at the Nazi dictator's Alpine residence in Germany.

blocks.text: Police in the south German state of Bavaria have detained a suspect during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.
Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 (19:15 GMT) on Friday, and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.
Difficult terrain was hindering efforts to extinguish the blaze and it was still burning early on Saturday, police said, with some 200 emergency personnel deployed. There were no reports of injuries.
The Nazi dictator used the retreat, which lies above the town of Berchtesgaden, as a part-time seat of government and met commanders there to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941.
A criminal investigation is under way to determine whether the suspect is connected to the fire.
Hitler also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — France saw some of the worst unrest in years as huge protests occurred across the country over the cost of living and underfunded public services. Nationwide demonstrations had erupted into riots on October 17, with a town hall torched, shops pillaged, and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country.
On October 18, French President Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm. “Looking at these images, we have all asked ourselves: What was going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?”
“Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it. Tonight, we all feel anger and shame.” Macron said in a televised address to the nation.

The unrest has been attributed to far-left groups, while the government faces criticism for underestimating public anger over living costs and declining services, leading to heightened tensions ahead of upcoming presidential elections.

Meanwhile, Pope Leo returned to St. Peter’s Square on October 21, waving to pilgrims and blessing babies from his open-air popemobile as he held his first general audience at the Vatican since undergoing lung cancer surgery eight days ago. articles.title: Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat catches fire, police say
articles.summary: Authorities have arrested a suspect as firemen try to put out the fire in Bavaria, near the Austrian border.

image.caption: The site once housed the Nazi leader's heavily fortified country residence [FILE: Jun 21, 2004]Image: Peter Kneffel/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A fire broke out at the Kehlsteinhaus retreat, more commonly known as Adolf Hitler's Eagle's Nest, on Friday evening, Bavarian police said.
The Kehlsteinhaus was engulfed in flames, a police statement read, adding that a suspect has been arrested and the incident was being criminally investigated.
What do we know so far about the Kehlsteinhaus fire?
A fire alarm went off at the Kehlsteinhaus on the Obersalzberg in Berchtesgaden at around 9:15 p.m. local time (1915 GMT) on Friday, the police said in a statement.
"The fire brigades, who were alerted immediately, could already see flames clearly visible at the Kehlsteinhaus as they approached," the police statement read.
Firefighters struggled to reach the Kehlsteinhaus, which sits at some 1,834 meters (6,017 feet) above sea level, with their engines.
Police added that the building and its immediate vicinity could only be entered while wearing respiratory protective equipment (RPE).
Police said they were unaware of any injuries as of yet.
The site once housed Hitler's heavily fortified country residence, where he is believed to have partially written his book "Mein Kampf."
It remains a symbol of the Nazi regime and is among only a few monuments of the Hitler era that survived the World War II bombing unscathed. Today, it is home to a popular restaurant.

articles.title: DepEd using data-driven criteria in determining classroom allocation --Angara
articles.summary: The Department of Education is using data-driven criteria in its construction strategy to determine classroom allocations according to school needs, DepEd Secretary Sonny Angara said.

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 10:37am
The Department of Education is using data-driven criteria in its construction strategy to determine classroom allocations according to school needs, DepEd Secretary Sonny Angara said.

Angara made the statement as he acknowledged the report of the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) on gaps in allocations for local government units (LGUs) with the highest estimated classroom shortages based on initial 2026 allocations.

The Education department said its classroom needs assessment and validated school-site priorities serve as basis for identifying projects to implement, including those through partnerships with qualified LGUs, as per DepEd Memorandum No. 038, s. 2026.

“We share the same mission with EDCOM. Through strategic partnerships with qualified LGUs, we ensure that resources go directly to where our schools and learners need them most,” Angara said Thursday.

“Ang alokasyon natin para sa mga silid-aralan ay dapat direktang tumutugon sa mga eskwelahang pinakamatindi ang pangangailangan. Kailangan naka-base sa tunay na datos ang ating mga desisyon para bawat pisong inilalaan natin, tunay na nararamdaman sa ating mga paaralan," he said.
(Our allocations for classrooms should directly meet the needs of schools with the greatest needs. Our decisions should be based on valid data so each peso allocated will be felt in our schools.)
DepEd said they will continue to weigh the severity of shortages, site readiness, project feasibility, and implementation timelines in deciding on classroom allocations.

It is deploying a multi-pronged strategy integrating Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH)-led construction, LGU partnerships, Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs), DepEd Learning Continuity Spaces (LCS),and collaborative initiatives with both government and private sector organizations.
The DepEd said allocations cover 439 LGUs, 1,955 schools, and 8,777 classrooms nationwide under the current LGU-led classroom construction initiative.

"This infrastructure rollout spans 81 provincial LGUs accounting for 4,043 classrooms across 1,022 schools, 127 city LGUs covering 3,123 classrooms across 468 schools, and 231 municipal LGUs encompassing 1,611 classrooms across 465 schools," it added.
DepEd also had agreements with Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (PAGCOR) and 48 LGUs which led to 576 classrooms to be built in priority communities.

The department said it requires regular physical and financial progress reporting, technical validation, and monitoring protocols across division, regional, and central office levels to strengthen transparency and accountability.

“To truly deliver for our learners, we need a transparent and evidence-based approach. It is the only way to ensure that available resources are directly translated into classrooms where they are needed the most,” Angara said. —KG, GMA News

articles.summary:
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled

Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more…

blocks.text: Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.

Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan.

blocks.caption: Waves generated by Typhoon Champi crash against a seawall in Keelung. Photograph: Ann Wang/Reuters

blocks.text: Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
