articles.title: Seven killed and 40 injured after gunmen open fire at church funeral in Jordan
articles.summary:
Footage broadcast on state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots

Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on…

blocks.text: Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said.
The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 180km (110 miles) south of the capital, Amman.

Footage broadcast on Jordanian state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots. A third man who appears to be holding a semiautomatic rifle then approaches and opens fire, and all three then run toward the church.
Video footage taken by witnesses shows broken glass and pools of blood on the floor of the church.

Dorgham Halasa, who was among the mourners inside the church, said intense gunfire erupted 15 minutes after the funeral had started, and then people started running. “It was a weird situation, and heavy gunfire,” Halasa said.

He did not see the gunmen, but said other people reported seeing four of them. The Associated Press could not independently verify the number of assailants, and Jordan’s security services did not immediately release details.

A government statement said that the attack was “carried out by unknown assailants,” but didn’t say whether any gunmen were captured or killed. It said that “investigations are under way at full speed”.
Jordan declared three days of national mourning, according to the kingdom’s Petra news agency.
Karak is home to a minority Christian population.

In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed those gunmen after a long standoff.
Jordan’s health minister Ibrahim al-Budour said two of those wounded are in critical condition.

King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan “will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties” and offered his “deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded”.

Jordan’s prime minister Jafar Hassan said during a security meeting in Karak on Friday evening that the attack was a result of terrorist ideology and blind extremism. He said the assailants will be punished and legal measures taken against those who seek to introduce extremism.
Condemnation of the slayings came from around the region, including from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman.

Ahmed al-Tayeb in Cairo, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, the Sunni Muslim world’s foremost religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of victims in Friday’s shooting, calling it a “heinous terrorist attack.”
Iraqi foreign minister Fuad Hussein called his Jordanian counterpart and “affirmed Iraq’s solidarity with Jordan in the face of terrorism”, Hussein’s office said in a statement.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the attack during a funeral as “especially heinous,” spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said. “The secretary-general also calls for all those responsible to be found and to be held to account.”

articles.title: Embattled Greens senator Jordon Steele-John confirms leave from parliament after allegations against him made public
articles.summary:
WA politician says he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be ‘unacceptable’

  • Get our

blocks.text: Jordon Steele-John has confirmed he will not attend parliament next week as the embattled Greens senator releases a letter detailing the allegations against him.
After days of confusion following historical complaints about alleged misconduct were publicly aired in the media, Steele-John posted a statement to social media late Friday night.

In the statement, the Western Australian senator said he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be “unacceptable”. He will instead focus on seeing through an independent investigation to its conclusion, he said.

“Over the past few days there has been a growing chorus calling on me not to attend parliament next week. I have explored attending digitally but have been informed that would also be unacceptable,” Steele-John said.
Steele-John said a precedent of keeping parliamentarians out of parliament after “allegations of allegations” are made had now been set.
“Had an allegation or complaint been made against me, I would have taken these actions immediately,” he said.

The 32-year-old senator’s attendance in parliament for the remainder of the year had been uncertain after a public stoush with the party’s leader, David Shoebridge, over whether he was on leave while an investigation was undertaken into allegations he had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.
The complaints are now subject to an independent investigation commissioned by the WA Greens and have been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission.
Shoebridge claimed Steele-John had requested leave and he accepted it last week after seven party members penned a letter to the leader urging an investigation into the claims.

The three-page letter sent on 13 October, and first published by the Nine newspapers, said the authors had been “made aware of multiple allegations of serious misconduct” against Steele-John about his “behaviour in the presence of women”.
The letter referred to an allegation of sexual harassment at a Greens campaign event in 2024 that the alleged victim had not reported out of fear and backlash. The letter provided no further detail.
In another, the authors referred to an allegation of “serious sexual misconduct” in 2025.
Also contained in the letter was a reference to a disparaging nickname for Steele-John – “feels on wheels” – which the authors said implied he had a reputation for acting inappropriately.

“To be clear, all signatories to this letter know that an allegation does not equate to a fact and/or guilt. We simply believe that it is in the party’s best interests to ensure that every allegation is investigated thoroughly, in alignment with community and member expectations,” the letter’s authors wrote.

Steele-John was defiant in a lengthy statement last Sunday, rejecting the allegations against him, denying he agreed to take leave from parliament and accusing an internal faction within the Greens of playing “nasty political games” in their decision to release the letter to the media.

Steele-John said any claims of his alleged behaviour should be investigated “fairly and thoroughly” but accused an “unofficial faction” within the WA branch had released the complaint letter to the media in a bid to oust him from the Senate.
Guardian Australia has confirmed the WA police told Steele-John the investigation was closed in May with no charges.

articles.title: Helen Haines’s condition improves days after losing both legs from alleged attack
articles.summary:
Independent MP now serious but stable, according to update from Melbourne’s Alfred hospital

  • Get our breaking news…

blocks.text: Independent MP Helen Haines’s condition has been downgraded to serious but stable after she lost both legs following an alleged attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria on Monday afternoon.
The Alfred hospital in Melbourne provided an update on Haines’s condition on Saturday morning.
“The patient is in a serious but stable condition at The Alfred on Saturday morning,” a spokesperson for the hospital said.

Haines, the federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a car in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon. Surgeons were trying to save her right leg on Tuesday, but both legs had to be amputated due to the seriousness of her injuries.

Police on Tuesday charged Brendan Nugent, 43, from nearby Tarrawingee with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official. Police have since charged him with two additional offences – cultivating and possessing cannabis – according to court documents.
Nugent appeared in court on Wednesday and did not apply for bail.
On Friday, an update on Haines’s social media accounts said her staff were working to reopen her electorate offices next Thursday.
“What happened on Monday has deeply affected Helen’s family and all of her staff. Many of us witnessed the incident and some were among the first to come to her aid,” the post read.

“As Helen takes the time she needs to recover, we will take time to look after ourselves and one another, too. Healing will take time, and we ask for your understanding as we navigate the days and weeks ahead.”
The alleged attack on Haines has reverberated through Australian politics, prompting conversations about the temperature of political debate and mental services in regional Victoria.

articles.title: White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom
articles.summary: From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on some products, including certain machinery, and placed on others, such as carpets.

blocks.text: The Trump administration is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods two weeks before the midterm elections, after a Republican candidate in a key US Senate race said she had lobbied for the change.
From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on products including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment", the White House said on Friday.
Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race to keep her seat in Maine, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.
The US imposed a 50% levy on $20bn (£15bn) worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries collapsed in August.
Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures in response to the US tariffs, which Prime Minister Mark Carney said were "necessary to protect our workers".
Last month, Carney matched the US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after the breakdown in talks. Trump had imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US car, dairy and alcohol exports.
The White House said that, while tariffs would be lifted from some items, including some packing crates and boxes, they would be introduced on other items such as carpets and "waste products".
It said the action reflected US President Donald Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade".
She wrote on X that the tariff exemptions were on products that were "crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers".

Collins' Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, responded: "Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire."

Maine borders the Canadian provinces New Brunswick and Quebec. Its economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the months-long trade war.
Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state.
Also on Friday, Trump said Canada was "working very hard" on a ⁠trade ​deal with the US.
Carney, who has sought closer ties with Europe since the tariff war erupted, said that Canada was open to a mutually beneficial deal, but was willing to wait it out.

"We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there," he said on Friday, according to Canadian broadcaster CBC. "If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that."

LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada.

articles.title: Rubio tells Cubans ‘now is the time’ to act to see political change
articles.summary:
US secretary of state makes comments after Trump tells US rally warships could intervene on return from Iran

Marco Rubio urged Cubans seeking political change in their country to act, saying…

blocks.text: Marco Rubio urged Cubans seeking political change in their country to act, saying “now is the time” moments after Donald Trump told a Friday rally for candidates in south Florida that US warships could intervene in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war.

The US secretary of state, in his social media post addressed “to those who seek to create positive change”, urged Cubans to capitalize on Trump’s plans. “The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA,” Rubio said.

The top US diplomat, whose parents left Cuba for the United States before the socialist revolution there, seemed to mistakenly use the word “discrete”, meaning separate, rather than “discreet”, meaning private or secret.

Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days before midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the US war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries.

“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”

Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would “be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.

In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of US military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous US presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it”.

Rubio told reporters separately that Cuba had been a national security threat for years because of its ties to US adversaries and that Trump was intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wanted to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the US could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.
Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a 29 September interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.

“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.

“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing. We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”

Rubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. But the US side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.

During his address to the United Nations general assembly last month, Trump said Rubio – son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership – was “deep into negotiations with Cuba”, saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep”.
Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal”, adding: “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”

Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana.

Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk , and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have immigrated, many to the United States.

articles.title: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
articles.summary: She was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo.

blocks.text: Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease.
A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said.
Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added.
All the cases were within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry said.
More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
Kenya's latest victim was a "direct contact and close family member of the first case (deceased) and was under quarantine when she developed symptoms" on 13 October, the health ministry said.

The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later.
Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner.
The US has warned its citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.

Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.

Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from DR Congo and nine other countries it considers to be at high risk: Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.

articles.title: Thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding predicted for much of Australia
articles.summary:
Parts of Queensland, Victoria and South Australia can expect severe storms on Saturday, moving into NSW and Tasmania by Sunday

  • Get our
articles.byline: Adeshola Ore with Australian Associated Press

blocks.text: Severe thunderstorms and heavy rain will sweep across most Australian states this weekend, adding to the deluge in an already drenched Queensland.

Flash flooding in south-east Queensland this week prompted hundreds of SES callouts and the closure of multiple schools. On Saturday morning, the Bureau of Meteorology had nine flood warnings in place for south Queensland.
The BoM is now warning of severe thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding across South Australia, Victoria, NSW, Tasmania.

Senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, David Crock, said severe thunderstorms and heavy rain were forecast across multiple locations in central and eastern Queensland on Saturday, including Rockhampton, Gladstone, Bundaberg, the Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Roma.

Severe storms could also sweep through parts of Victoria, including Melbourne’s eastern suburbs and central and eastern South Australia. Heavy rain is expected to develop in Tasmania overnight into Sunday morning.
“There’s plenty of rain across the south-east, as well as plenty of showers and storms and rain across much of Queensland as well, after what’s already been a really wet week,” Crock said.
The cold front will move across NSW on Sunday, bringing severe thunderstorms to the west of the state as well as north-eastern Victoria, Sydney and Brisbane.
“Tomorrow is a threat for thunderstorms right across eastern Australia, with severe thunderstorms likely through a wide part of inland eastern Australia,” he said.
This week, multiple areas in Queensland were hit by more than twice their average October rainfall across a few days.
“It was an incredibly wet week in Queensland. Much more typical of summer or January or February than this time of year,” Crock said.
The Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Caboolture were hit by flash flooding and recorded a seven-day rainfall total of 300-400mm of rain, with some areas reaching 450mm.

“It’s been notable how persistent this weather pattern has been, how much moisture has pumped in … then how those rainfall totals have accumulated across seven to 10 days through Queensland and northern New South Wales,” Crock said.
On Thursday, torrential rain in south-east Queensland caused flash flooding, water rescues and hundreds of calls for help while several schools were forced to close on Friday.
Thursday’s heavy rain stretched from Caboolture down to the Border Ranges, with some places copping well over 200mm falls.
The Queensland fire department carried out more than 16 swift-water rescues, including using a raft to retrieve an elderly man clinging to the roof of his vehicle at Caboolture.

articles.title: Are California voters about to impose world's first 'tax on billionaires'?
articles.summary: Voters are about to decide if the mega-rich among them should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
BySareen Habeshian
Reporting fromLos Angeles
Few places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US state known for glamour, coastal mega-mansions and being home to many rich and famous.

Now voters are about to decide if the mega-rich among them - names that include media mogul Oprah Winfrey, Meta head Mark Zuckerberg, Skims cofounder and reality television star Kim Kardashian and filmmaker George Lucas - should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.
Proposition 40 is aimed at levying a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of all of California's billionaires.

There are a little more than 200 such individuals in the state - but that hasn't stopped the measure from dividing leaders and causing some of its ultra-wealthy residents to flee. One billionaire businessman says he's brought jobs to California, but the proposition made him feel "a little bit like I wasn't wanted".
But the vote is also offering regular everyday residents a voice on an issue that has riled politics for decades.

"I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap.

The state has the largest economy in the country - and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the whole of the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the globe. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps.

Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system.

Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill.
"If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she told the BBC.

blocks.caption: A "Yes to 40 This Lawn Is Watered By Billionaire Tears" yard sign among merchandise for sale during a "Yes on 40 for Ballots Over Billionaires" rally in San Francisco, California, US, on Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images

While the ballot measure has many supporters - including some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - it has faced fierce opposition from a variety of figures, from billionaires to the state's liberal governor.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin has given more than $100 million to a political nonprofit funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax, the Los Angeles Times reports, external.

California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose tenure is coming to an end, is perhaps the most notable political leader opposing it. He has voiced concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.

A September poll, external from the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times found the proposition has not clearly won over a majority of voters, with 45% of likely voters in favour of the tax, 42% opposed and 13% undecided.
The statewide ballot measure would need to be approved by a majority of residents.

California is not the first place to toy with the idea of taxing the rich. Also on the West Coast, voters in US state of Washington are considering whether to accept or reject a "millionaires tax" - a 9.9% tax on income over $1m a year.

While wealth taxes were once a fairly common form of taxation in Europe, they have rapidly fallen out of favour and now only exist in three European countries – Spain, Norway and Switzerland, says Dr Kristian Niemietz, head of political economy at the Institute of Economic Affairs.

Niemietz believes wealth taxes are "more trouble than they are worth" because they cause administrative issues, suppress investment, lead to capital flight and, in the end, do not raise much revenue, she said.

In the case of Norway, a local news organisation found that an increase in the wealth tax led to more super wealthy people leaving the country in 2022, external than in the preceding 13 years combined. A study on Switzerland, external found that a 0.1 percentage point increase in a wealth tax reduced taxable wealth by 3.5%.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly  given more than $100 million to a political nonprofit funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax

blocks.text: Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly given more than $100 million to a political nonprofit funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax

The California measure, if approved, would apply retroactively to those with a net worth of at least $1bn who resided in California as of 1 January 2026. At least six of the state's 200 plus billionaires have reportedly left California ahead of that deadline to avoid the tax.
They include Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, venture capitalist Peter Thiel, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Hankey Group founder Don Hankey.
Hankey, a Los Angeles billionaire who has lived in California all his life, told Forbes he left for the state of Nevada as a result of the proposed wealth tax.

"I think we've created a lot of jobs in California. We have a few thousand people working for us and we have a profit sharing plan. And I have to leave the state," he added, saying the measure made him feel like he wasn't "wanted" in the state.

Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg told the company's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California over the proposed tax. To prevent him from leaving the state - where the company is headquartered - Meta agreed to a new stock deal that gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn, even more shares in the company to make up for the billions he would lose if the measure passes in November. Estimates say he could owe as much as $12.5bn.

DoorDash cofounder Andy Fang, who has an estimated net worth of $1.6bn, has called the measure "stupid" and wrote on X that "proposals like this make it irresponsible for me not to plan leaving the state".

blocks.caption: Chart of California billionaire's wealth

blocks.text: Meanwhile, businessman Tom Steyer, who ran an unsuccessful bid for California governor earlier this year, is one of the few billionaires who has said, external he would vote in favour of the tax. Steyer said that although he believes the way the measure is written is "problematic", it is necessary to protect vulnerable Californians.
Huang, too, has expressed support of paying the levy.

"I don't mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I'm okay with that," the Nvidia chief executive said in an interview with the BBC's news partner in the US, CBS. "I am the ultimate American Dream."
Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a vocal champion against income inequality, has campaigned in support of Prop 40.
While at a Los Angeles rally, Sanders said billionaires "believe, like the monarchs of the 19th century, that they have a God-given right to rule".
"They have all the wealth; they got all the power, and who the hell do you think you are challenging them? Well, I think on Nov 3 they're going to learn a very powerful lesson".

Income inequality in the US is at some of its highest levels, external in over three decades, with the top 1% of households owning nearly 32% of all US wealth in the third quarter of 2025. It is also near historic highs in California.

Economic inequality is a concern among most Californians, with 72% believing that the gap between the rich and poor is widening and a similar share holding that state government should do more to reduce the gap, according to a statewide survey, external from the Public Policy Institute of California.
Trebbi says it is an "anti-elite, anti-system sentiment that is behind a policy" like Prop 40.
"This is really not about Prop 40," he says. It's about trying to "re-balance the scale a little bit".

articles.title: Ruins of Limoges city hall a symbol of France divided by national protests
articles.summary: Younger Limoges residents see the destruction of their town hall as unfortunate collateral damage in a wider movement. For others, the fire was an unacceptable tragedy.

blocks.text: For weeks, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly young, have engaged in protests that have only increased in size and scope. What started off as a demonstration over the poor state of high schools has expanded to a general frustration, even anger, over how challenging and expensive life has become.

In the backdrop is a daunting fiscal deficit, one of the biggest in Europe, and political candidates from across the spectrum claiming to have the answers ahead of presidential elections in six months' time.
In the middle is a centrist government, which is short on solutions, a majority in the National Assembly and time. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu visited Limoges on Friday evening.

Officials have banned demonstrations in various cities and promised to boost police numbers over the weekend to avoid a repeat of the rioting. That includes in Limoges, where overnight curfews have been announced, along with a limit on gatherings to 10 people in the centre.

Proud as the French are of their politics being rooted in street demonstrations, many in Limoges felt the town hall's destruction went far beyond the parameters of reasonable protest. But not everyone.
Whether the destruction of Limoges town hall changes the course and tone of an increasingly polarised political debate depends on who you ask.
"Of course it was really sad, it's a symbol of the republic, but what is more important: a town hall or people living in poverty?" asks Alexander, 24.

It is student night at the Lord John pub, and Alexander is one of several wearing a faluche, a colourful, traditional French student beret. Many chatting under the mist from their vapes took part in the demonstrations last weekend.
I ask Alexander whether the widespread looting and fires seen last weekend, with €500,000 (£420,000) of reported damage in Limoges, helped his argument?
"For some people it's a catastrophe and some things are not acceptable," he admits.
Jade, a 19-year-old, medical student, has a similar opinion: "I think burning the town hall is sad, but it's not the saddest part of the protests."
She complains of having to live on €300 per month.
"I feel we are not respected as young adults."

Their views on the town hall's fate are not replicated in Limoges' imposing market halls, where neat, narrow timbers sitting upon studded steel girders have been painted a duck-egg blue, using the same engineering approach as the Eiffel Tower.
This has been a "week of chaos" that 63-year-old Jean Roger Faucher would like to forget.
In a region renowned for producing beef, his family has run his fishmonger stool here for more than a century.
"It left us stunned," he says. "I got married in the town hall, so it had an unimaginable effect on us."
Asked whether he had sympathy for the protesters, Faucher said it was more complicated than that.
"On one side you have people with grievances you can understand, but from the moment there is vandalism and the lives of local residents are put at risk, then we can't accept it," he adds.
Among those tending to their iced displays of fresh produce or quietly sipping a steaming coffee, there is a desire for the temperature of the demonstrations to decrease.
"Of course, life is expensive!' says Pascale Vuylsteke, 59. "Life isn't all a calm river, it's complicated, but we grit our teeth and we work," she tells me leaning over shelves of butchered pork.
Pascale says she works 100 hours a week and struggles to understand why so many others have taken to the streets so easily.

Limoges has found itself at the heart of social action before. In the 19th Century, around the time the town hall was built, the development of its industries, notably in porcelain, led to it becoming a major centre for the French labour movement.

In 2026, the town sits centre-stage once more in a political rupture, although there is a broad hope that the loss of a prominent piece of its history will steer the demonstrations away from destruction and back to debate.
With France's political polarisation set to continue and further protests planned, it is a scenario far from assured.
Additional reporting by Paul Pradier.

articles.title: Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election
articles.summary: The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests to form the biggest challenge to Vučić's rule.

blocks.text: Ilija Srdanović may head the list of candidates – but he is not the movement's leader and would not necessarily be first choice prime minister if they won.

Srdanović insists that the Student List has a clear vision: "We offer to our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time."

The other candidates on the Student List range from academics to athletes – and economists to engineers. None of them has a political background. But the students who selected them believe that is a strength, rather than a weakness.

"We've gathered people who are actually the best in their fields, and we really think that they are competent enough to rule the country," says Aleksandra, a student at Novi Sad University who only wants to give her first name.

"All of them are gathered around the same vision of a country where the freedom of speech is ruling, where you can walk to your home in the middle of the night and you will not be beaten up by some hooligans," she adds.
The Student List and its supporters say that Aleksandar Vučić and the SNS dominate state institutions and media coverage.

At the last parliamentary election in 2023, the International Election Observation Mission noted "overwhelming ruling party advantage" due to "bias in the media" and "misuse of public office and resources".
The BBC approached leading figures in the SNS for an interview but was not offered a response.
Protests followed, with participants accusing the authorities of corruption and having "blood on their hands".
"This is a problem for the government," says Magda Anastasijevic, the Eastern Europe analyst for the conflict monitor, ACLED.
"Vučić has survived this in the past, he was always able to find a scapegoat and blame whatever problems on them. This was not the case for the canopy."
On the diplomatic front, he has performed a delicate balancing act.

Membership talks with the EU continue, albeit fitfully, even as Serbia retains close ties with Russia and China – both countries that refuse to recognise Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia.
Vučić has warned those links could be severed if the Student List took power.
"When you ask them: will you impose sanctions on Russia? Silence, umming and ah-ing, but no answer," he told the audience at a pre-election rally.
"You know what the Chinese think, you've heard what Vladimir Putin said. So you decide. Think about who has our best interests at heart."

The final rallies of the campaign saw the SNS stage an event at Belgrade Arena, with Aleksandar Vučić as the only speaker. But on the other side of the Sava River, the Student List attracted a reported 150,000 people in Slavija Square to listen to a mixture of students and candidates.
The contrasting visions were clear to see: the strong, sole leader – or a collective approach. Now Serbia's electorate must decide which they prefer.

articles.title: Father who killed Oregon school shooter describes anguish over children he couldn't save
articles.summary: Kaylub Giamanco, has been hailed as a hero for killing a teenager who fatally shot three children and a teacher.

blocks.text: A father who fatally shot a gunman at his daughters' school in the US state of Oregon has described his anguish over being unable to save more pupils after "hearing children pleading for their lives".
Three students and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student at Silver Rail Elementary School earlier this month. The attacker was then killed by Kaylub Giamanco.

"I want to apologise for not saving their babies," Giamanco, who has been hailed as a hero, said of his thoughts for the parents of the children killed, in an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) that aired on Friday.
"The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save."
Giamanco, 36, said he wanted to meet the victims' families and "cry with them and hold them".
He credited a teacher who fought the attacker with giving him the chance to intervene without losing his own life.
"I would love to give her a hug because that's a real true hero," he said.

The students who were killed were all boys, aged five, eight and 11. They were among six people in total who were shot in a classroom at the school, police said. Alongside the teacher who was killed, another child and a teacher were wounded.
Giamanco told OPB that the day of the attack began with breakfast and making packed lunches. He and his wife had spent extra time getting their daughters ready because it was school picture day.
The carpenter had taken lunch to work but decided to go home to eat with his wife instead. That decision brought him past the school as the attack began.
He initially wondered whether someone carrying a long gun was playing a prank. Then he saw him fire at a pickup truck and head towards the school.
Giamanco retrieved a handgun from his vehicle and called emergency services.
"I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die'," he told the broadcaster.
He followed the attacker, who shot through the school's locked glass doors. Hearing children pleading for their lives and more gunfire, Giamanco crawled towards the building.
"I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do," he said.
Giamanco crawled through a shattered window and reached the classroom, where a teacher was locked in a struggle with the gunman. He opened the door and fired.
Giamanco told OPB he fired again when the attacker reached for his weapon. He then placed his own gun on the ground and raised his hands as an officer appeared.
He described feeling like the "last line of defence" between the children and the gunman, and said he "was supposed to be there" that day.
Afterwards, he called his wife to say he would not be home for lunch and that she needed to get to the school immediately. He then called his mother to tell her what had happened.
"Mum, I just had to take the life of what I think is might be a child because he ran into my daughter's school with a gun," he said.
Police identified the gunman as Griffin J John II - a former pupil who had attended special education classes at the school. His motive remains under investigation.

Police said the teacher who confronted the attacker had thrown her phone at him, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said she "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
The youngest victim was Rhoam Summer, aged five. His father said the family was "broken and lost".
Megan Lambert, 25, the teacher who was killed, was working in what her family described as her "dream job".
"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said.
The other two boys have not been publicly named at their families' request.
The injured teacher has been named as Becky Drury, 54. She said in a statement shared with US media that the gunman shot her as she tried to shut her classroom door.

articles.title: France to deploy 70,000 police officers ahead of protests
articles.summary: With new protests in France planned for this weekend, the authorities pledged to do everything in their power to prevent looting, violence and vandalism.

image.caption: France has seen several peaceful protests since the violent clashes of October 17Image: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS

blocks.text: As France braces for new protests on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned that calls for violence and looting were circulating online and pledged to deploy 70,000 police officers to secure order across the country.
"We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all those who commit acts of violence," Nunez told reporters on Friday.
France: Why students are taking to the streets

The regular police officers will be reinforced by elite units, mounted police and heavy vehicles, and also equipped with helicopters, water cannon, drones and anti-drone systems, according to the minister.
"We will be extremely vigilant," he added, vowing to "let absolutely nothing pass."
Paris storekeepers prepare for more looting
The apparent show of force comes a week after riots ripped through Paris and other major cities.

While the ongoing political standoff started with students demanding better facilities, more teachers, and other improvements to the country's education system, it has grown into a general outpouring of anger over the cost of living.
Last Saturday, the protests escalated into violent riots, with authorities accusing radical militants and bands of young looters of taking advantage of the protesters' anger to sow chaos.
Police have faced groups of masked looters burning cars and buildings. Thousands of stores were ransacked.
French business owners share harrowing accounts of violent protests
Addressing reporters on Friday, the interior minister said that the unrest was "completely unacceptable" and said the authorities "will do everything in our power" to avoid a repeat of the violence.

Meanwhile, Paris shopkeepers were seen boarding up their windows. The city council called on residents and business owners to remove objects that could be set on fire or used as either projectiles or barricades.
Who will be marching on Saturday?
Nunez also said authorities will maintain curfews in designated areas of the city. This will include restrictions between 11 pm and 6 am in two central Paris squares, according to the local police.
After days of rioting, France introduces localized curfews

The police approved only one protest march, organized by labor union CGT, on a limited route through Paris on Saturday. The authorities rejected requests by France's biggest student union UNEF and its anti-establishment Yellow Vest movement to hold their own rallies.
However, UNEF pledged to go ahead with its protest regardless, while Yellow Vest supporters were expected to join the official march.

Authorities had banned all protests in France's second largest city, Marseille, before walking the decision back and allowing a union demonstration. Authorities also intend to keep protesters away from the center of Lyon, France's third most populous city.
Students 'not satisfied' after meeting Macron
The government, led by centrist President Emmanuel Macron, sought to differentiate between what they see as legitimate protests and the violent unrest.
Macron himself also dismissed the narrative that Islamist extremists and migrants were driving the violence. He has, however, pointed to far-left groups and accused them of trying to stage a coup.
On Friday, Macron also held his first-ever meeting with representatives of secondary school students. However, the meeting ended with the pupils calling for more protests.
"We are not satisfied," said student representative Nathanael Combary, president of campaign group High School Renewal.
Violent unrest rocks France after nationwide protests
He told reporters that the president had been "attentive" but that the students were still waiting for concrete proposals to be presented at their meeting with the prime minister on Monday.
He urged his fellow students to "continue to mobilize" and maintain a "standoff" with the government.

articles.title: ICC prosecution seeks admission of expert report, 3 witness testimonies
articles.summary: Prosecutors of the International Criminal Court (ICC) are asking judges to admit an expert report and the previously recorded testimonies of three witnesses into evidence in the crimes against…
articles.byline: JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN, ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 5:19am

Prosecutors of the International Criminal Court (ICC) are asking judges to admit an expert report and the previously recorded testimonies of three witnesses into evidence in the crimes against humanity case against former President Rodrigo Duterte.

In two public redacted filings dated October 23, the Office of the Prosecutor asked Trial Chamber III to admit the materials under Rule 68(3) of the ICC’s Rules of Procedure and Evidence, while still allowing limited live questioning of the witnesses in court.
In the first document, the prosecution sought to introduce the expert report of witness P-1400 and 15 associated items for its fourth application under Rule 68(3)
The witness’s field of expertise, as well as much of the subject matter covered by the report, was redacted from the public filing.
Prosecutors said the report was relevant, reliable, and probative, and would help the Chamber determine the issues in the case.
They also asked for two hours to conduct a focused supplementary examination of P-1400, instead of an estimated five hours of direct examination.

“Granting the Request will enhance the expeditiousness of the proceedings by reducing the length of the witness’s direct examination from five hours to two hours, saving approximately three hours of court time,” the filing stated.
The prosecution said P-1400 would first adopt the expert report before being asked supplementary questions on matters requiring clarification or elaboration.

It said this would avoid having the witness repeat every issue already addressed in the written report while preserving the opportunity for the defense, victims’ lawyers and the judges to question the witness.

The prosecution also argued that admitting the report would not prejudice Duterte’s rights because his lawyers had agreed in principle to the introduction of expert reports under Rule 68(3) and would still be able to question P-1400.
Three witnesses on alleged murders

In a separate fifth Rule 68(3) application filing, prosecutors asked the Chamber to admit the prior recorded testimonies of witnesses P-1155, P-1156 and P-1157, together with associated materials. The three would still appear in court and remain available for questioning and cross-examination.
The prosecution said their evidence relates to alleged murders charged under Count 3, although the particular incident and several details remain redacted.

Prosecutors said P-1155 and P-1156 provide direct evidence on the killings and on Duterte’s alleged knowledge and intent, while the three witnesses also give evidence concerning the alleged policy to “neutralize” suspected criminals through violent crimes.
Prosecutors said P-1155’s statement covers, among other matters, alleged orders “from above,” police instructions and a reward linked to the incident.
P-1156’s account concerns alleged orders, planning, preparations and payment, while P-1157 provides evidence on a killing and a planned police operation against the targets.
Much of the surrounding detail in the three witnesses’ testimonies remains redacted.

The prosecution said the three testimonies are “internally consistent” and mutually corroborative, and argued that admitting them would not prejudice Duterte because his lawyers would still be able to cross-examine the witnesses in court.

The filings come ahead of the final status conference scheduled for November 2, where the Chamber is expected to address remaining trial-preparation concerns before proceedings open for Duterte’s case on November 30.
The ICC has said the Chamber will resolve pending matters and adopt procedures needed for the fair and expeditious conduct of the trial before it begins.
Trial Chamber III, composed of Presiding Judge Joanna Korner and Judges Keebong Paek and Nicolas Guillou, has yet to rule on the two prosecution requests. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Ebola: Kenya announces second death
articles.summary: Kenya has recorded a second Ebola death, ‌the ⁠health ⁠ministry said late Friday. ​The 65-year-old ​woman had developed ​symptoms ‌during quarantine and was a close ‌relative of a ‌Kenyan ​man who…

image.caption: There are still seven people receiving treatment for Ebola in KenyaImage: Monicah Mwangi/REUTERS

blocks.text: Kenya has recorded a second Ebola death, the Health Ministry said on Friday.
Officials said the 65-year-old woman had developed symptoms during quarantine and was a close relative of a Kenyan man who died of Ebola earlier this month.
"Sadly, she succumbed to ⁠the ​disease early ​this evening," the ministry said.
Seven people continue to receive treatment for the illness in Kenya.
What else do we know about the 2nd Kenyan Ebola death?
The woman began showing symptoms 10 days ago. She began receiving supportive care at an infectious disease unit in the capital, Nairobi.
Medical personnel "did everything possible to save her life," the ministry said, adding that it had notified her family and would arrange a safe and dignified burial in consultation with relatives.
Kenya's first Ebola case was announced on October 6. A 40-year-old Kenyan man living in Congo travelled to Kenya via Uganda, arriving on October 3.
He tested positive for the disease on October 5 and died on the same day.
Of some 135 who were identified as contacts with the patient, 118 were placed in quarantine, with eight testing positive. They included four health workers and four close family members.
The latest death is believed to have been among those quarantined family members. The ministry said she developed symptoms on October 13.
The remaining seven cases are all within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry added.

articles.title: Argentina drops investigation into President Milei over crypto fraud
articles.summary: Javier Milei had denied acting fraudulently when a cryptocurrency nosedived after he deleted a social media post about it.

blocks.text: A criminal investigation into Argentine President Javier Milei and his sister's links to a cryptocurrency scandal has been dropped.
The case against Milei and his sister Karina Milei was dismissed by federal judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi at the request of prosecutors, court records show.
The Argentinian president had denied promoting the newly launched cryptocoin $Libra , which collapsed shortly after he mentioned it in a social media post in February 2025.

He said he had acted "in good faith" when the cryptocurrency rose in value before crashing and causing huge losses for the majority of its investors. Milei is yet to respond to news of the case being dropped.
Dismissing the case, the judge said "the reported events do not fall under a legal category", and concluded that no "criminally relevant deception" had been proven.
Accusations of fraud arose when Milei posted on X, formerly Twitter, about the $Libra coin, which he said at the time would help fund small businesses and start-ups.
The cryptocurrency's price subsequently shot up when the Argentine president shared a link to buy it.
But, within a few hours, he deleted his post and the crypto nosedived in value, losing investors most of their money.

It led opposition members of Congress to plan impeachment proceedings, while some online accused Milei of a "rug pull" - where promoters of a cryptocurrency draw in buyers, only to stop trading activity and make off with the money raised from sales.
The Argentinian president, though, insisted: "I didn't promote it, I merely shared it" in an interview with local media Todo Noticias'.
The presidential office insisted that Milei was in no way involved in the development of $Libra and announced that the Anti-Corruption Office would determine if the president had acted improperly.
Milei himself defended deleting his post, saying that at the time he did not know "the details of the project and after learning about it, I decided not to continue promoting it".
And, in a TV interview, he insisted that those who invested in $Libra had done so "voluntarily" and knew of the risks.

articles.title: Trump eases Canada tariffs ahead of US midterms
articles.summary: The move comes as Trump's Republican Party scrambles to maintain control of the US Congress, with a Republican candidate in a key Senate race saying she had lobbied to lift the tariffs on Canadian…

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has lifted some of the tariffs imposed on Canada amid an economic row with the US' neighbor to the north, which peaked this summer.
The White House on Friday said the easing of tariffs will apply to products including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment."
The changes will take effect on October 30.
US-Canada trade war: The cost of fighting back
What do we know about the Canada tariffs relief?
The White House said the president was seeking to offset "the burden to US commerce while better serving the public interest.''
The move comes less than two weeks ahead of the November midterm elections, where Republican candidate Susan Collins is locked in a tight race with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson in Maine.

Collins said on Friday she'd addressed the tariffs with Trump's top trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, adding that she raised with the due the issue of "the toll tariffs are taking on Maine families, businesses, farmers, and growers.''

"Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," Collins said.
She added that she had asked for tariff relief and vowed to "encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner."
While the latest move reliefs some of the tariffs, it also imposes new levies on goods including carpets, certain valves and waste products, the White House said.

articles.title: Freed US citizen was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say
articles.summary: Ukrainians held alongside the American say they witnessed beatings and sexual humiliation by Russian guards during his detention.

blocks.text: Ukrainians held alongside freed US prisoner Stephen Hubbard have said they witnessed him being beaten and humiliated by Russian guards during his four-year detention.
Dmytro Khyliuk first met Hubbard at the Novozybkov prison in Bryansk, not far from Russia's border with Ukraine, in September 2022.
"We heard it from the guards. They came during inspections and were asking: in which cell is the American? And then they used obscene words. They threatened him, they mocked him from the first days."
Ihor Shyshko also remembers Hubbard's arrival at the jail and says his nationality marked him out to the officers.
"It attracted such attention because they mocked him, forced him to learn the Russian language, sing the national anthem and repeat the rules of the prison schedule, which he could not read."
Hubbard was captured in April 2022, when Russian soldiers occupied the eastern city of Izyum, where he was living with his Ukrainian partner.

He was accused of serving in Ukraine's armed forces and convicted in a trial in Moscow before being sentenced to six years and 10 months. Shyshko and Khyliuk were held alongside Hubbard as he awaited trial.
Shyshko said he witnessed and heard Hubbard being beaten by prison guards and electrocuted with a stun gun.
"They beat him on the legs, on the back, on the arms," he said. "Of course, they didn't give him food, they didn't give him medical care. They kept him in the cold.
"He was always treated more harshly, because he was an American. They claimed he was a mercenary, and said 'let's beat him'."
Shyshko, a captured Ukrainian soldier, alleges Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of the prison staff.
Accounts from the two former Ukrainian prisoners corroborate statements made by Hubbard's family that he was tortured in prison.
The 74-year-old was released by the Kremlin after four-and-a-half years, on the day US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss the war in Ukraine.
Witkoff praised the Russian President as a "humanitarian", despite the ongoing full-scale invasion and daily Russian attacks across Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump said he had asked Putin to free Hubbard during a phone call the week before.
Khyliuk, a journalist, was held in the earliest days of the invasion, when Russian troops advanced towards the capital Kyiv.
He said he knew Hubbard's health was declining over the months they were initially held in nearby cells because he heard his complaints and the guards calling him more often to see the prison doctor.
Khyliuk described broken windows and biting cold, with detainees using time out of their cells to huddle together in the bathroom for warmth.
"It was very difficult conditions in Novozybkov, worse than in the next prison. It was very cold there in winter, terribly cold," he said.
Both men encountered the retired English teacher again at their next prison, Pakino, where Shyshko says Hubbard's condition worsened.
"There was not a single spot on his knees or on his feet without rot," he said.

"Everything was rotten. We all had scabies. It was very, very difficult for him. I even bandaged him once at the medical centre, because the doctor didn't want to do it. He just couldn't do it himself, and I had to help. He was quite weak then and he almost couldn't move."
They detailed a harsh regime and a meagre diet of porridge, bread and potatoes, with a daily routine of beatings and humiliation, being forced to run or hold stress positions.
"There's a handler with a dog, who lets go so it can bite you on the buttocks, on the elbow, or bite your leg. Then these wounds fester very badly," Shyshko said.
Khyliuk claimed that soon after their transfer to Pakino, Hubbard was hidden to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors.
"I would like to say that an international humanitarian organisation that receives a lot of funding could do better. They saw only what was shown to them and they were happy with that," he said.

The International Committee of the Red Cross said in a statement that "in any situation where the ICRC has been granted access, we request to see every individual and assess the conditions they are held in. We continue our discussions with parties to the conflict on this issue."
Khyliuk said Hubbard disappeared from the prison in 2024 and he thought he must have been released. Khyliuk was returned to Ukraine in August 2025 in a prisoner exchange.
He likened their treatment to the regime of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin.

"Russian captivity is a torture machine. From the first second of your detention, they do everything to suppress you, to intimidate you. This is torture in all its manifestations, from psychological to physical. Beatings, hunger, cold, lack of any information, lack of the opportunity to communicate even with other prisoners".
Khyliuk said he was pleased to see Hubbard finally released and heading to the US.
"I understand what it is like to be in terrible captivity. Moreover, it was not his war. He ended up in the wrong place and at the wrong time," he said.
But he described the timing as "shameful PR of the US president, who is losing votes in elections to Congress".
Shyshko said he hoped one day their torturers would face justice.
"Evil must be punished, and so it will be. I have hope for that".

articles.title: This Ontario township isn't voting for a mayor or councillors — for the 3rd election in a row
articles.summary: Enniskillen is a mainly agricultural community located in Lambton County.

blocks.text: Windsor·Video
Enniskillen is a mainly agricultural community located in Lambton County.
The mayor and 4 councillors were acclaimed after running unopposed
Meet the Lambton County community that hasn't had a municipal election in 10+ years
Voters across Windsor-Essex, Chatham-Kent and Sarnia-Lambton will be deciding the fate of their municipal leaders on Monday — except in the Township of Enniskillen.
The mayor and all four councillors are acclaimed for the third time in a row — though voters will still vote to fill regional school board positions.
The last time voters voted for a mayor and council in the small southwestern Ontario township was 2014.

Enniskillen is a mainly agricultural community in Lambton County squished between Petrolia and Oil Springs. Many of the approximately 1,100 households and 2,800 residents either work in agriculture or make the short commute to “chemical valley” in the Sarnia-area.

The township is one of 19 municipalities in the 2026 election that has seen acclaimations for all council positions, according to the Association of Municipalities of Ontario. That does not include school board posts.

items: Ontario municipal elections see modest gains in competition: report

blocks.text: Kevin Marriott has been the mayor of Enniskillen since 2011.
This year's election marks the third straight time he hasn't had to campaign for support or worry about losing his seat.
“It makes me feel pretty lucky, really, when I see the struggles that some of my colleagues in the county are going through,” said Marriott, who also serves as the warden of Lambton County.
Kevin Marriott is the mayor of the Township of Enniskillen, Ont. He's been in the position since 2011 and has run unopposed in the past three elections. (Dalson Chen/CBC)

Marriott said he thought there would be more interest for this cycle, but in the end, there wasn’t; he added he’s been told people are "fairly happy" with the state of affairs around their council table.
“I don't let my personal opinion interfere with what I gather from the general public," he said.
"I try to take a wide poll from talking to constituents to make sure I know the way they feel on a particular issue.”
Marriott said he’s unsure what he’ll do come the 2030 municipal election.
“I actually am thinking I'm getting close to, 'Maybe I should let somebody else take over,''' he said.
"I take each four years at a time. I won't comment [officially] until we get closer to 2030.”
LISTEN | Concerns around Ontario's 2026 municipal election:
Ontario Morning8:10Concerns around Ontario’s upcoming municipal election
Tim Williams is a fourth generation farmer, lifelong Enniskillen resident, and also a councillor.
He was selected by his peers in the midst of this past term when another councillor retired.
Williams said he wasn’t shocked that no one ran against him or his three fellow councillors.
“Municipal politics is pretty basic,” he said. “We have no big issues in our area right now. Things run fairly smoothly.
“I think that the councillors that were in place were great leaders. When people saw who was running … there wasn't no issue with who was going to be in there.”
Tim Williams is a councillor for the Township of Enniskillen, Ont. He took the seat in the midst of the last term and was unopposed for the 2026 election. (Dalson Chen/CBC)
Most local voters are probably happy not to have to deal with an election "or see some of the carryings on that are going ... on in other communities,” he added.
Arnold Syer, 73, is a would-be voter who’s lived in Enniskillen his entire life.
He’s also a former mayor, who said he’s happy to not have an election weighing over the township yet again.
“[They're] all good, reputable people,” he said of the current leaders, adding he knows all of them on a first-name basis.
“Why fix something that isn't broke, you know?”

Arnold Syer supports all positions being acclaimed for the 2026 municipal election in the Township of Enniskillen. The local resident is also a former mayor of the southwestern Ontario community. (Dalson Chen/CBC)
Syer said he has faith in the current council and mayor.
He added that people aren't happy about the rise in farmland taxes but they blame the province for withdrawing funding from rural municipalities.

“I think the people are smart enough to know we got to have a certain amount of money to run the place," he said, "and we don't see millions of dollars being squandered in any way. It's a real shift in taxation, and it's a fact of life.”
If the same people stay in their roles four years from now, Syer said he’d support not having an election in 2030, too.
“There's worse places you could be,” he said.

items: Prediction markets are taking big bets on Ontario municipal races. Here's what the rules say

blocks.text: University of Windsor political science professor Lydia Miljan said there are a few circumstances that lead to acclamations and low voter turnout in general — especially when it comes to civic politics.

“What we know about municipal races is that the incumbent advantage is very strong. And so in some instances, they have a 90 per cent chance of re-election — especially in a small community [where] everybody knows everybody,” she said.

items: Why some withdrawn candidate names will still be on the ballot
What these Ontario tenants want out of this municipal election

blocks.text: There's also a sort of democratic deficit for communities with consistent incumbents," she said.
“The time where you actually get a race and you get people putting their name forward is when ... an incumbent says, ‘I'm not going to run again.’"
According to Miljan, the burden for municipal politicians can be great when everybody knows who you are.
“They're going to complain at you all the time," she said.
"You do have to have a thick skin and ... get some work-life balance, and it becomes more difficult in a small town versus a bigger city.”
The municipal office for the Township of Enniskillen located within the mostly farming community in southwestern Ontario. (Dalson Chen/CBC)
She added the lack of tax credits in municipal campaigns — compared to those at the provincial and federal levels — could also dissuade people from running.
Miljan said she’s becoming increasingly convinced that municipalities need term limits.
Changing the Municipal Act to limit the number of years and/or times someone can be a councillor or mayor would force governments and constituents to focus on succession planning.
“The research shows in countries that do have term limits, you get ... more diversity in terms of candidates," she said.
"You get younger people. You get more women because they finally think, ‘I have a fighting chance.’ It isn't just going to be the same old, same old.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bob Becken is with CBC's digital team. Previously, he was an executive producer with CBC Windsor, and held broadcast and digital news director duties with Bell Media and Blackburn Media. You can reach him at bob.becken@cbc.ca.
With files from Dalson Chen

articles.title: Russia's attacks on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, are intensifying. DW asked people on the ground what life is like
articles.summary: Russia's attacks on the Ukrainian capital are hitting harder and more frequently, making 2026 one of the long war's bloodiest years for Kyiv. DW asked people on the ground what life is like.

image.caption: Russian attacks have turn Ukraine's capital into a front-line cityImage: Marina Asmolowa/DW

blocks.text: Until a few months ago, life was relatively peaceful in Kyiv when compared with the situation near the war's front lines elsewhere in Ukraine. Now, as Russia expands its attacks on the capital, Kyiv has increasingly become a front-line city.

With too few shelters for the 4 million residents of Kyiv, subway stations double as makeshift dormitories. Starting at about 10 every night, people create sleeping areas with mattresses and small tents. Children snuggle up to adults; pets seek comfort from their owners or find a spot among strangers between the cold walls.

"We're alive," Halyna told DW, holding her 5-year-old son, Roman, close. "We've been lucky once again." Most evenings — even when no air-raid siren has sounded — she takes the boy to the nearest subway station. Her apartment is located in the Lukyanivka district, which Russia has systematically targeted over the war's four years and eight months.

blocks.caption: People lie on mattresses in the capital's subway system during the nightImage: Marina Asmolowa/DW

blocks.text: 'These sick monsters don't care who they kill'

In September, 14-year-old Daniel Umanskyj was doing homework in his room when a Russian drone struck the apartment building in the central district of Pechersk. A neighbor named Vlad happened to be in the hallway with his daughter at the time of the strike. "We were late that day — and this saved our lives," Vlad said. "Daniel's death is a tragedy." He added: "These sick monsters don't care who they kill." Flowers have been planted in front of the damaged apartment building in memory of Daniel.
Russia also targets places where children gather. In early October, a drone struck a school building in southwestern Kyiv. Fortunately, pupils and teachers were already in shelters at the time.

"We've been teaching all the pupils in person because we have a large shelter that can accommodate more than 500 students," Valentyna Chorna, the school's principal, told DW. As there is enough space in the shelter for everyone, students in the first through ninth grades are able to go to school, she said.

blocks.caption: 14-year-old Daniel was killed when an attack hit his building in KyivImage: Marina Asmolowa/DW

blocks.text: Danger at home, at school — everywhere

Whether classes take place depends not only on the decision of the parents and the school administration: It also depends on whether shelters are available and how long the air-raid siren continues to sound. If an alarm sounds in the morning while children are still at home, they may not be able to go to school that day.
"This is an enormous burden for parents," said a colleague from the DW bureau in Kyiv, whose daughter attends school. "You have to go to work — and the child stays home alone."

"Even the walk to school is dangerous because an air-raid alarm can go off at any time," she said. Her daughter attends a school not far from the Antonov aircraft factory. "One day she texted me: ‘You can't imagine what a huge explosion that was!'" she said. "I don't know if something was shot down or if there was a strike somewhere." She added: "Things like that really scare children." And staying home brings its own risks.

In September, a Russian drone struck their building. The apartment itself wasn't damaged, and her daughter was at school that morning, but it was another reminder of just how much survival has become a matter of luck. When an air-raid siren sounds, no one knows who will be spared, she said.

blocks.caption: Attacks on Kyiv target civilian infrastructure, schools and places where children spend free timeImage: Marina Asmolowa/DW

blocks.text: Kyiv's population persists

Russia's attacks have become deadlier in 2026. According to the military administration in Kyiv, 140 people were killed in the capital during the first eight months of the year, compared with 172 for all of 2025. If this trend continues, 2026 could become Kyiv's deadliest year since the start of the Russian invasion in 2022.

Attacks on warehouses have led to shortages in supermarkets on a scale not seen since the early months of the war. At the end of September, emergency power outages resumed in Kyiv. The subway was paralyzed by a Russian attack. Given the strikes on the energy infrastructure, it is unclear how the capital can reliably supply residents with heat, electricity and water during the upcoming winter.

Despite Russia's attempts to render Kyiv uninhabitable, 72% of the city's residents said in September that they are prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary, the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology reported in early October. The authorities are striving to maintain normal life in the city, where the curfew has been shortened and now runs from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m.

Some facilities have even been allowed to continue operating during "yellow" alerts. During "red" alerts, however, people must immediately seek shelter: This could mean ballistic missiles, cruise missiles or massive combined attacks.
Russia strikes Ukraine with massive aerial attack
This article was originally written in Ukrainian.
